title: Does a Learned Corrector Beat a Simple Retreat? Evidence from a Frozen VLA
summary: Before deploying runtime recovery for a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy, one must establish that an intervention improves success beyond ordinary run-to-run variation and that its complexity adds value over a simple action. We evaluate these questions on frozen $π_{0.5}$ across four RoboTwin tasks. For each test seed, we pair rollouts with and without correction and include a same-seed base-policy re-run as a placebo. Seed-cluster intervals and prespecified comparison rules assess net gains against stochastic outcome changes. Across 3,888 paired episodes, the full pipeline raises success on beat_allowbreak block_allowbreak hammer by $+13.5$\,pp (95\% interval $[+9.4,+17.7]$), with no detectable gain on the other three tasks at the deployed weight. Among failed base episodes on the responsive task, $43.2\%$ succeed on a plain re-run, compared with $63.5\%$ after correction; many nominal rescues therefore reflect the base policy's own variability. A fixed-time trigger and scripted return to an earlier joint configuration produce a net gain with no detected difference from the learned pipeline across two rounds, although our prespecified equivalence criterion is not met consistently. Pausing and a constant-action control do not yield comparable gains. On this benchmark, the decision to intervene depends strongly on the task, and a paired placebo plus a simple retreat baseline are needed to establish what learned correction contributes.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are usually deployed frozen: the weights that were trained are the weights that run. When such a policy fails, it often fails quietly. The arm slows, hovers, or repeats a motion without completing the task. A natural remedy is runtime correction: watch the rollout, decide that it is failing, take over for a few dozen steps, and then hand control back. When and how control returns is the hand-back rule. Several recent systems report that it raises success rates~ FailSafe,VLACorrector,ReCoVLA . The base policy, however, is stochastic: in our setting three runs of the same seed with no intervention disagree on the outcome for 39--60 of seeds (Section~ sec:placebo ). A rollout that ``was rescued'' may be one that would have succeeded on a second try anyway. Three things are missing from how runtime correction is evaluated. First, a placebo. Failure-detection work evaluates alarm accuracy~ SAFE,Sentinel,ActProbe,FAILDetect , and recovery work reports success before and after intervention. None of the runtime-correction studies we surveyed subtracts how often the base policy's outcome flips on a plain re-run. Second, the simplest counterpart. Learned correctors are compared with the base policy, rarely with a non-learning script under the same trigger and hand-back rule. Retreat-and-retry is well established~ BGR,RewindIL,CycleVLA,SPR,CoRe , but has not been put head-to-head against a learned corrector under one paired protocol with an equivalence margin. Third, paired statistics. Benchmark practice reports the mean of 100 rollouts per task~ RoboTwin20,SimpleVLARL . Because the base success rate on identical seeds drifts between rounds (separate launches of the evaluation, Section~ sec:placebo ) by more than binomial sampling explains, unpaired means cannot resolve effects of the size we report (Section~ sec:main ). Related work Failure detection scores VLA features with conformal calibration~ SAFE , action statistics without training~ Sentinel , the action space~ ActProbe , or uncertainty scores without failure data~ FAILDetect ; our trigger is one task-specific threshold plus five shared constants, judged only by what follows the alarm. For recovery, PLD is closest in structure to our pipeline: a residual reinforcement-learning teacher whose recoveries are distilled back into the base~ PLD . Others fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) helper on injected failures~ FailSafe , re-plan by gradient inside a frozen ~ VLACorrector , train a residual recovery policy from VLM-compiled rewards~ ReCoVLA , or augment demonstrations into failure--recovery trajectories~ RACER . Only two keep the base frozen at deployment~ VLACorrector,ReCoVLA , and none of the five reports a same-seed placebo or a non-learning counterpart under the same trigger and hand-back rule. The mechanism that reproduces our gain is not new. A scripted retreat can be fired from a value function~ BGR , replayed from a VLM-certified checkpoint with a frozen ACT policy~ RewindIL , reverse-executed to a subtask start with a fine-tuned VLA~ CycleVLA , or learned by LoRA fine-tuning on progress stalls~ SPR . Learned recovery policies handle states outside the training distribution~ BackToManifold or target safety rather than completion~ RecoveryRL , and a stateless push-back is a training-free retry~ ProbeAct . Two comparisons come closest to ours. In CoRe's ablation an anchor rollback, a simulator reset that also restores objects, matches the full method within about a point on 270 paired episodes, but both conditions are training-free and the numbers are means without intervals~ CoRe . In FAR a naive retry trails a learned retry by 4--6\,pp, but that condition updates weights at test time, with no pairing or intervals~ FAR . Harness VLA re-positions the arm with analytic primitives on RoboTwin under a different base policy~ HarnessVLA . On the data side, interactive imitation learning admits corrections by rule~ RaC,Sirius,IntervenGen,CUPID,Dream2Fix ; ours instead replays each rescue along the rescue branch and two no-rescue branches (Section~ sec:admission ). Distilling a privileged teacher into a sensor-limited student is standard~ LearningbyCheating , and learned gates for when to ask a human stay within one task with a human fallback~ ThriftyDAgger,AIM,SiriusFleet . Adjacent reinforcement-learning control work studies when to update a controller and how to reject disturbances. Tang and colleagues combine actor--critic control with disturbance observers for output stabilization and tracking under mismatched disturbances~ Tang2024Stabilization,Tang2024Tracking ; a time-delay extension adds predictive compensation~ Tang2024Delay . Bai et al. update an adaptive-dynamic-programming controller only when a state-dependent error crosses a threshold~ Bai2026Event , and a robotics-focused survey places such methods in the context of manipulator and mobile-robot constraints~ Chan2026ADPSurvey . Earlier observer-based iterative learning for magnetic bearings and tracking control for roll-to-roll coating address disturbance rejection in physical systems~ Tang2019Bearing,Tang2026Coating . Closer to learned robot policies, Guided Action Flow uses a critic to guide inference in a frozen VLA, while WAM-OPD distils a world-action model on states visited by its student~ Yang2026GuidedFlow,Yang2026WAMOPD . These studies motivate the trigger, robustness and distillation aspects of our pipeline; our paired placebo and scripted-retreat comparisons test which parts improve task completion after a brief hand-back. This paper We fill all three gaps by building a complete pipeline of the kind in~ PLD,FailSafe,VLACorrector,ReCoVLA and taking it apart. The pipeline (Section~ sec:pipeline , Fig.~ fig:overview ) keeps ~ pi05 frozen and adds four components. Two run only during data collection: a privileged teacher that plans rescues with cuRobo~ cuRobo from the simulator state, and a counterfactual admission step that replays each rescue to check it was needed, keeping 87 of 175. Two run at deployment: a stall monitor, and a camera-free joint-space corrector distilled from the admitted rescues and deployed as one weight file on all four tasks. The protocol (Section~ sec:protocol ) pairs every seed with and without intervention, with a same-seed re-run as the placebo and rules written down before the test seeds ran. Across 3,888 paired episodes (Section~ sec:main ), the pipeline is significant on one task, beat block hammer (hereafter bbh, \,pp, 95 interval ), and indistinguishable from zero on the other three: rotate qrcode (qr), place a2b left (a2b) and place a2b right (a2br), taken one at a time or pooled (Table~ tab:main ). Our contributions are three, none of them a new corrector. (i) An evaluation protocol for runtime intervention on frozen policies: per-episode pairing (as in~ CoRe ) and interval reporting (as in~ RaC ), plus a same-seed re-run placebo, a rescue/breakage decomposition with a break-even identity, preregistered equivalence rules and disjoint seed sets. It is needed here: the naive rescue rate is three times the placebo-corrected one. (ii) A component-by-component dissection on the one recoverable task: the gain is reproduced by retreating to the pre-stall configuration. A more elaborate trigger, privileged planning, counterfactual admission and this distilled corrector add no benefit we can detect. (iii) Evidence that, on this benchmark and for the deployed weight, recoverability follows the task, not the repair: a distilled corrector and a hand-written retreat help on the same one task and show no detectable gain on the other three (with exceptions, Section~ sec:tasksagree ). A 324-pair pre-deployment check picks out the one clear case. To our knowledge no prior work makes this comparison on one frozen VLA under a preregistered \,pp equivalence margin. Method sec:pipeline Trigger: monitor and timer sec:trigger Both triggers share one task-specific quantity, a time threshold , where is the 75th percentile of the step at which successful base rollouts finish on training seeds. This gives 148, 177, 177 and 183 steps on bbh/qr/a2b/a2br. Slash lists follow this order throughout. The monitor adds five hand-set constants shared by all tasks (velocity ratio, window, progress fraction, warm-up, earliest snapshot step) and fires when motion inside the window collapses after the threshold. These five were fixed on screening seeds (Section~ sec:tasks ) before any test seed ran. The timer keeps only and fires at step . On 400 held-out seeds with no intervention the monitor missed 0 of 208 failures (95 exact binomial upper bound 2 , Clopper--Pearson) and fired on 18 of successes, ranging from 3 on a2b to 37 on a2br. Those false alarms are episodes that would have recovered on their own, which we call self-healing, and suppressing them does not pay (Section~ sec:check ). Privileged teacher sec:teacher During data collection only, the teacher attempts a rescue whenever the monitor fires. It is privileged: it reads the simulator state, which the deployed corrector never sees. It plans with cuRobo~ cuRobo through a four-rung fallback sequence: (1) re-plan the scripted grasp-and-place from the current state, (2) retract along a short backtrack and re-plan, (3) retract further and return both arms home before re-planning, and (4) run a task-specific routine for a knocked-over object. The teacher is not an upper bound: used online at every alarm it lowers success (Section~ sec:ladder ). Rungs 2 and 3 are themselves retreat-then-retry procedures (Section~ sec:tasksagree ), and they supply 27 of the 87 admitted rescues. Counterfactual admission sec:admission Admission asks whether each rescue was needed and worked. From the alarm state we replay three branches three times each: two no-rescue branches (the base policy continuing) and the rescue branch. A rescue is admitted only if each no-rescue branch succeeds at most once in three and the rescue branch succeeds at least once in three. Because one success in three is enough, the admitted set is permissive: most admitted rescues succeeded once or twice in three, which is one reason the teacher is unreliable when used online. Of 175 teacher rescues on bbh, qr and a2b, 87 pass; the rejected ones are all cases in which the base policy recovered on its own. title: SWAP: Stepwise Action Policy Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Robot manipulation systems using Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model backbones typically use just one VLA for task execution. However, individual VLAs do not perform well across different task states and environments. We introduce a framework for dynamically composing multiple VLA policies during execution: StepWise Action Policy Routing (SWAP). SWAP formulates policy routing as an offline reinforcement learning problem, learning a routing critic that selects the most appropriate policy at each decision step given the current observation. SWAP enables robots to select new policies to execute online rather than committing to a single policy for the duration of an episode. We evaluate SWAP on both real-world DROID manipulation tasks and LIBERO simulation experiments. SWAP improves over fixed-policy execution and routing baselines, giving absolute improvements in real-world task success up to 33% while reducing successful trajectory robot action step length by 28.3%.
full_text: Robot manipulation systems using Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model backbones typically use just one VLA for task execution. However, individual VLAs do not perform well across different task states and environments. We introduce a framework for dynamically composing multiple VLA policies during execution: . SWAP formulates policy routing as an offline reinforcement learning problem, learning a routing critic that selects the most appropriate policy at each decision step given the current observation. SWAP enables robots to select new policies to execute online rather than committing to a single policy for the duration of an episode. We evaluate SWAP on both real-world DROID manipulation tasks and LIBERO simulation experiments. SWAP improves over fixed-policy execution and routing baselines, giving absolute improvements in real-world task success up to 33 while reducing successful trajectory robot action step length by 28.3 . Policy Routing, VLAs, Inference Introduction Robot manipulation systems are increasingly powered by large foundation models such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. These systems have demonstrated impressive generalization across manipulation tasks, but they are typically deployed under a restrictive assumption: that a single policy should control the robot for the duration of execution. In practice, however, no individual policy performs consistently well across every episode. A policy that performs well under one scene configuration may fail under another, while a stronger policy overall may still make poor decisions in specific states. For robots operating in dynamic environments, effective execution may therefore require not a single policy, but a collection of complementary policies that can be selectively composed during execution. Existing approaches largely ignore this setting by training a single large generalist VLA. Recent progress in scaling VLA models has focused on improving the capability of individual policies through larger datasets~ droid, open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023 , better architectures~ kim2024openvla, octo , broader pretraining~ black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t , and better post-training~ physicalintelligence2025pi0.5 , and has shown increasingly capable general-purpose manipulation systems. However, these approaches implicitly assume that a single policy can robustly handle the full distribution of task states encountered during deployment. This assumption is particularly limiting in real-world manipulation, where distribution shift, compounding execution errors, and recovery behaviors can substantially alter the execution over time. Even when multiple policies are available, selecting one at the start of an episode commits the robot to a fixed behavior regardless of how execution evolves. In this work, we instead formulate a policy routing problem for robot manipulation. Rather than selecting a single policy for an entire episode, we consider the setting where a robot has access to multiple candidate policies and must dynamically determine which policy should act at each decision step. This introduces a new challenge: routing decisions must account for long-horizon downstream results, since a chosen locally-reasonable policy may ultimately lead to failure, while an alternative choice may enable recovery or successful completion. To address this, we introduce Step-Wise Action Policy Routing (SWAP), a framework that formulates policy routing as an offline reinforcement learning problem over a discrete action space of policy identities. SWAP learns a routing critic from offline robot interaction data containing successful and failed executions from multiple candidate policies. At deployment, the routing critic evaluates the current observation and dynamically selects the policy predicted to maximize task success. This enables the robot to compose complementary behaviors across policies within a single trajectory. We evaluate SWAP in both real-world and simulated manipulation settings. On a real-world DROID~ droid setup, SWAP improves task success from 63.3 for the best standalone policy to 96.7 , while reducing successful trajectory length by 28.3 . Across large-scale LIBERO simulation experiments, we further show that learned policy routing is effective. Together, these results suggest that robust robot execution may emerge not solely from building stronger individual policies, but from learning how to effectively route between them. Background and Related Work sec:related_work Recent progress in robot foundation models has produced a growing collection of policies with diverse capabilities and failure modes. Our work draws connections between VLA models, routing methods in language models, and value-function-based decision making in robotics. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models have demonstrated strong generalization across manipulation tasks by directly mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions~ brohan2022rt1, kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, physicalintelligence2025pi0.5, octo . Work on evaluating robot policies has found that VLAs often remain brittle on certain types of distribution shifts such as language rephrasing, lighting changes, or increased clutter~ wilbert_colloseum, simpler_env, anwar2024contrast, anwar2025efficient, kress2024robot, parekh2024investigating,xie2024decomposing,taxonomy2025arxiv,mitra2025roboticsteering, fei25libero . Finetuning VLAs on a new target task to mitigate these shifts can reduce robustness on the original training distribution~ mitra2025roboticsteering . Our key insight relies on leveraging the diverse behavior of existing VLAs during a single task rollout. Routing in LLMs Recent work in large language models has explored routing mechanisms that dynamically select among multiple models, experts, or inference strategies at test time. Rather than relying on a single model for all inputs, these approaches allocate queries to specialized experts based on the current context~ jiang2023llm,feng2025graphrouter,jitkrittum2025universal , estimated difficulty~ ding2025best,zhuang2025embedllm , or predicted downstream performance~ jiang2023llm, ong2024routellm, lu2024routing, shnitzer2023large,zhang2026dips . Routing has been studied with model cascades~ shen2025sater,yue2024large,moslem2026dynamic and multi-model systems~ aggarwal2023automix,ding2024hybrid,ong2024routellm,jiang2023llm that balance cost factors~ chen2023frugalgpt,ding2024hybrid such as latency and capability by selecting the most appropriate model for a given request. A common theme across this literature is that different models exhibit complementary strengths, and that adaptive routing can outperform any individual model alone. In this work, we propose an adjacent problem of policy routing for robotics, where the routing decision must be made online throughout robot motion, as the robot's actions directly influence future observations and task outcomes. Policy routing is also related to mixture-of-experts architectures, which learn a gating network jointly with the experts; in contrast, SWAP treats the candidate policies as fixed black boxes and learns only the router, so new policies can be added without retraining any expert. Value Functions for Robotics Value functions play a central role in robot learning by estimating the long-horizon consequences of actions and policy decisions. Model-free offline RL algorithms~ kumar2020conservative, nakamoto2023cal, kostrikov2022offline, fujimoto2019off, kumar2019stabilizing, nair2020awac, awr typically require value functions to train a robot policy. These value functions enable these policies to predict actions that maximize long-term rewards. Recent work builds more general value~ physicalintelligence2025pi0.5, ghasemipour2025selfimproving and reward~ zhang2025rewind, liang2026robometer, lee2026roboreward functions. Beyond policy optimization, value functions have been used to guide high-level decision making and planning. SayCan combined language model outputs with learned value functions to select skills that are both relevant and executable~ ahn2022can . Value functions have been used for failure detection~ gokmen2023asking , and more recently have been used to steer policies of larger VLAs at deployment time~ nakamoto2024steering . We take inspiration from these works leveraging value functions at test-time, and focus on learning a routing critic that enables selection among multiple candidate robot policies for policy routing. Robot Policy Routing sec:related_work While modern VLA policies can exhibit strong generalization, no single policy is uniformly optimal across all task states, environments, or execution regimes. A policy that performs well during coarse free-space motion may fail during contact-rich manipulation, while another may excel at precise object interaction yet behave conservatively during exploration or recovery. More broadly, policies trained with different data distributions, architectures, or objectives may exhibit complementary strengths and failure modes, motivating policy routing. Rather than committing to a single policy for an entire episode, we argue an agent should dynamically select which policy to execute next based on the current observation context, enabling multiple policies during a single rollout. We formalize action taking in this setting as a Markov decision process (MDP), , where at timestep , the robot observes state and executes action . Rather than learning a single policy , we assume access to a finite library of candidate robot policies, where each represents a pretrained robot controller. In our setting, these policies may correspond to distinct VLA models trained with different architectures, datasets, or algorithms. Our key insight is to leverage the assumptions that each policy induces different behavior under identical observations and that no single dominates across all reachable states. We aim to learn a routing policy, , that selects which robot policy to execute at each timestep. The routing policy is defined as where denotes the selected policy index at time . The robot action to take is then sampled from the chosen robot policy: We pose an objective to maximize long-horizon task performance for the routing policy: This formulation differs from standard policy learning in that the action space of the router is not low-level motor control, but policy selection itself. The router operates at a higher level of abstraction, deciding which controller should act rather than directly predicting robot actions. SWAP: Stepwise Action Policy Routing We instantiate the policy routing framework as Step-Wise Action Policy Routing (SWAP), an offline reinforcement learning approach for selecting among candidate robot policies during robot action rollouts (Figure~ fig:overview ). SWAP learns a routing critic that estimates which policy is most likely to lead to successful task completion given the robot's current execution state. Training is performed entirely offline from logged robot interaction data from pretrained VLAs, after which the learned critic is used at deployment to dynamically swap between VLA policies during execution. The central component of SWAP is a routing critic that estimates the long-horizon utility of selecting a candidate robot policy given the current observation. Given an observation , the critic predicts the expected future returns of executing robot policies from that state onward. Offline Dataset Construction. To train the routing critic, we construct an offline dataset from robot interaction trajectories collected using each candidate policy across the target manipulation tasks that includes both successful and failed executions across all policies. title: Learning Modular Policy for Multi-Floor Object Navigation:A Factorized Framework for Diagnostic Study
summary: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) in multi-floor scenarios presents a challenge due to sparse rewards caused by long-horizon decision-making. In this paper, we propose a diagnostic study based on a modular framework with an effective learnable policy to analyze failure factors in multi-floor scenarios. To achieve an effective policy for diagnosis, we design the hierarchical factorization policy that deconstructs a single global policy into an intra-floor exploration policy and an inter-floor switching policy. To providing an effective initialization for Reinforcement Learning (RL), the lightweight intra-floor policy is learned by distilling the exploration logic of Visual Language Models (VLMs). Under idealized assumptions, we show that the factorized policy is theoretically equivalent to a single global policy at the policy-representation level. Experiment results indicate that perception performance and stair climbing stability are the primary bottlenecks in multi-floor navigation.
full_text: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) in multi-floor scenarios presents a challenge due to sparse rewards caused by long-horizon decision-making. In this paper, we propose a diagnostic study based on a modular framework with an effective learnable policy to analyze failure factors in multi-floor scenarios. To achieve an effective policy for diagnosis, we design the hierarchical factorization policy that deconstructs a single global policy into an intra-floor exploration policy and an inter-floor switching policy. To providing an effective initialization for Reinforcement Learning (RL), the lightweight intra-floor policy is learned by distilling the exploration logic of Visual Language Models (VLMs). Under idealized assumptions, we show that the factorized policy is theoretically equivalent to a single global policy at the policy-representation level. Experiment results indicate that perception performance and stair climbing stability are the primary bottlenecks in multi-floor navigation. Introduction Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an agent to reach an object goal in an unseen environment. Real-world scenarios often contain multiple floors, requiring the agent not only to make intra-floor decisions but also to determine when to switch floors. The main challenge lies in long-horizon decision-making, where the consequences of each decision may emerge only after many steps. Such long-horizon processes typically involve sparse rewards, making timely feedback difficult and ultimately causing leading to the failure of policy training. The recent emergence of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provides a promising paradigm for addressing these challenges. Without task-specific training, they can be directly used for decision-making, leading to the emergence of zero-shot methods with modular structures based on VLMs~ gong2025stairway,zhang2024mfnp,zhang2025apexnav,yokoyama2024vlfm . Meanwhile, learning-based end-to-end methods have achieved strong performance through large-scale imitation learning, reinforcement learning, or VLM fine-tuning~ yokoyama2025filmnav,yadav2022ovrl,yadav2023ovrlv2,ramrakhya2023pirlnav,wasserman2023xgx . Although modular designs improve interpretability and end-to-end methods achieve superior performance, the performance differences among existing methods do not directly reveal where the dominant bottlenecks arise in multi-floor scenarios. In particular, policy decision-making, perception, and low-level execution are coupled in the complete navigation process. Therefore, a diagnostic study with an effective framework is required to identify the main performance bottlenecks in modern multi-floor navigation methods. To conduct a detailed diagnosis, an intuitive approach is to design a modular framework with an effective learnable policy, which can decouple performance bottlenecks induced by policy from other factors. However, due to the lack of supervised datasets for multi-floor navigation, it is impractical to directly train a single global policy through imitation learning (IL), and using online reinforcement learning (RL) to train a single global policy requires millions of environmental interactions, resulting in high time and computational costs. Given these limitations, exploiting the environment’s inherent structure to decompose a single global policy is a feasible approach for the learning of an effective policy. We address these constraints by designing the hierarchical factorization policy. Specifically, we decompose a single global policy into an intra-floor policy and an inter-floor policy based on the natural structure of the environment. To provide an effective initialization for subsequent RL, we utilize IL for knowledge distillation, transforming the exploration logic of VLMs into a lightweight intra-floor policy. After IL initialization, we use alternating RL as a practical optimization strategy, freezing one policy while updating the other to decouple floor-switching and sub-goal learning. Crucially, under idealized assumptions, we show that the factorized policy is theoretically equivalent to a single global policy at the policy-representation level. Once the factorized policy converges, our modular framework enables systematic diagnosis of multi-floor navigation bottlenecks. The results show that the main limitations lie not in decision-making, but in perception and stair-climbing stability. With GT perception and ideal stair climbing, our framework outperforms existing methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We provide a diagnostic study for multi-floor ObjectNav, which utilizes an effective learnable policy and a modular structure to decompose failure modes, indicating that perception reliability and stair climbing stability are two main bottlenecks. We design the hierarchical factorization policy that deconstructs the policy into an intra-floor policy and an inter-floor policy, and show that, under idealized assumptions, the factorized policy is theoretically equivalent to a single global policy at the policy-representation level. We obtain a lightweight intra-floor policy by distilling the exploration logic of VLMs, enabling effective RL fine-tuning. Related Works Modular Zero-shot Methods Previous studies have focused on solving intra-floor and inter-floor decision-making problems based on the zero-shot paradigm. For intra-floor navigation, SG-Nav~ yin2024sgnav prompts an LLM with an online-constructed 3D scene graph to reason about potential sub-goals. VLFM~ yokoyama2024vlfm uses a pre-trained VLM to produce a value map for scoring frontiers toward the object goal. ApexNav~ zhang2025apexnav further improves zero-shot exploration efficiency by adaptive switching between semantic-driven and geometry-driven exploration. For inter-floor navigation, MFNP~ zhang2024mfnp extends zero-shot navigation to multi-floor environments with a rule-based inter-floor mechanism. ASCENT~ gong2025stairway emphasizes floor-aware exploration through hierarchical semantic mapping and LLM-driven coarse-to-fine frontier reasoning, enabling efficient multi-floor decision making without additional training. End-to-End Methods End-to-end approaches directly map observations to actions using IL or RL. The OVRL series~ yadav2022ovrl,yadav2023ovrlv2 demonstrates that visual representation can achieve robust ObjectNav performance without explicit modules. PIRLNav~ ramrakhya2023pirlnav pretrains policies with IL and further improves them through RL fine-tuning. XGX~ wasserman2023xgx proposes a learning-based exploration and exploitation coupling, where policies are jointly optimized to improve goal-conditioned exploration and approach behavior. Although end-to-end methods are simple and scalable, they lack explicit multi-floor representations and separate inter-floor and intra-floor decisions, making multi-floor decision-making less controllable. Based on prior work, we diagnose the main bottlenecks using a modular framework with a hierarchical factorization policy consisting of inter-floor and intra-floor policies. Task setup ObjectNav requires an agent to reach an object goal in an unseen environment. At each episode start, the agent is randomly initialized and assigned a goal category. At time , the agent receives , where is the RGBD image and is its pose, and selects from six actions: MoveForward, TurnLeft, TurnRight, LookUp, LookDown, and Stop. An episode succeeds if the agent stops within distance of the goal and is limited to steps. Methodology Overview Fig.~ Framework illustrates our framework, which uses a diagnostic paradigm to identify the main bottlenecks in multi-floor navigation. It employs a hierarchical factorization policy composed of inter-floor and intra-floor policies, followed by the low-level navigation policy described in Sec.~ sec:low_level_nav . Diagnostic Paradigm First, we validate policy effectiveness through multiple rounds of alternating intra-floor and inter-floor training. The policy is considered effective if each round improves performance and our method outperforms the zero-shot method. Secondly, hypotheses will be proposed based on experimental results. If our method has limited improvement compared to the zero-shot multi-floor baselines and still has a significant gap compared to the end-to-end baselines, we believe that factors other than the policy cause the performance bottlenecks. Furthermore, combined with the failure cause statistics, if the success rate using ground-truth (GT) perception exceeds that of YOLO-based perception during training, then perception is hypothesized as one of the causes of performance bottlenecks. Similarly, if the learned and greedy inter-floor policies perform comparably under GT perception and waypoint mode, while both improve with teleportation, stair-climbing stability is hypothesized as another performance bottleneck. Finally, we validate these hypotheses through a series of experiments. A clear advantage over zero-shot multi-floor baselines under GT perception identifies perception as a primary bottleneck, while gains from teleportation over waypoint mode indicate stair climbing as another bottleneck. Hierarchical Factorization Policy We design the hierarchical factorization policy with an intra-floor policy and an inter-floor policy. Below we describe map representation, intra-floor policy, inter-floor policy, network architecture and training paradigm. Representation. We maintain a local sliding-window multi-floor map representation , where , , and correspond to floors , , and , respectively. full_text: World action models jointly learn visual prediction and robot actions, providing a way to use observations of scene evolution for policy learning. Their video and action losses, however, provide no explicit target for the geometric consequences of a demonstrated action sequence. Moreover, visual features taken after temporal attention can contain future observations, making them unsuitable as the sole current visual input to an auxiliary predictor. We introduce and its auxiliary objective, the Action-Conditioned Geometric Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture ( ), which predicts geometric features at several horizons from the current observation and intervening actions, using the future slot of a frozen VGGT encoding of each current and future image pair as the target. We apply this supervision from the head and wrist cameras to a shared visual embedding before temporal mixing, and remove the teacher and auxiliary modules at inference. On 50 RoboTwin~2.0 tasks, achieves 93.46 success in clean scenes, with the best randomized success (92.68 ) and mean across both settings (93.07 ) among the compared methods; across three tasks on a real robot, it achieves 85.00 success and 91.67 partial completion score, exceeding Motus by 10.00 and 9.17 percentage points, respectively. Code: . Website: . Introduction Robot manipulation requires actions that change the scene in a useful way: a grasp must secure an object, and a placement must leave it in the intended position. Generative policies learn action sequences from images and language instructions~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . World action models (WAMs) also predict future observations, coupling visual forecasting with action generation~ bi2026motus,li2026causal,zhu2025uwm . This joint formulation gives policy training access to how objects and robot hands move between observations, in addition to the demonstrated control commands. For manipulation, the relevant change is often a spatial relation: a hand closes around an object, a container receives it, or one object becomes supported by another. Spatial representations have proved useful for such tasks~ ze2024dp3,goyal2023rvt,ke2025diffuseractor . In bimanual manipulation, these relations also connect the two arms: moving an object with one arm changes the conditions for the other's next action. The question is how to make geometric information a useful training signal for a WAM while retaining its existing observation and action interface. Two challenges arise when adding this supervision. First, video and action losses do not explicitly require a representation of the geometric change associated with an action interval. From the same observation, a robot can approach, lift, or move an object; the starting image alone does not specify which outcome a predictor should learn. An additional prediction target must therefore describe a future scene in the context of both its starting observation and the actions that connect them. Even over the same duration, different action sequences can lead to different stages of an interaction. The action interval identifies the demonstrated movement, while its duration specifies how far ahead the predictor should look. Second, the location of the supervised policy feature matters. During joint video and action training, attention mixes tokens from current and future frames. A token assigned to the current frame can consequently contain future visual information after this mixing. Using that token as the visual input to an auxiliary predictor would let it use part of the observation it is supposed to predict. For this supervision to benefit action generation, its gradients must reach the visual features shared with the policy. These challenges motivate two complementary choices. For the first, we predict a geometric representation of a future endpoint conditioned on the intervening action sequence. A frozen teacher jointly encodes the two images, allowing the future representation to use the current scene as context. Sampling different endpoints associates the same current observation with both short interactions and longer action sequences. This exposes the visual embedding to changes that develop over different portions of a manipulation sequence, from the initial approach to later object transport. For the second, we supervise the visual embedding before the backbone mixes frames. The student then receives features computed from the current image alone, while the teacher can use the future image to form a target. The head camera describes the shared workspace, including the target region and the relation between the arms; wrist cameras reveal local configurations of the grippers and manipulated objects. Together, these views provide spatial evidence about both the overall arrangement and the immediate interaction. Supervising the shared embedding with these views connects geometric prediction to the visual input used by the deployed policy. We implement these choices as , a Motus policy trained with the objective. Frozen VGGT~ wang2025vggt encodes the current and future images jointly within each camera. We retain its future slot, pool the features from each view, and train a predictor using the current visual features, demonstrated actions, and a temporal horizon. The auxiliary loss updates the shared visual embedding alongside the base video and action objectives. The teacher and predictor are discarded at inference, so the policy uses its original inputs and action generation path. Figure~ fig:teaser shows this connection between training and deployment. We evaluate the resulting policy on 50 RoboTwin~2.0 tasks and three tasks on a real robot. It reaches 93.46 clean success and leads the compared methods in randomized success (92.68 ) and the mean across both settings (93.07 ), with 85.00 mean success on the robot. Ablations on six simulation tasks examine action conditioning, temporal horizons, and the geometric target. Together, these evaluations test whether geometric endpoint supervision benefits task completion under visual variation and execution on physical hardware. In summary, our main contributions are: Geometric dynamics conditioned on actions. We introduce a joint embedding objective that predicts geometric targets over several horizons from the current observation and intervening actions. A frozen teacher jointly encodes current and future images to provide explicit supervision for world action modeling. Geometric distillation from multiple views. We connect targets from the head and wrist cameras to policy features computed from the current observation before temporal mixing. Auxiliary gradients update the shared visual embedding, while the teacher and predictor are removed at deployment. Benchmark and real robot evaluation. We evaluate the policy on 50 RoboTwin~2.0 tasks and three manipulation tasks on a real robot. It achieves the best randomized and mean success among the compared methods on RoboTwin~2.0 and the highest average SR and PCS on the robot. Ablations on six simulation tasks support the Joint target design, action conditioning, and supervision at multiple horizons. RT-2 and OpenVLA use different approaches to transfer~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla ; and focus on continuous control and adaptation~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld . Motus combines understanding, generation, and control in a latent WAM, while LingBot-VA studies causal world modeling for robot control~ bi2026motus,li2026causal . We use Motus as the backbone and add geometric supervision during training. Predictive Representations and Alignment Joint embedding methods predict features instead of reconstructing pixels. title: ProactiveVLA: Augmenting Embodied Memory through Proactive Environment Exploration
summary: Rapid adaptation to a new environment requires a robot to acquire useful knowledge about local objects, states, and interactions from limited experience. Systems that combine a reasoning agent with a frozen vision-language-action model (VLA) can adapt through execution feedback and memory, making the choice of experience central to their effectiveness. Repeated practice of a target task may refine a familiar solution while leaving other interactions relevant to changed conditions untested. We introduce ProactiveVLA, which uses proactive environment exploration to acquire reusable knowledge for deployment-time adaptation. After completing an initial task, the agent allocates the remaining interaction budget to self-proposed goals covering object affordances, state-changing interactions, and compositions of interactions. It verifies execution outcomes and consolidates both task-directed and exploratory experience into memory that guides subsequent planning and control. ProactiveVLA outperforms the baselines under the same turn budget on LIBERO-Pro and RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen. On LIBERO-Pro Goal-T, with at most one VLA primitive invocation allowed during evaluation, ProactiveVLA completes 48% of instances, compared with 19% for the state-of-the-art task-refinement baseline.

Systems that combine a reasoning agent with a frozen vision-language-action model (VLA) can adapt through execution feedback and memory, making the choice of experience central to their effectiveness. Repeated practice of a target task may refine a familiar solution while leaving other interactions relevant to changed conditions untested. We introduce ProactiveVLA, which uses proactive environment exploration to acquire reusable knowledge for deployment-time adaptation. After completing an initial task, the agent allocates the remaining interaction budget to self-proposed goals covering object affordances, state-changing interactions, and compositions of interactions. It verifies execution outcomes and consolidates both task-directed and exploratory experience into memory that guides subsequent planning and control. ProactiveVLA outperforms the baselines under the same turn budget on LIBERO-Pro and RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen. On LIBERO-Pro Goal-T, with at most one VLA primitive invocation allowed during evaluation, ProactiveVLA completes 48 of instances, compared with 19 for the state-of-the-art task-refinement baseline. Introduction sec:introduction A robot deployed in an unfamiliar environment must use its existing capabilities with new objects, layouts, and task requirements. Vision-language-action models (VLAs), including OpenVLA and , provide pretrained manipulation capabilities learned from broad robot data kim2024openvla,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . However, possessing these capabilities does not establish how they work in a particular deployment environment. The robot needs experience with local object uses, action outcomes, and interaction sequences to guide its decisions. Grounding decisions in available skills and environment feedback helps connect language-level knowledge to feasible robot behavior ichter2023saycan,huang2023innermonologue . With limited opportunities for interaction, rapid adaptation depends on acquiring information that supports task execution beyond the specific conditions already encountered. Recent advances in agentic robotics use language models to organize perception, planning, and control through executable robot interfaces~ liang2022codeaspolicies,singh2023progprompt,fu2026capx,zhang2026harnessvla . Such systems make experience acquisition an explicit design choice, since the agent determines which interactions to attempt and what knowledge to preserve. Harness VLA provides a state-of-the-art agentic framework for adapting frozen VLAs, exposing the VLA as a callable manipulation primitive and combining it with analytic control and execution memory. During its exploratory bootstrapping phase, Harness VLA searches for a working solution on a reference task instance and refines its execution memory across attempts zhang2026harnessvla . We refer to experience acquisition that keeps the provided task objective fixed while improving its execution as task refinement. Although this can improve a working solution, the resulting experience may remain concentrated around the same task requirements. For example, practicing placement with an unobstructed target can refine grasping and release but may provide little direct evidence about clearing space when the target becomes obstructed. Handling this change may require an interaction absent from the successful trajectory. Improving a familiar solution and expanding the conditions under which the robot can act are therefore different uses of the same interaction budget. Self-directed play already provides a route to acquiring reusable robot skills, as demonstrated by RATS zhang2026playful . For rapid adaptation of a VLA-based agentic system, we focus on using limited deployment-time interaction to acquire knowledge relevant to the local environment and its tasks. This knowledge concerns the roles objects can serve, the changes an interaction can produce, and the ways interactions can be combined. Under a limited interaction budget, actively acquiring diverse and reusable environment knowledge can improve adaptation to changes in tasks and execution conditions beyond practicing a single solution. We introduce , an adaptation framework that enables agentic VLA systems to proactively acquire and organize environment knowledge through interaction. The agent first tries the target task to obtain concrete experience with the local environment and controller. It then uses the remaining budget to propose and execute goals at three levels, covering object affordances, state-changing interactions, and interaction compositions. Visual outcome checks connect each proposal to observed execution evidence. A memory-management process organizes experience within scenes, synthesizes candidate knowledge across scenes, and uses an independent critic to review proposed rules before they guide subsequent execution. Both initial task experience and exploration outcomes contribute to this memory. Adaptation takes place through the agent's acquired knowledge while the VLA remains frozen. The experiments show that ProactiveVLA outperforms Harness VLA under the same adaptation-turn budget on LIBERO-Pro. Under the same limited VLA primitive invocation budget, ProactiveVLA achieves higher task success, with an advantage when only a small number of VLA calls are available. Our contributions are threefold. First, we study deployment-time adaptation as the acquisition of reusable environment knowledge under a fixed interaction budget. Second, we develop a task-guided proactive exploration method that couples three levels of goal generation with outcome verification and memory consolidation. Third, we evaluate on LIBERO-Pro and RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen, covering controlled task and spatial variations as well as multi-step household tasks, and analyze how exploration structure and memory consolidation affect adaptation. Related Work Vision-language-action models and generalization. Vision-language-action models learn language-conditioned visuomotor policies from large collections of robot trajectories and vision-language data. RT-2 introduced the VLA formulation by jointly representing language and robot actions, while Open X-Embodiment expanded cross-embodiment robot data at scale brohan2023rt2, openx2023 . OpenVLA provided an open generalist VLA, and subsequent models such as and scaled continuous action generation and heterogeneous robot training kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, physicalintelligence2025pi05 . These models obtain strong manipulation capabilities from pretraining, but robustness can decrease when deployment changes task bindings, object arrangements, or compositional requirements. LIBERO-Pro explicitly evaluates such changes through controlled perturbations of LIBERO tasks liu2023libero, zhou2025liberopro , while RoboCasa365 provides diverse multi-step household manipulation tasks in kitchen environments nasiriany2026robocasa365 . Agentic adaptation around robot policies. Language-model agents provide another route to generalization by composing perception and control interfaces around pretrained robot capabilities. Language-model agents interleave reasoning with actions and environment feedback yao2023react . In robotics, this interaction connects high-level decisions to perception and control interfaces. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt use executable programs or program-like plans to connect language-model reasoning with robot APIs liang2022codeaspolicies, singh2023progprompt . More recent systems increasingly treat the policy as one component inside a persistent execution harness. Harness VLA exposes a frozen VLA as a contact-rich manipulation primitive and combines it with high-level agent reasoning, analytic control, and execution memory zhang2026harnessvla . Recent agentic systems further explore self-improvement through interaction feedback, skill discovery, runtime recovery, and experience accumulation lu2026aspire,xiao2026enpire,zhang2026playful,ding2026zetta . studies adaptation efficiency under a limited interaction budget, focusing on what experience should be acquired from a new environment. It allocates this budget to acquiring reusable environment knowledge rather than concentrating additional experience on a single task. Autonomous exploration and reusable experience. Prior work has also studied how agents can autonomously acquire experience beyond a single externally specified task. Plan2Explore uses task-agnostic exploration to learn a world model for later adaptation sekar2020plan2explore . ELLM uses language models to propose semantically meaningful exploration goals, showing that language-guided exploration can improve the usefulness of pretraining experience du2023ellm . Voyager combines automatic curriculum generation, environment interaction, and a persistent skill library for open-ended embodied learning wang2023voyager . More closely related to robot manipulation, recent agentic systems use self-directed interaction to discover reusable skills or behavioral knowledge that can later support downstream tasks lu2026aspire, zhang2026playful . Experience can also be consolidated through reflection and verification. Reflexion retains verbal reflections in episodic memory, while ReasoningBank distills reasoning strategies from self-judged successful and failed attempts and updates memory across tasks shinn2023reflexion,ouyang2026reasoningbank . REFLECT summarizes multimodal robot experience to diagnose failures and guide subsequent correction liu2023reflect . ProactiveVLA shares the premise that interaction should create reusable knowledge, but studies a budgeted preparation problem. Methodology sec:method supports rapid adaptation by acquiring environment experience, consolidating it into a global memory, and using that memory to guide subsequent behavior. A high-level agent interacts with the environment through a set of robot primitives, such as moving to a target pose, adjusting the robot posture, controlling the gripper, and VLAs. Each adaptation instance consists of a scene and an environment-provided task, with a shared budget of interaction turns for task execution and autonomous exploration. The method comprises three stages, illustrated in Figure~ fig:architecture . Exploration collects task-directed and self-directed experience, memory management consolidates the evidence across adaptation scenes, and deployment uses the resulting global memory. Proactive Environment Exploration sec:exploration sec:initial sec:goals The agent first attempts the target task . Following some attempts at turns, it retains the task-execution experience and allocates the remaining turns to exploring other scene-related goals. A language-model proposer uses the observed scene and accumulated execution feedback to generate these goals at three levels. Object affordances. The first level explores atomic or local interactions that reveal how individual objects can be used. Examples include grasping a bowl, opening a cabinet door, or pressing a faucet control. These interactions provide concrete evidence about the roles and operations supported by objects in the current scene. The goal at this level is to establish basic object--action relations that later exploration can build upon. State-changing interactions. The second level explores larger but reasonable changes to the scene to understand its functional semantics. The agent autonomously proposes goals involving storage, placement, opening, closing, or other meaningful state changes. These interactions provide evidence about how objects and fixtures can be used to establish different scene states. For example, a Level-2 task may ask the agent to ``place the bowl into the already opened top drawer and verify that the bowl is stably contained inside.'' Interaction compositions. title: LEAP: Making Privileged Geometry Supervision Effective for Visuomotor Learning
summary: Privileged 3D supervision uses additional geometric information during training to guide RGB-based visuomotor policy learning, without requiring geometric inputs at deployment. However, low reconstruction error does not ensure that visual representations capture geometry useful for control. We identify three limitations that weaken this supervision: proprioceptive shortcuts, dominant-view reliance, and reconstruction objectives dominated by task-irrelevant geometry. To address these limitations, we propose Latent Encoding with Aligned Privileged Geometry (LEAP). Our framework uses an auxiliary decoder to reconstruct point clouds within the manipulation workspace from visual features alone, while retaining proprioception for action prediction. Alongside full reconstruction, we introduce wrist-view dropout and partial reconstruction targets matched to the retained wrist, encouraging the encoder to capture complementary local geometry. The auxiliary decoder is removed at inference, leaving only RGB observations and robot state as policy inputs. Extensive experiments on RoboTwin, ManiSkill, and real-world tasks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements over Diffusion Policy and ACT, with only a small increase in parameter count and no reduction in inference speed.
full_text: Privileged 3D supervision uses additional geometric information during training to guide RGB-based visuomotor policy learning, without requiring geometric inputs at deployment. However, low reconstruction error does not ensure that visual representations capture geometry useful for control. We identify three limitations that weaken this supervision: proprioceptive shortcuts, dominant-view reliance, and reconstruction objectives dominated by task-irrelevant geometry. To address these limitations, we propose Latent Encoding with Aligned Privileged Geometry ( ). Our framework uses an auxiliary decoder to reconstruct point clouds within the manipulation workspace from visual features alone, while retaining proprioception for action prediction. Alongside full reconstruction, we introduce wrist-view dropout and partial reconstruction targets matched to the retained wrist, encouraging the encoder to capture complementary local geometry. The auxiliary decoder is removed at inference, leaving only RGB observations and robot state as policy inputs. Extensive experiments on RoboTwin, ManiSkill, and real-world tasks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements over Diffusion Policy and ACT, with only a small increase in parameter count and no reduction in inference speed. Introduction sec:introduction Reliable robotic manipulation depends on the 3D relationships among objects and the robot. RGB-based imitation learning methods, such as Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusion and ACT~ zhao2023act , learn complex skills from demonstrations, but their training objectives do not explicitly require visual features to encode these relationships. Point-cloud policies such as DP3~ ze2024dp3 provide explicit geometric inputs, but require depth sensing and point-cloud processing at deployment, adding sensing requirements and computational cost. Privileged geometry supervision instead uses 3D information during training, through auxiliary geometric prediction~ li2025qdepth,he2026foresight,kim2026pri4r or representation alignment~ li2025spatialforcing , while retaining an RGB policy at deployment. Without explicit 3D observations at deployment, an RGB policy must infer task-relevant geometry from its images. A low geometric training loss does not establish that it has done so. (1) when does fail to make the visual representation capture task-relevant 3D structure? (2) how can privileged 3D supervision be formulated to circumvent this failure? e identify three limitations of privileged geometry supervision: proprioceptive shortcuts, view dominance, and task-irrelevant global prediction. A proprioceptive shortcut occurs when geometry decoder uses robot state to reduce reconstruction error without extracting the corresponding geometry from images. Such shortcuts have been studied in action prediction~ zhao2025statefree , but their effect on privileged geometry supervision remains underexplored. View dominance occurs when the broad-coverage camera explains much of a fused reconstruction target, leaving the contribution of other views unclear. Finally, task-irrelevant global prediction can devote much of the objective to background and robot geometry while giving little weight to the local contact and occlusion geometry needed for control. Together, these limitations allow low geometric loss without ensuring that the visual features preserve the geometry relevant to manipulation. e propose , a training framework that directs privileged geometry supervision toward task-relevant visual learning. Its geometry decoder receives only visual features, limiting proprioceptive shortcuts. During training, we randomly mask views and matches a partial geometry target to the remaining views, making wrist contributions easier to identify. At deployment, the policy uses only multi-view RGB images and robot state. Our contribution can be summarized as follows: We identify proprioceptive shortcuts, view dominance, and task-irrelevant global prediction as limitations of privileged geometry supervision for multi-view visuomotor learning. We introduce , combining visual-only geometric reconstruction, view dropout with visibility-aligned partial reconstruction, and workspace-constrained supervision. We evaluate these limitations and the corresponding designs through abundant controlled experiments and policy evaluations across simulation and real-robot settings with different RGB-based policy architectures. Related Work sec:related_work Explicit 3D Inputs for Robotic Manipulation. shridhar2023peract voxelize RGB-D inputs, goyal2023rvt render virtual views from point clouds, and gervet2023act3d use sensed depth to lift visual features into a 3D field. GNFactor shares a voxel representation between reconstruction and control~ ze2023gnfactor . Other policies encode point clouds~ ze2024dp3,wang2024rise , predict trajectories from 3D scenes~ ke2024diffuseractor , or combine point maps with RGB~ jia2025pointmappolicy . These approaches retain geometric observations or representations at deployment. LEAP uses geometry only for training supervision and acts from RGB and proprioception. Multi-View Learning and Camera Availability. Multi-view observations provide complementary evidence for manipulation. hsu2022hands show that hand-centric and global views differ in their coverage and generalization behavior. MV-MWM seo2023mvmwm reconstructs masked views, while 3D-MVP qian2024threedmvp and DiffuView zhang2026diffuview use multi-view pretraining to learn spatial representations. MAD almuzairee2025mad learns fused and per-view features for missing-camera robustness, and Multi-Camera View Scaling xie2026multicamera uses synchronized views to increase the effective training data. akinola2020multicamera use camera dropout to make RGB policies robust to missing views. ur concern is the geometric objective under such masking: a low loss on a fused scene may leave the contribution of a wrist view unclear. Geometric Representation Learning for RGB Policies. Geometric supervision can improve RGB policies without requiring 3D observations at inference. DPR and SPA pretrain encoders through depth prediction and multi-view rendering, while eVGGT and GP3 transfer pretrained geometric knowledge~ wang2024dpr,zhu2024spa,vuong2025evggt,qian2025gp3 . wang2025monolift distill depth-guided spatial, temporal, and action cues into an RGB policy. During policy learning, methods predict depth, future scenes, or 3D motion~ li2025qdepth,he2026foresight,qian2025geopredict,kim2026pri4r,he2026elan4d , align features with geometric teachers~ li2025spatialforcing,wang2026vega,wang2026track4action,shi2026thinkvla , or use training-only 3D Gaussian prediction heads~ jiang2026gaussiandreampp,zhang2026gaussianwam . Other methods focus on interaction-relevant structure: object geometry~ ding2026mindvla,liu2026sam3dalignment , subtask-relevant regions~ gao2026focalvla , or affordances and goal regions~ zheng2026gift . yang2026mvucf combine depth and cross-view correspondence supervision, while xu2026actiongeometry jointly predict actions and future point maps from features that include proprioception. LEAP instead reconstructs workspace and view-matched partial point clouds from visual features alone, encouraging geometric learning from complementary camera views. Proprioceptive Shortcuts in Visuomotor Learning. Prior work identifies proprioceptive over-reliance~ lin2024spawnnet and optimization-driven visual suppression~ lu2026gap . State-free Policy~ zhao2025statefree removes proprioception to improve spatial generalization, while ReViP~ li2026revip rebalances vision and proprioception to reduce false task completion. We instead examine, both theoretically and empirically, how proprioceptive shortcuts can weaken privileged point-cloud supervision in multi-view imitation learning. To mitigate these shortcuts and focus supervision on task-relevant geometry, reconstructs workspace point clouds from visual features alone and supplements full reconstruction with visibility-aligned partial supervision under wrist-view dropout. This design encourages complementary local geometric representations while retaining proprioception for action prediction. Background sec:background Visuomotor Imitation Learning. In this work, we mainly consider imitation learning for two-arm robots equipped with a head camera and two wrist cameras. A visuomotor policy comprises a visual encoder and an action predictor trained on expert demonstrations. Let index the head, left-wrist, and right-wrist cameras, and let denote their RGB observations. The proprioceptive state includes measurements such as joint angles and gripper configurations. title: Hierarchy-GBP: Accelerating Factor Graph Inference via Abstraction and Recovery
summary: Gaussian Belief Propagation (GBP) is a distributed inference algorithm that passes messages in graphical models, making it attractive for scalable spatial intelligence. However, we find GBP most effective locally: it rapidly smooths message errors that vary sharply between neighbor variables, but corrects global errors across distant graph regions incrementally through long-range message propagations. We propose Hierarchy-GBP (H-GBP), an iterative, two-stage framework that accelerates GBP by first solving these global errors with a coarse graph approximation (abstraction) and projecting the results back to the original graph (recovery), then refining the remaining local errors with GBP. We prove H-GBP convergence to the optimum by deriving the combined matrix operator of our abstraction and recovery steps and analyzing its spectral radius. Experiments on linear sparse graphs show that H-GBP converges fundamentally faster than standard GBP. Moreover, we validate H-GBP on two important spatial problems: Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) and Bundle Adjustment (BA). H-GBP markedly accelerates large-scale PGO and achieves state-of-the-art runtime across all tested BA scales.

Experiments on linear sparse graphs show that H-GBP converges fundamentally faster than standard GBP. Moreover, we validate H-GBP on two important spatial problems: Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) and Bundle Adjustment (BA). H-GBP markedly accelerates large-scale PGO and achieves state-of-the-art runtime across all tested BA scales. Introduction Gaussian Belief Propagation (GBP) is an efficient distributed graphical inference algorithm pearl2022reverend, yates2026belief that has been successfully applied in error-correcting decoding frey1997revolution , multiuser detection bickson2008multiuser , and solving large-scale linear systems shental2008gaussian . Inference proceeds by passing Gaussian distributions between nodes in a probabilistic graphical model, iteratively updating each variable's marginal belief. This local, decoupled, and scalable computational model makes GBP a highly promising inference and reasoning framework for future spatial intelligence systems davison2019futuremapping . GBP has the desirable property that, if it converges on a Gaussian graph, it converges to the global optimal mean weiss1999correctness . However, its convergence rate is compromised by graph structures like local loops or long graph diameters johnson2005walksum,malioutov2006walksums,du2018vectorvalued , and GBP can often require many iterations elkurdi2012relaxed,liu2012feedback . Algebraically, GBP behaves as a smoother: it quickly damps local (high-frequency) errors that vary sharply between neighboring nodes, while global (low-frequency) errors across distant graph regions require many iterations to reduce. We observe the local-versus-global error separation in many spatial inference problems, including SLAM, 3D computer vision, and sensor networks. This motivates a two-level view of GBP (see Fig. fig:teaser_image ). The fine space is the original variable space where GBP performs local message passing, while the coarse space is a low-dimensional graph approximation suitable for removing low-frequency errors. We solidify this idea with a localized low-rank abstraction. Variables are grouped locally and abstracted via their most prominent eigenvalues, forming a coarse problem that captures low-frequency errors briggs2000multigrid,nataf2011dtn,spillane2014geneo . Our algorithm Hierarchy-GBP (H-GBP) alternates coarse residual correction with fine-level synchronous GBP. For linear Gaussian factor graphs, we derive an operator describing a `V-cycle' of alternating coarse and fine steps, which lets us compute the spectral radius and predict a large improvement in convergence rate compared to standard GBP on the fine graph. Experiments on sparse spatial factor graphs dellaert2017factorgraphs, davison2018futuremapping,papadimitriou2025spatial,jiao2026opennavmap verify this predicted acceleration in linear problems. We also show that the abstraction-and-recovery principle extends to practically important, non-linear Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) (see Fig. fig:experiment_figure ) and Bundle Adjustment (BA) (see Fig. fig:experiment_figure2 ). Specifically, our main contributions are: H-GBP framework We introduce a multilevel GBP framework for general sparse factor graphs. H-GBP builds a low-rank coarse space from low-eigenvalue modes, and alternates coarse corrections with GBP updates on the original fine graph. Empirical validation H-GBP converges faster than standard GBP on sparse linear factor graphs empirically. Extensive experiments on PGO and BA benchmarks show H-GBP's speed and accuracy benefits, and demonstrate the potential for broader spatial intelligence applications. Convergence theory For linear factor graphs, we establish a global precision convergence rate and derive a reduced cycle operator whose spectral radius is a geometric global convergence criterion. We prove the local convergence of H-GBP on manifolds. Related Work GBP on linear-Gaussian graphs has a strong theoretical foundation. weiss1999correctness shows that when loopy GBP converges on a Gaussian graphical model, it recovers the correct posterior means, though the variances can be overconfident. Subsequent work connected GBP to walk-sum expansions and linear/quadratic solvers, clarifying that its behavior is governed by global coupling structure rather than by any single local loop in isolation malioutov2006walksums,shental2008gaussian, moallemi2009convergence . More recent analyses extended these perspectives to vector-valued Gaussian models, which arise in estimation problems du2018vectorvalued, yates2026belief . Our H-GBP analysis takes a matrix-operator view of the underlying dynamics. A second line of work improves GBP efficiency while remaining on a flat graph. Representative ideas include residual scheduling elidan2006residual , relaxation or damping elkurdi2012relaxed , and structural modifications such as feedback message passing liu2012feedback . These methods can reduce oscillation or avoid unnecessary updates, but they do so by reordering or partially restructuring message passing on the original graph. They do not build a coarse representation to divide and counter long-range, low-frequency error components. H-GBP is inspired by domain-decomposition methods, where local smoothers remove high-frequency errors and coarse spaces correct slowly varying components briggs2000multigrid . The closest prior work combines GBP with multigrid for PDE/FEM systems elkurdi2014parallel,elkurdi2015parallel . In contrast, H-GBP constructs the hierarchy directly on sparse factor graphs and derives the coupled coarse/fine message dynamics. To our knowledge, it is the first multilevel GBP framework formulated and analyzed for general sparse factor graphs beyond PDE/FEM discretizations. Our work is also related to the factor-graph optimization literature in robotics tazaki2022spanning . Factor graphs have become a standard abstraction for large-scale estimation and SLAM, while sparse nonlinear solvers such as g2o and Ceres remain the dominant practical baselines dellaert2017factorgraphs,kuemmerle2011g2o, ceres . Recently, there has been renewed interest in GBP as a distributed inference engine for spatial estimation, including multi-robot localization, continuous-time SLAM, and bundle adjustment on graph processors murai2024distributed,hug2024hyperion, ortiz2020bundle . H-GBP sits between these threads: it preserves the locality and parallelism of GBP with an abstract-then-recover acceleration mechanism.
