title: SharedKV-BT: Node-Local Typed Decisions for Behavior-Tree Agents
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Last updated on October 5th, 2026
summary: Agent tasks require sequences of interdependent decisions. Autoregressive models support more flexible decision interfaces than conventional classifiers but incur the latency of token-by-token generation. Recent shared-prefix methods reduce this cost by reusing encoded context and scoring multiple decisions in parallel, but do not model decision dependencies or verify execution. We propose SharedKV-BT, where each active node of a behavior tree (BT) exposes stage-local fields and candidates, and Shared-KV scores the candidates in parallel and passes the selected decision to a separate execution system. We tested SharedKV-BT on robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks. Across three tasks, SharedKV-BT made typed decisions 2.36-4.15 times faster than prompt-matched autoregressive decoding. On the manipulation task, node-local Shared-KV improved joint decision accuracy from 75% to 94% and closed-loop success from 0% to 60%. Fixed-score policy replay showed that stage gating prevented out-of-order actions and external postconditions prevented premature completion.
full_text: Agent tasks require sequences of interdependent decisions. Autoregressive models support more flexible decision interfaces than conventional classifiers but incur the latency of token-by-token generation. Recent shared-prefix methods reduce this cost by reusing encoded context and scoring multiple decisions in parallel, but do not model decision dependencies or verify execution. We propose SharedKV-BT, where each active node of a behavior tree (BT) exposes stage-local fields and candidates, and Shared-KV scores the candidates in parallel and passes the selected decision to a separate execution system. We tested SharedKV-BT on robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks. Across three tasks, SharedKV-BT made typed decisions \(2.36\)--\(4.15 \) faster than prompt-matched autoregressive decoding. On the manipulation task, node-local Shared-KV improved joint decision accuracy from 75 to 94 and closed-loop success from 0 to 60 . Fixed-score policy replay showed that stage gating prevented out-of-order actions and external postconditions prevented premature completion. behavior trees, structured decisions, shared KV cache, robot agents, computer-use agents Introduction introduction Agents must make sequences of interdependent decisions to achieve a goal. A robot cannot place an object before grasping it, and a computer-use agent cannot paste a file before selecting its source and opening the destination. An appropriate action and its arguments, such as the target object or destination, need to be selected based on the current execution stage and environment state. Conventional classifiers select from a predefined set of classes bishop2006pattern . Open-set recognition extends this setting by rejecting inputs from classes not seen during training scheirer2013toward,geng2021recent , but it still does not provide application-defined, stage-specific decision interfaces. Autoregressive models support flexible interfaces specified through text brown2020language , but sequential token decoding incurs inference latency that increases with output length~ stern2018blockwise,leviathan2023fast . More recently, typed-decision systems such as Jev ask a model to fill named fields by choosing among application-defined candidates, avoiding token-by-token generation typesafe2026system . Typed-decision interfaces, however, focus only on choosing the value of each field and do not manage execution itself typesafe2026system . They do not define when a decision should be made, which candidates are valid at that point, or whether the chosen action succeeded. As a result, they can act out of order, repeat a completed action, or stop because the model claimed success. Behavior trees (BTs), on the other hand, are commonly used to structure agent execution through conditional branching and failure recovery iovino2022survey,colledanchise2017hybrid,colledanchise2014robustness . In this paper, we propose SharedKV-BT, which combines a Jev-style typed-decision interface with BT control (Fig.~ fig:architecture ). Each BT node defines the current execution stage and exposes only the fields and candidates that are valid at that stage. For example, in the schematic pick-and-place example, , , and nodes expose different skills and arguments. This node-local design focuses the model on the decisions relevant to the current stage. The model encodes the instruction and observed state once as a task-state prefix and reuses the resulting key-value (KV) cache to score complete candidates in parallel. A separate execution system executes the selected action, while the BT's external postcondition checks the system state after execution and controls progression and retry. Section~ tasks specifies the experiment-specific interfaces. Our findings answer three questions: . How much does shared-prefix reuse reduce decision cost? On model inputs saved at decision points, Shared-KV was \(2.36\)--\(4.15 \) faster than prompt-matched constrained autoregressive decoding; a controlled comparison using identical candidate batches isolated a \(1.29\)--\(2.09 \) benefit from cache reuse alone (Section~ decision-efficiency ). . Does exposing only the current node's choices improve decisions and execution? Yes. Relative to an interface that exposed all fields and candidates at every decision (the global interface), node-local Shared-KV improved correct joint typed decisions from 75 (90/120) to 94 (113/120) and closed-loop completion from 0 to 60 (Section~ node-local-interface-routing ). . Which errors do stage gating and external postconditions prevent? Stage gating prevented out-of-order actions, while external postconditions prevented model-reported completion from advancing an unsatisfied task (Section~ control-of-candidate-sets-and-completion ). The contributions of this paper are: . An architecture in which each active BT node provides a typed-decision interface with predefined candidates, while a shared task-state prefix supports parallel candidate scoring. Controlled evidence for the three corresponding mechanisms: prefix reuse for efficiency, node-local interface routing for focus, and stage gating with external postconditions for execution authority. End-to-end evaluations across robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks, with decision errors separated from downstream execution failures. Related Work related-work Robot Execution Architectures robot-execution-architectures Robot architectures separate fast action-level skills from higher-level decision making. Subsumption uses priority-ordered layers brooks1986robust , whereas Gat's three-layer architecture gat1998three and 3T bonasso1997experiences place an executive between planning and real-time control. BTs formalize periodic updates (ticks) and success or failure returns marzinotto2014unified and have been studied for sequential composition colledanchise2017hybrid , robustness and safety colledanchise2014robustness , and robotic applications iovino2022survey . BT learning includes branch and tree design dey2013qlbt and continuous action-node parameters iannotta2025adaptation . In a separate line of work, task and motion planning (TAMP) methods jointly search over discrete action sequences and continuous robot motions, propagating geometric failures back to task-level search~ kaelbling2011hierarchical,garrett2021integrated . SharedKV-BT instead operates at a different layer, selecting among candidates exposed by a predefined BT rather than planning action sequences or trajectories. Language-Model Planning and Skill Selection language-model-planning-and-skill-selection Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have generated or revised task procedures from prompts, demonstrations, fine-tuning, or heuristic planning cao2023robot,izzo2024btgenbot,cai2024hbtp,ao2025llmbtplanner , including runtime-generated visual-condition nodes wake2025vlmdriven , language-model action sequences wake2023chatgpt , and multimodal plans from demonstrations wake2024gpt4vision . Reusable skill libraries separate task descriptions from hardware execution takamatsu2026skillagents , and Plan-and-Act studies when to invoke an LLM sasabuchi2025planandact . Other systems span free-form code or plan generation liang2023code,vemprala2024chatgpt,driess2023palme,huang2022zeroshot and predefined skill selection: SayCan combines language-model scores with scores of whether an action is feasible ahn2022saycan , ProgPrompt specifies available actions in program-like prompt context singh2023progprompt , and Inner Monologue conditions later reasoning on feedback huang2022innermonologue . Unlike these methods, SharedKV-BT combines fast candidate scoring through Shared-KV with stage-constrained decision making through the BT. Complete-Candidate Scoring and Shared-Prefix Inference complete-candidate-scoring-and-shared-prefix-inference Complete-candidate likelihood scoring is not novel brown2020language ; prior work has also examined alternative label wordings and prompt-dependent calibration holtzman2021surface,zhao2021calibrate . Related structured-generation methods constrain outputs through token masking or schemas, including XGrammar, Outlines, and Structured Outputs dong2024xgrammar,willard2023guided,openai2024structured , while Toolformer learns when to insert tool calls during generation schick2023toolformer . Jev frames structured inference as typed decisions over application-defined candidates typesafe2026system , and concurrent work scores candidate identifiers in parallel li2026llm2jev . Shared-prefix inference has also been studied at the systems level. PagedAttention manages KV caches kwon2023pagedattention , SGLang reuses prefixes through RadixAttention zheng2024sglang , Hydragen separates shared-prefix from candidate-specific computation juravsky2024hydragen , and ArborKV manages caches for branching search chen2026arborkv . SharedKV-BT applies shared-prefix reuse to multi-step agent execution, with each BT node exposing multiple typed fields and candidates that share a task-state prefix. SharedKV-BT System materials-and-methods SharedKV-BT can be applied to autoregressive models that provide a probability for each token and allow reuse of their KV caches. All primary experiments used the open-weight Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct qwen2024qwen25 . As an additional model-robustness check, we repeated Adaptive PickPlace with Qwen3-4B in non-thinking mode using its native chat template yang2025qwen3 . Shared-KV Complete-Candidate Scoring shared-kv-complete-candidate-scoring A typed decision fills named fields by choosing from predefined candidates; for example, a grasp node may expose skill = \ GRASP, ORIENTED GRASP\ and operand (action argument) = \ CUBE A, CUBE B\ . The model represents the common instructions and system state as text and encodes them as a task-state prefix \(x\). For each field \(f\), its name and candidates form prompt \(p_f\). If candidate \(c_i\) has tokens \((t_ i,1 , ,t_ i,m_i )\), its score within field \(f\) is \[ s(c_i f)= m_i _ j=1 ^ m_i P(t_ i,j x,p_f,t_ i,<j ). \] The KV cache for \(x\) is computed once and reused while the candidate completions for all fields are evaluated in one batch. Only candidate tokens contribute to the mean log score, which reduces preference for shorter labels and distinguishes labels sharing their first token. SharedKV-BT records mean and per-token scores and selects the highest-scoring candidate in each field. These scores rank the supplied candidates; we do not treat them as reliable probabilities of correctness or as evidence that the candidate set contains a valid action. Notably, independent fieldwise argmax does not, in general, guarantee cross-field compatibility. Arbitrary interfaces therefore require an explicit compatibility check. The node-local interfaces used in our experiments, however, are designed so that all exposed field combinations are executable. To isolate the benefit of KV reuse, we compare four methods for answering the same typed decision. Autoregressive (AR) generation produces the answer one token at a time without constraining it to the candidate set. Prompt-matched constrained AR starts from the same task-state prefix, field suffix, and candidates as complete-candidate scoring, then selects the highest-probability next token at each step (i.e., greedy decoding) while a token trie (i.e., a prefix tree) blocks every sequence outside the candidate set. Sequential scoring evaluates each candidate but recomputes the task-state prefix for every candidate. Shared-KV encodes the task state once and reuses its KV cache to score all candidates in one batch. Behavior-Tree Decision Interface behavior-tree-decision-interface The BT determines when a decision is requested and exposes only the fields and candidates of the active node. The model selects their values but neither generates the procedure nor certifies the outcome. An external execution system executes the selected decision;

title: MoonGS: High-quality Representation of the Lunar Surface via Gaussian Splatting Using Robust Depth Features from Image Pairs
summary: High-quality 3D reconstruction of lunar terrain from sparse rover images is indispensable for autonomous lunar exploration, but remains challenging because viewpoint overlap is insufficient, surface textures are weak, and data volume is limited. We propose MoonGS, the first feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework tailored to lunar scenes. Given only two input images, MoonGS predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass and renders photorealistic novel views without any per-scene optimization. MoonGS (i) adopts an adaptable backbone design that seamlessly integrates advanced vision foundation models to extract robust depth features; (ii) integrates semantic priors in two manners: merging semantic cues with visual features to refine Gaussian parameter estimation, and adopting a semantic ranking loss that regularizes background depth; and (iii) employs an entropy-guided heuristic resampling strategy to augment sparse observations by selecting the most informative distant viewpoints with negligible overhead. Experiments on the LuSNAR benchmark and our synthetic weak-texture MoonBlender dataset show that MoonGS surpasses state-of-the-art feed-forward NeRF/3DGS baselines by +4.9 dB PSNR, +0.29 SSIM, and 40\% lower LPIPS while maintaining sub-second inference. Furthermore, we validate the broad applicability of our framework by demonstrating that it effectively leverages state-of-the-art backbones, including VGGT, to significantly boost performance. Qualitative evaluations on Chang'e mission imagery also show the best visual quality among compared methods, indicating robustness on real lunar data. The source code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/InRobots/MoonBlender.
full_text: MoonGS: High-quality Representation of the Lunar Surface via Gaussian Splatting Using Robust Depth Features from Image Pairs Yun Jiang, Bo Zheng, Yingying Zhang, Xueming Xiao, Tao Hu, Hutao Cui, Zhiguo Meng, Ke Gao, Yang Gao, and Meibao Yao High-quality 3D reconstruction of lunar terrain from sparse rover images is indispensable for autonomous lunar exploration, but remains challenging because viewpoint overlap is insufficient, surface textures are weak, and data volume is limited. We propose MoonGS, the first feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework tailored to lunar scenes. Given only two input images, MoonGS predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass and renders photorealistic novel views without any per-scene optimization. MoonGS (i) adopts an adaptable backbone design that seamlessly integrates advanced vision foundation models to extract robust depth features; (ii) integrates semantic priors in two manners: merging semantic cues with visual features to refine Gaussian parameter estimation, and adopting a semantic ranking loss that regularizes background depth; (iii) employs an entropy-guided heuristic resampling strategy to augment sparse observations by selecting the most informative distant viewpoints with negligible overhead. Furthermore, we validate the broad applicability of our framework by demonstrating that it effectively leverages state-of-the-art backbones, including VGGT, to significantly boost performance. Qualitative evaluations on Chang’e mission imagery also show best visual quality among compared methods, indicating robustness on real lunar data. The source code and dataset are publicly available at . Lunar Exploration, Novel View Synthesis, Feed-forward Gaussian Splatting, Vision Foundation Model. INTRODUCTION Lunar exploration through robotic rovers is a cornerstone for future long term lunar residency activities. We investigate the problem of high-fidelity novel view synthesis from sparse image observations in lunar environments with higher real-time performance, as shown in Fig.~ overall , which can enable rovers to achieve comprehensive terrain understanding~ 4399223 , precise visual localization~ mur2017orb , and improved real-time decision-making. As an integral part of 3D scene reconstruction, novel view synthesis is a task dedicated to inferring previously unseen viewpoints of a scene from partial observations. Classical dense 3D reconstruction methods, including point cloud or voxel representations~ vineet2015incremental, whelan2015elasticfusion, dai2017bundlefusion , typically depend on local image similarity metrics. However, these approaches can hardly handle scenes containing repetitive textures or limited overlapping regions, resulting in poor-quality novel view synthesis. Recent advances in neural rendering, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)~ mildenhall2021nerf , have the ability to model complex scenes and render realistic images. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d , an emerging method extending NeRF, significantly accelerates rendering speed and improves efficiency, while still maintaining high fidelity. However, since 3DGS requires training from scratch for each new scene, it currently cannot meet real-time application requirements. Additionally, it requires densely captured images to ensure quality, making it unsuitable for common scenarios with extremely sparse observations in lunar exploration missions. Feed-forward radiance field methods partially address the challenges posed by sparse data and limited real-time capability. For instance, NeRF-based approaches (e.g., MuRF~ xu2024murf and PixelNeRF~ yu2021pixelnerf ) address these challenges by performing efficient inference directly from sparse observations. In comparison, feed-forward 3DGS methods enable more photorealistic and efficient novel view synthesis by explicitly utilizing 3D Gaussian scene representations. Leading scalable reconstruction models in this category (e.g., pixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat and MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat ) employ feed-forward architectures to efficiently generate Gaussian primitives for scene representation. Despite recent progress, lunar scene reconstruction still faces several distinct and unresolved challenges: (i) limited viewpoint overlap during exploration often invalidates traditional epipolar constraints, hindering accurate cross-view feature matching; (ii) lunar background regions exhibit weaker textures compared to foreground objects, complicating depth estimation and geometric reconstruction due to sparse visual cues; (iii) mission-imposed resource constraints severely limit the number and quality of observations, further challenging the accurate representation of lunar surfaces. To overcome these critical challenges, we propose MoonGS, a feed-forward 3DGS framework that synthesizes novel views from sparse lunar surface images and rich semantic information with high fidelity, while achieving real-time performance, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview . To begin with, (i) MoonGS leverages robust cross-view depth features provided by an off-the-shelf vision foundation model to achieve a reliable scene representation, particularly in regions lacking sufficient viewpoint overlap. Moreover, (ii) to further enhance performance, we integrate semantic information into our method in two critical ways: firstly, semantic priors are used to improve the prediction of Gaussian parameters, resulting in more stable scene geometry; secondly, a semantic ranking loss is introduced to regularize depth estimation in weak-textured background regions (e.g., the sky), significantly reducing geometric errors. In addition, (iii) we propose a heuristic resampling strategy to effectively augment sparse lunar surface observations, substantially enhancing the fidelity of synthesized novel views. Meanwhile, (iv) we also introduce a new synthetic lunar dataset as an extension to existing lunar datasets, deliberately designed with extremely sparse sky textures to specifically evaluate reconstruction performance under weakly textured conditions. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We introduce MoonGS, a feed-forward 3DGS framework specifically designed for the Moon, which represents scenes using Gaussian primitives and enables high-quality synthesis of novel views from sparse viewpoints in real time. We fully exploit robust depth features from an off-the-shelf vision foundation model to address insufficient viewpoint overlap, effectively integrate semantic priors and a semantic ranking loss to handle unreliable depth estimation in weakly textured regions, and adopt a heuristic resampling strategy to overcome data sparsity. We provide a dataset named MoonBlender as an extension of existing lunar datasets, specifically designed to evaluate the performance of scene representation methods under weakly textured conditions. Related Work Celestial Surface Reconstruction Based on Radiance Fields Reconstructing celestial surface environments is critical for tasks such as geological analysis~ kang2018coarse and navigation simulation~ 8701525 , providing essential data for robotic perception~ 10746318, 10610211,XIAO20192535, YANG20241327, 10210278, 9646256, 10360155, LIU2023492 and mission planning~ XIONG2024167, dynamic_SLAM . Early approaches to novel view synthesis were based on light fields, initially using densely sampled data~ 10.1145/3596711.3596759, 10.1145/383259.383309 and subsequently allowing unstructured capture~ 10.1145/3596711.3596764 . The advent of structure-from-motion (SfM)~ 10.1145/3596711.3596766 opened the door to synthesizing novel views from photo collections, by estimating a sparse point cloud during camera calibration. Building on SfM, multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques~ Goesele2007MultiViewSF enabled the development of full 3D reconstruction pipelines and further advanced view synthesis algorithms~ 10.1145/3272127.3275084, kopanas2021pointbasedneuralrenderingperview . These methods typically reproject and blend input images based on the recovered geometry, producing high-quality results in many scenarios. However, they can still suffer from unreconstructed regions or artifacts caused by inaccuracies in the MVS-generated geometry. Neural radiance field methods achieve higher fidelity and have shown promise in novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction, and pose estimation~ 10680902 . Mildenhall et al. mildenhall2021nerf encode a scene as an MLP-based implicit function and use volume rendering, which is computationally expensive due to extensive ray sampling. Subsequent techniques muller2022instant, yu2021plenoctrees accelerate radiance field methods, and among these, 3DGS~ kerbl20233d employs Gaussian primitives with a rasterization approach to circumvent ray sampling, reconstructing scenes from dense posed images. Radiance fields have also been applied to celestial environments for high-fidelity visualization. For instance, MaRF~ giusti2022marf reconstructs Martian landscapes from NASA’s PDS, and Zhang et al.~ zhang2024neural extends neural radiance fields to lunar surface scenes. However, existing approaches often suffer from data sparsity and lack real-time performance. To address these issues in lunar applications, we format sparse lunar data as image pairs and design a specialized model architecture to exploit this sparsity. As a result, our method synthesizes high-quality lunar images in real time, strengthening robotic perception in lunar exploration. Feed-forward Radiance Fields To enable real-time reconstruction, researchers have explored feed-forward radiance field methods that reconstruct a scene from a single forward pass. PixelNeRF~ yu2021pixelnerf uses one or few input images to form an entire scene, integrating pixel features into rendering and showing that radiance fields can be learned from sparse views. Du et al. du2023learning adopt epipolar sampling and a lighter renderer for better results, and MuRF xu2024murf constructs a cone volume of the target view, achieving strong performance via convolutional neural networks. However, all these NeRF-based methods rely on ray sampling, resulting in slower performance. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233d is significantly faster in both training and rendering. Consequently, many sparse-view reconstruction methods have adopted 3DGS. For instance, Splatter Image szymanowicz2024splatter employs U-Net to directly infer pixel-wise Gaussian parameters from a single view for object-level reconstruction, while PixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat learns epipolar attention from two related views to predict depth distributions. However, ambiguous feature-to-depth mappings can misposition Gaussians and blur the final images. MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat constructs a cost volume for more precise geometry, and MVSGaussian~ liu2024mvsgaussian similarly uses cost volumes for depth estimation. Yet, end-to-end MVS approaches struggle with limited overlap in planetary data and are not tailored to these scenarios. In contrast, MoonGS leverages a vision foundation model for depth-related features, inferring reliable depth even with sparse observations. It also uses rich lunar semantics as prior knowledge and employs a heuristic resampling strategy. These techniques yield superior reconstruction results for lunar scenes. title: PlaySuite: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Interactive Visual Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models yield strong performance on static perception and reasoning benchmarks, yet such evaluations largely overlook a central aspect of intelligence: acting competently in dynamic environments over extended time horizons. We introduce PlaySuite, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating interactive visual intelligence across more than 5K open-source video games curated from PyWeek and itch.io. Spanning diverse genres and engines, including Pygame, HTML5, Godot, and Unity, these independent games are largely out-of-distribution for current models, reducing the likelihood that success can be achieved by retrieving memorized walkthroughs or web-scale training artifacts. To enable scalable evaluation across heterogeneous titles, we develop a unified closed-loop interaction framework optimized for HPC clusters alongside a Video-LLM-as-a-judge protocol that maps observable gameplay milestones to standardized progress levels. We evaluate fourteen recent open models spanning vision-language models, computer-use agents, and vision-language-action models. Our results yield strong evidence of a perception-action gap: despite strong reasoning capabilities, current models struggle to make sustained progress and exhibit recurring failures in spatial grounding, action execution, and self-correction. PlaySuite provides a reproducible and extensible testbed for measuring progress from visual perception to goal-directed interaction, and a foundation for developing models that can act, adapt, and generalize in dynamic visual environments.

Our open-source benchmark for interactive visual intelligence comprises four stages: (1) Open Game Catalog: A diverse library of 1.7M video games sourced from itch.io and PyWeek. (2) Data Curation: An automated filtering and sandboxing pipeline that distills the catalog into approximately 17.5K executable, safe, and reproducible environments, of which 5,734 are used in our evaluation. (3) Interactive Agent Harness: A high-performance, closed-loop system where foundation models interact via standard keyboard/mouse interfaces for optimized large-scale HPC evaluation. (4) Evaluation Artifacts: A comprehensive suite of gameplay videos, action traces, and a Video-LLM-as-a-judge mechanism to quantify goal-directed performance. fig:playsuite Introduction Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have rapidly expanded their capabilities beyond static visual understanding toward multimodal reasoning and interaction. Modern models can operate graphical user interfaces across desktop, mobile, and web platforms and control embodied agents over extended tasks~ bai2025qwen2,zhou2026qwen, qin2025ui,intelligence2025pi_ . Yet, many multimodal benchmarks still primarily evaluate perception and reasoning over static inputs yue2024mmmu, liu2024mmbench . Real-world intelligence~ lake2017building , by contrast, is interactive and temporally dependent: actions alter future observations, decisions require adaptation to feedback, and agents must recover from mistakes over time. Recent agent benchmarks~ xie2024osworld,zhouwebarena,zheng2025v,zhang2025videogamebench are increasingly incorporating assessment of such closed-loop capabilities, but doing so across large and diverse sets of environments remains challenging. This motivates a central question: how well do current multimodal models translate their perceptual and reasoning capabilities into goal-directed interaction? Games provide a particularly rich testbed to address this question. They combine computer use with spatial reasoning, temporal dynamics, and goal-directed behavior in interactive environments. Recent frontier systems have demonstrated sustained interaction in complex games from visual observations and natural-language goals~ tan2024cradle,bolton2025sima,anthropic2026fable, openai2026astra , but these demonstrations remain concentrated in a small number of environments. Existing game benchmarks similarly span only a limited number of distinct games~ Guss_Houghton_Topin_Wang_Codel_Veloso_Salakhutdinov_2019,fan2022minedojo,zheng2025v,paglieribalrog,park2025orak,zhang2025videogamebench,wang2026visgym , raising questions on how broadly these capabilities generalize. We introduce , a large-scale benchmark for interactive visual intelligence across 5,734 distinct video games, over two orders of magnitude more game environments ( ) than prior multi-game benchmarks. These environments are drawn from a larger pool of approximately 17.5K launchable games validated by our pipeline, providing substantial room for future expansion. An illustration of is presented in Figure~ fig:playsuite . We construct from games hosted on~ pyweek and~ itchio . PyWeek contributes lightweight Python-based games, while itch.io substantially expands the visual, mechanical, and engine diversity of the benchmark with games developed using Unity, Godot, GameMaker, RPG Maker, and other frameworks. Together, these ecosystems provide a broad distribution of independently developed, human-designed environments, ranging from simple 2D games to visually complex 3D and physics-driven settings. Evaluating agents across thousands of heterogeneous games introduces two key challenges: scalable interaction and comparable evaluation. Different engines expose disparate execution and control interfaces, motivating a common interaction layer that enables agents to operate across games using standard keyboard and mouse actions. At the same time, games do not share a common reward or scoring interface. We therefore introduce a progress-based Video-LLM-as-a-judge methodology~ zheng2023judging,lin2023mcu , which extracts observable gameplay milestones and maps them to progress levels. Together, these components enable scalable and comparable evaluation across thousands of diverse game environments. Using this new infrastructure, we benchmark fourteen recent open models spanning general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs), computer-use agents (CUAs), and vision-language-action models (VLAs). Despite strong visual reasoning capabilities, current models achieve meaningful gameplay progress on only a minority of games. Qualitative inspection of gameplay traces further identifies recurring difficulties in spatial grounding, control selection, action execution, and adaptation over time, highlighting the gap between interpreting an environment and acting effectively within it. Nearly a decade after OpenAI Universe~ openai2016universe , revisits the vision of broad-environment evaluation in the setting of pretrained multimodal agents that can be deployed across heterogeneous games without environment-specific training. We release as an open and extensible benchmark, including environment wrappers, evaluation protocols, and high-performance cluster tooling. In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) a large-scale benchmark spanning over 5K heterogeneous interactive visual environments; (2) a unified, HPC-optimized infrastructure for closed-loop evaluation across diverse game engines; and (3) a scalable milestone-based Video-LLM evaluation protocol for measuring gameplay progress without environment-specific rewards. The benchmark is designed to grow as new environments and increasingly capable interactive models emerge. Related Work models in interactive environments. LLMs have shifted from passive information retrieval toward agentic interaction in closed-loop systems~ wang2024survey . Early work focused on reasoning-chain planning, decomposing natural language goals into executable sub-steps~ huang2022language, xie2023translating , but requiring recursive feedback to adapt to environment shifts~ yao2023react, wang2023describe . With the emergence of multimodal foundation models, research has shifted toward unified perception-action policies mokaria2026survey . General VLMs~ bai2025qwen2, gemma2025 ground linguistic instructions in raw visual pixels, while specialized GUI agents~ qin2025ui,lin2025showui, wuatlas predict control tokens directly. Despite these advancements, models still struggle with the fundamental challenges of interactive intelligence: translating granular perception into effective action, maintaining long-horizon planning, and exhibiting robust spatial reasoning in dynamic environments. This persistent gap highlights the need for an open-source, large-scale, and heterogeneous benchmark to evaluate and refine these capabilities across interactive scenarios, moving beyond narrowly defined domains toward truly general-purpose agency. -based benchmarks. To address performance saturation and data contamination in traditional evaluations, the field has pivoted toward dynamic, interactive suites that require real-time decision-making~ wong2025reasoning, chen2025recent . Digital navigation benchmarks~ he2024webvoyager, zhang2025appagent, zhouwebarena, yao2022webshop assess tool-use and GUI automation, while embodied AI frameworks focus on atomic physical interactions~ yang2025embodiedbench . Games have emerged as a primary testbed due to their inherent complexity and high-frequency temporal dynamics. Early benchmarks were restricted to 2D or grid-based environments~ costarelli2024gamebench, nasir2024gametraversalbenchmark, hafner2021benchmarking, kuttler2020nethack, wang2025large, chollet2025arc . While these provided essential testbeds for logic and planning, they failed to capture the spatial nuances of the real world~ zhang2024ing, wang2025large . Recent 3D environments require agents to process perspective, depth, and occlusion~ qiao2023gameeval, hugamearena, Xie_Zhang_Chen_Wan_Li_2024 , but remain constrained to single titles~ fan2022minedojo, Guss_Houghton_Topin_Wang_Codel_Veloso_Salakhutdinov_2019 , or small sets of games requiring bespoke per-title engineering and hand-crafted rewards~ zheng2025v, paglieribalrog, park2025orak, ying2026ai . Modern modular harnesses decouple perception and reasoning to tackle diverse games without domain-specific engineering~ zhang2025general, zhang2025videogamebench, lu2025cultivating, foundation2026arc , often adopting the LLM/VLMs-as-a-judge paradigm to assess agentic competence~ zheng2023judging,pan2024autonomous,lin2023mcu . synthesizes these advancements into a scalable paradigm, replacing bespoke engineering with a unified, judge-based assessment across a large variety of game mechanics. A comprehensive comparison of the existing video games benchmarks against is provided in Table~ tab:literature_comparison , highlighting our contributions in scale, infrastructure, and dynamic evaluation. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on domain-specific simulators or restricted game lists, provides a unified interaction framework that standardizes communication across heterogeneous engines. Each game is executed in an isolated sandbox using a virtual display, enabling efficient and scalable execution across GPU clusters without requiring physical displays. To ensure the benchmark captures a broad spectrum of common-sense interactive intelligence across different tasks, we curated a library of 5,734 open-source games from ~ pyweek and ~ itchio . title: Sim-to-Real Transfer of Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments Using an Ackermann-Steered Mobile Robot
summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to navigate through environments using natural language instructions, making human-robot interaction intuitive. Traditional VLN models often rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization which pose significant challenges when adapting these models to real-world settings. This work addresses these limitations by performing a simulation-to-real domain shift of a VLN approach that operates in continuous environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views. The proposed system integrates vision-language models that align visual inputs and linguistic instructions within a shared embedding space, facilitating natural language-driven navigation. We employ a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) based architecture trained on an existing dataset in a simulated environment and fine-tune it using real-world data collected from a custom-built Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and a LiDAR sensor. By utilising linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a limited number of episodes, our model successfully adapts to real-world environments, achieving effective navigation while running offline on dedicated hardware. Experimental results, evaluated using Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) metrics, demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of our approach. Keywords: Vision-Language Navigation, Cross-Modal Attention, Natural Language Instructions, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Autonomous Navigation, Ackermann-steering.

Keywords: Vision-Language Navigation, Cross-Modal Attention, Natural Language Instructions, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Autonomous Navigation, Ackermann-steering. INTRODUCTION sec:intro Vision-Language Navigation (VLN), where robots navigate through an environment by following natural language instructions, has garnered significant attention due to its intuitive approach to robotic control. This emerging field leverages the ability of vision-language models to map visual data (from images captured by the robot) and language instructions into a shared embedding space, enabling the prediction of actions within a specified action space. Most early VLN studies use simulated environments, which were often discrete~ li2023kerm,chen2022think, anderson2018vision, zhu2021soon, qi2020reverie . These implementations frequently rely on: (i) oracle navigation, which is capable of accurately traversing multiple meters in the presence of obstacles; (ii) known topology, where agents operate on a fixed network of traversable nodes (graph); (iii) ideal 360-degree panoramic RGB imagery and depth information; and (iv) perfect localization, where agents are given their precise location and heading at all times. These assumptions present a major challenge when transferring VLN models trained in simulated environments to real-world continuous environments. Transferring a VLN agent from a simulated environment to the real world (sim-to-real) introduces additional complexities anderson2021sim . Visual domain gaps can exist between the simulated training environment and the real world due to differences in the camera quality, dynamic range, and lighting conditions. Viewpoint variations, even slight ones, can degrade the agent's performance. In simulations, the VLN agent is trained with a high-level discrete action space, yet real robots operate in a continuous low-level motor control space. While the sim-to-real work by Anderson et al.~ anderson2021sim is notable for being one of the first such implementations, it relies on SLAM DurrantWhyte2006SimultaneousLA for navigation in physical world. To bring VLN significantly closer to real-world scenarios, Krantz et al.~ krantz2020beyond introduced VLN-CE, which removes the need for discrete graph assumptions while adopting a more generalized approach for navigation in continuous environments. It uses a 3D continuous environment simulator (Habitat) savva2019habitat for the VLN task. Nevertheless, as a simulation-based work, it cannot be directly applied to an embodied real-world implementation due to the aforementioned sim-to-real challenges. In this work, we present a real-world VLN framework leveraging VLN-CE while addressing sim-to-real complications. Our model encodes the image and depth information using two ResNet50 networks and encodes natural language instructions using a Bi-LSTM encoder. Then, through cross-modal attention, we predict an action among a discrete action space. We train our model using the VLN-CE anderson2018vision dataset in simulated environment. Then, through linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning, we enhance the model performance in real-world settings. We used a custom Ackermann-steered mobile robot to implement the sim-to-real VLN system utilizing Robot Operating System (ROS) Quigley2009ROSAO framework. We validate the efficacy of our approach through experiments demonstrating the robot's ability to interpret and follow language instructions across diverse real-world settings. The contributions of this work are as follows: We introduce a VLN sim-to-real architecture without navigation graphs and 360-degree views. We demonstrate successful navigation in real-world indoor environments using an Ackermann-steered mobile robot with minimal fine-tuning in sim-to-real transfer. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to attempt VLN using an Ackermann-steered robot. We provide a ROS implementation for offline VLN system deployment, enabling practical applications. RELATED WORK The key developments in VLN can be explored, highlighting the evolution of methods from discrete action spaces to continuous environments, while identifying existing challenges and research gaps. Vision-Language Navigation The concept of VLN was first introduced by Anderson et al. anderson2018vision , and their work laid the foundation for the VLN task, where the agent perceives its surroundings through RGB images and navigates based on high-level language commands. This pioneering effort utilized the Room-to-Room (R2R) anderson2018vision dataset, a benchmark for training and evaluating VLN models in simulated environments. Subsequent research in VLN li2023kerm,chen2022think,vln-pano2real has largely focused on enhancing the model's ability to interpret language and visual inputs more effectively. Early models, such as those based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention mechanisms, demonstrated the feasibility of combining visual and linguistic modalities for navigation tasks krantz2020beyond,krantz2021waypoint . However, these models were often constrained to discrete environments and action spaces, limiting their application to pre-defined environments with fixed viewpoints and requiring navigation graphs for path planning. Navigation Graphs Models operating in discrete action spaces rely on predefined navigation graphs that map out possible routes within the environment chen2021topological, daniuvsis2021topological . These navigation graphs consist of nodes (representing specific locations) and edges (representing navigable paths between nodes), facilitating structured movement from one point to another. This approach faces significant limitations when applied to real-world scenarios. Moreover, the reliance on 360-degree views and exact localization is often unachievable in real-world applications, where visual input may be obstructed or incomplete due to environmental factors. Sim-to-Real Transfer Sim-to-real transfer has been a crucial focus in VLN to bridge the gap between performance in simulated environments and real-world applications. Early works in VLN achieved notable success by training agents in high-fidelity simulated environments with controlled settings, predefined maps, and panoramic images chen2022think, li2023kerm, anderson2018vision, hermann2020learning . These simulated environments allowed researchers to evaluate navigation tasks using structured visual data and idealized conditions, but transitioning these systems to the real world introduced substantial challenges. Visual domain gaps can exist between the simulated environment and the real world due to differences in the camera quality, dynamic range, and lighting conditions. One of the main difficulties is the sim-to-real gap, which encompasses discrepancies in visual quality, and the sensor fidelity of real-world environments. Anderson et al. anderson2021sim addressed these challenges by employing domain randomization to handle visual differences and using a subgoal prediction model to translate high-level actions from simulation into the continuous, real-world action space required by physical robots. Their work demonstrated that sim-to-real transfer is feasible with the support of pre-mapped environments and annotated navigation graphs, but performance degraded significantly when these aids were removed, underscoring the limitations of sim-to-real strategies in previously unseen settings. LM-Nav~ shah2023lm leverages pre-exploration and large pretrained models to enhance navigation in complex environments, relying heavily on external processing and prior knowledge. In contrast, our implementation does not depend on precomputed maps, allowing the robot to operate autonomously in unknown environments with limited processing power. Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments The transition from discrete, graph-based navigation to continuous environments has been a significant step forward in the development of VLN systems. VLN in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) by Krantz et al. krantz2020beyond, krantz2021waypoint , comes first in that transition. VLN-CE krantz2020beyond focuses on enabling agents to operate in more realistic, unbounded settings where actions are not restricted to a set of predefined paths. The action space of VLN-CE results in significantly longer-horizon tasks, with an average of 55.88 steps compared to the 4-6 steps typical in discrete environments (R2R). While recent research enhances VLN in continuous environments, it still relies on the use of pre-computed navigation graphs an2024etpnav, irshad2021hierarchical, an2023bevbert and 360-degree panoramic visuals krantz2021waypoint , and remains limited to simulation-only implementations. METHODOLOGY Our goal is to build an embodied VLN implementation for unseen environments that carries out navigation tasks using only the egocentric view of the robot and natural language instruction without having the restriction of a predefined navigation graph. We propose a cohesive framework to achieve this task by leveraging cross-modal attention across a natural language model and computer vision models to predict a discrete action within a predefined action space. Our framework also includes the safe execution of this predicted action through a ROS action handler integrated with a fail-safe algorithm for obstacle avoidance. We deploy our system on a custom Ackermann-steered robot platform for testing and evaluation. The following subsections describe these methods in detail. Fig.~ fig:The system architecture shows the overall system architecture. Generalized System Architecture The architecture processes multimodal inputs, including RGB images, depth data, and natural language instructions, to predict navigation actions in continuous environments. RGB and depth data captured through camera sensors undergo photometric adjustments, and are encoded using dual ResNet50~ he2016deep networks pretrained on the ImageNet~ deng2009imagenet and PointNav~ wijmans2019dd datasets. Precomputed instruction embeddings (GLoVE embeddings~ pennington2014glove ) are encoded using a Bi-LSTM~ graves2005framewise , which captures context from both sides of the instruction for accurate language understanding in a memory-efficient manner, enabling deployment on resource-constrained standalone devices. Then, these multimodal inputs are processed using a cross-modal attention-based architecture to generate navigation actions, enabling the robot to move through the environment as per the instructions. title: AeroBuoy: A Drone Deployable, 3D Printed, Autonomous Robotic Buoy for Environmental Inspection in Remote and Hazardous River Systems
comment: 7 pages. Accepted version. Published in the 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Winner of the IROS 2025 Best Paper Award on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics in memory of Motohiro Kisoi. Reuben O'Brien and Angus Lynch contributed equally
summary: Monitoring of waterways such as remote and hazardous rivers and streams is important so as to assess the impact of external factors including construction runoff or climate change. Versatile, autonomous robotic boats can offer excellent environmental inspection and monitoring solutions for remote, dangerous, or access protected water bodies but they have several shortcomings in terms of maneuverability. This paper proposes an environmental inspection system consisting of an autonomous data collection buoy which is designed to be deployed to inaccessible river systems using a drone. The system can perform a drop off and pickup of the buoy depending on the requirements of a particular location and monitoring task. Utilising the natural flow of the river the buoy autonomously steers down, using GPS and magnetometers so as to maintain the desired trajectory. The buoy is capable of measuring water temperature but it can also be equipped with a range of sensors such as water oxygen meter, sonar for river bed inspection, or turbidity for water clarity. This paper describes the system design, presents an analysis of the self-righting capabilities of the buoy, and shows a full system demonstration at the Ōrewa River in Auckland, New Zealand.

Introduction sec:introduction Environmental monitoring in remote and dangerous rivers and other aquatic environments is a critical task for which robotic systems can provide a reliable, low-cost solution. Traditional methods, such as deploying boats or canoes for data collection or water sampling, present numerous challenges. These conventional platforms are often oversized relative to the narrow and winding nature of rivers, making them difficult to maneuver, particularly in confined spaces and turbulent waters. Additionally, their directional design can limit their ability to navigate sharp turns or reverse course, and they are highly susceptible to becoming entangled with floating debris and aquatic plants. To mitigate some of these issues, jetboats have become a common choice for river navigation. Jetboats, with their impeller-based propulsion systems, are capable of operating in shallow waters and executing tighter turns. However, even these specialized vessels are not without their drawbacks. Their size and operational characteristics can still be suboptimal for the complex and dynamic environments often encountered in rivers, where factors such as shallow areas, debris, and rapid currents can pose significant risks. The need for more efficient, adaptable, and resilient platforms for environmental inspections is evident, especially in locations where traditional methods are impractical or unsafe. The development of such systems can offer new possibilities for routine monitoring and rapid deployment in response to emerging environmental concerns. Furthermore, as rivers are often difficult to access, particularly in remote or hazardous regions, the ability to deploy and retrieve monitoring systems remotely would be highly advantageous. This capability would not only enhance the safety and efficiency of environmental monitoring efforts but also provide a consistent stream of valuable data over time. This paper presents a novel 3D-printed, autonomous robotic buoy (Fig. fig:cover ) for environmental monitoring in inaccessible rivers. Its key novelty lies in the combined functionality of drone-based deployment/retrieval on both water and land along with a robust, self-righting design, enabling operation in debris-ridden waters. The buoy autonomously traverses downstream, driven by the river's flow, collecting temperature, imagery, and flow data. In this paper the design and experimental validation of the system is detailed. Related Work sec:related Environmental monitoring using autonomous systems has gained traction, particularly in remote and hazardous locations. Unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) and autonomous drones have emerged as viable platforms for gathering data in inaccessible environments. According to Jain2021 , applications for these technologies span seven categories: rescue, military, patrolling, disaster relief, environmental monitoring, inspection, and water sports rescue. Their primary benefits include reduced human involvement, faster response times, increased flexibility, and the ability to cover vast areas. Several fixed autonomous systems have been developed to monitor environmental conditions. For example, Shukla2023 describes a stationary, moored buoy designed for continuous water quality monitoring. This system includes sensors to ensure safe drinking water standards are maintained in rivers. Despite its effectiveness, stationary solutions like this are constrained by their inability to move, making them less suitable for large or dynamic environments like rivers. Larger mobile systems have also been explored for monitoring aquatic environments, in Si2023 , a USV raft capable of traversing oceanic environments while measuring various parameters at different speeds was presented. These larger systems, although effective in open waters, are less suited for narrower or obstacle-laden rivers due to their size and limited manoeuvrability. The propulsion systems, like wave gliders hine2009 , which rely on ocean waves for long-distance travel, also fall short in river environments where wave energy is minimal. Smaller, motorized buoy systems have shown promise in autonomous monitoring. For example, in Guan2022 a motorized buoy with dual thrusters was developed that optimizes path planning and manoeuvrability. However, even with improved efficiency, systems designed for calm lakes may struggle in dynamic and debris-filled river environments. This is where leveraging natural river currents could significantly reduce energy consumption. MIT designed and built the `BoB' system offering a significant innovation in the buoy movement. Designed for omnidirectional travel, this 7.4 kg system uses three points of propulsion to achieve high stability in calm waters Zoss2018 . It was later upgraded to be a 3.3 kg system Kwa2020 . Although it shows promise in lake environments, its application to river systems remains limited by its inability to navigate turbulent waters. Research on autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) specifically designed for rivers is ongoing. Systems such as madeo2020low provide a low cost, monitoring system, but it is limited by its size and weight. In Schneider2016 , the authors proposed a method for using ultrasonic sensors to help ASVs monitor oil spills while avoiding obstacles like rocks and branches. This sensor-based navigation is critical for buoys and drones in river environments, where river currents sanjou2021portable and debris create unpredictable challenges, within the river boundaries zhang2023river . Drone integration with buoys has gained attention as an effective deployment strategy in remote or hazardous areas. In Franek2023 a stationary monitoring buoy that is deployable and retrievable by a drone was demonstrated. It featured floats for safe water landings, showcasing the potential for drone-based buoy deployment in dynamic environments. However, other drone systems, like Ajgaonkar2020 , which deployed lifebuoys using a servo mechanism, lacked retrieval capabilities and required manual loading. Simulated dynamic models for a tethered buoy and drone are presented in, Kourani2021 , kourani2021bidirectional , showing potential in both calm and wave conditions. Real-world testing of a similar system has been done in `The Bathy Drone' Diaz2022 , which demonstrates a tethered drone system capable of bathymetry. The sonar is attached to a multi-hull boat that is towed over open water. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV's) or `drones' have been developed to have many different ways of implementing aerial grasping and manipulation. In aerial-grasp-review , the authors review many of these methods, involving all kinds of mechanisms and actuation methods. In lynch2024 , a grasping mechanism on a drone is implemented using a dynamixel motor, where the drone uses it's grasper to perch onto a power line. In 6385963 a system where multiple drones support a net using tethers mounted to the underside of the drone is shown. 10018625 presents a drone which is able to lower a net based mechanism, suspended from a cable below the drone to pickup packages for delivery. The mechanism is actuated by motors mounted onto the net itself, so would be unsuitable to pickup or drop off into water. 9650012 presents the design of a three-fingered claw mechanism installed on a drone for picking up objects, particularly debris from power lines. A similar approach could be adapted for aquatic buoy retrieval by integrating a larger tether, ensuring the drone remains at a safe distance from the water. This paper proposes a novel approach to addressing the challenges of river-based environmental monitoring. Section III delves into the design of the proposed system, focusing on its novel aspects. Section IV discusses the experimental validation of the platform in the Ōrewa River and presents the results. Finally, Section V concludes the paper, discussing the potential impact of this solution on future environmental monitoring efforts. Design Modelling sec:design Buoy Design The environmental inspection AeroBuoy is comprised of one main hull shown in Fig. fig:design-explode , that is 3D printed from polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) as discussed in obrien2024 . A flotation ring is mounted around it and attached via four external mounting points to provide greater stability while ensuring that the buoy will always float regardless of any damage to the main hull. Most importantly it acts as a barrier to rocks, branches, or other obstacles that system might unexpectedly collide with, damping the impact to the electronics and protecting the hull at the waterline. The lid is sealed using a custom sized foam o-ring that seals from the compression of the 10 flange bolts around the rim. To allow for grasping the lid and flange are circular and reinforced with a 10 mm overhang for the claws to hook onto. On top of the lid is an enclosed camera which can either be a piloted first person view (FPV) or a logger connected to the companion computer. A global positioning system (GPS) is mounted alongside the telemetry radio with no physical obstructions. This allows clear communication to an off-board computer and strong satellite communication. Above the camera's lid two mild steel strips that have been coated with paint and allow for the claw's magnet to locate itself centrally. To provide a stable landing and take off, a 3D printed base with connecting carbon rods provide the standoff. Additionally, the landing gear acts as protection to the propulsion system which is a ducted propeller and a rudder that is controlled via a double o-ring sealed shaft. Speeds of up to 1.5 m/s can be achieved in steady water with operation possible against river flows of up to 1 m/s. Water quality sensors are also protected with the temperature and moisture probe extending through the base of the hull. Internally, the system is powered by two 2.6 amp hour, lithium-polymer batteries that power the propulsion, navigation, and sensing electronics. They are able to provide up to one hour of run time at steady speeds of 0.5 m/s. title: What the Elevation Map Cannot See: Semantic-Aware Locomotion and Execution-Aware Navigation for Humanoid Robot
summary: Navigation for humanoid robots is critical, yet large-scale evaluation on physical hardware is often impractical due to cost and safety concerns, making simulation benchmarks essential. Existing VLN benchmarks achieve physically executable navigation, but still assume (1) all hazards are observable from elevation maps; (2) realized motions closely match desired motions. In real environments, however, fallen bottles may be ambiguous in elevation maps, while phones and water spills may be difficult to differentiate; hazard avoidance by the locomotion policy can cause the robot's actual trajectory to deviate from the path intended by the VLN policy. Such command-execution mismatch can accumulate and lead the robot toward unintended locations. To expose these failure modes, we introduce a benchmark that models both elevation-subtle hazards and execution deviations, together with a closed-loop VLN + locomotion control framework that continuously realigns high-level navigation with the robot's actual state. We evaluate navigation in simulation and further validate the locomotion policy on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Results show that semantic input reduces contact with hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, while anti-deviation improves navigation success. These findings highlight the need to evaluate humanoid navigation jointly in terms of route completion and hazard avoidance.

Introduction Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to assist people in everyday household environments, where navigation requires moving through rooms and corridors while avoiding furniture and floor-level hazards. Small objects and water spills in these environments may be poorly represented in depth-derived elevation maps, posing challenges beyond geometric obstacle avoidance. Although humanoids offer mobility advantages over wheeled platforms, large-scale real-world evaluation is costly, time-consuming, and potentially unsafe. Simulation benchmarks therefore enable repeatable, scalable evaluation before physical deployment. Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) allows robots to navigate according to natural-language instructions rather than predefined metric goals. Early VLN benchmarks moved agents between predefined viewpoints, abstracting away locomotion and obstacle interaction anderson2018vision . Continuous-environment VLN replaced this graph-based formulation with local actions in continuous 3D environments krantz2020beyond . More recently, physics-based benchmarks such as VLN-PE~ wang2025rethinking , VLNVerse~ lin2025vlnverse , and VLN-CE-Isaac~ cheng2025navila further introduce robot kinematics, collision dynamics, and continuous motion, advancing VLN toward physically executable navigation. Nevertheless, physics-based VLN evaluation retains two implicit assumptions. First, obstacle observability assumes that locomotion hazards are detectable from depth or elevation maps. Yet wet floors and small objects such as phones or cables may have weak or absent geometric signatures, so geometric traversability does not imply safety. Second, command-execution consistency assumes that realized motion matches high-level commands. Safe humanoid locomotion may instead require sidesteps, shorter steps, or turns. Repeated avoidance can accumulate pose and heading errors, shift observations away from those expected by the VLN policy, and undermine navigation. These limitations are coupled: avoiding a semantically detected hazard can alter the trajectory assumed by the VLN policy. Existing benchmarks emphasize geometric traversability and collisions rather than this perception-execution feedback loop. Strong simulation performance may therefore conceal missed non-geometric hazards or lost task progress when subsequent decisions ignore avoidance-induced deviations. We introduce a humanoid VLN benchmark that exposes these failure modes through hazards with different levels of geometric observability, including those weakly represented or absent in elevation maps. It distinguishes commanded from realized motion, enabling controlled evaluation of execution deviations caused by safety-aware low-level behavior. This formulation measures whether an agent reaches its language-specified destination while remaining safe and recovering its navigation state after local deviations. We develop a hierarchical framework coupling a high-level VLN module with a semantic-aware whole-body locomotion policy. The VLN module generates relative target poses from language instructions and visual observations, while the locomotion policy tracks the derived velocity commands with local terrain and hazard awareness. Closed-loop feedback of the robot's realized state corrects avoidance-induced deviations. We evaluate navigation in simulation and validate locomotion on a physical Unitree G1 with hazards poorly represented by geometry alone. Our contributions are two-fold: Semantic-aware locomotion + anti-deviation VLN: The semantic branch provides a "steppability" prior to fill the blind spots of the elevation map, while anti-deviation correction compensates local deviations before they accumulate into navigation drift or render subsequent commands unsafe. Hazard taxonomy and benchmark: Incorporate "geometrically invisible hazards" and "physical disturbances" into the VLN evaluation benchmark, complemented by new metrics such as the Hazard Contact Rate. Evaluation: Navigation is evaluated in simulation, while locomotion is evaluated in both simulated and real-world environments. Related Works Humanoid Navigation Benchmark VLN datasets such as RxR ku2020rxr and REVERIE qi2020reverie extend language and object grounding without modeling humanoid execution. HumanoidBench sferrazza2024humanoidbench evaluates physical control but not language-guided navigation. Recent physics-based VLN benchmarks incorporate robot embodiment and locomotion wang2025rethinking,cheng2025navila,lin2025vlnverse,humanoidvln , complementing these language- and control-focused evaluations. These benchmarks advance physical evaluation but cover a more limited range of perturbations and obstacles. We introduce richer perturbation and obstacle settings to jointly diagnose semantic hazards and safety-induced execution deviations. We target hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, such as wet surfaces and small objects, and evaluate safety and navigation recovery when low-level avoidance alters commanded motion. Humanoid Locomotion and Whole-Body Control Perpetual Humanoid Control (PHC) luo2023perpetual provides motion imitation and fall recovery for simulated avatars. ExBody cheng2024expressive combines upper-body imitation with velocity-tracking locomotion on hardware, while OmniH2O he2024omnih2o learns deployable whole-body control from retargeted human motion and privileged teachers. HOVER he2025hover unifies velocity, pose, and upper-body control interfaces; ExBody2 ji2026exbody2 and TWIST ze2025twist emphasize motion tracking and coordinated locomotion--manipulation. Their primary focus is reference tracking rather than semantic navigation hazards. Terrain-aware methods incorporate environmental geometry. Humanoid Parkour zhuang2025parkour uses vision-based reinforcement learning for obstacle traversal. Attention-Based Map Encoding (AME) he2025attention attends to elevation maps for foothold selection, and AME-2 zhang2026ame2 adds uncertainty-aware mapping. Hiking in the Wild zhu2026hiking instead maps depth and proprioception directly to humanoid joint actions. Geometry alone, however, cannot distinguish similarly shaped surfaces with different semantic risks. Related quadruped systems address complementary aspects: ViNL kareer2023vinl couples visual navigation with locomotion that steps over household clutter, while Yang et al.\ yang2023semantics learn terrain-semantic speed and gait selection from human demonstrations. Our focus is humanoid foot-level hazard avoidance using aligned geometric and semantic maps, coupled with realized-motion feedback for correcting deviations during language-guided navigation. Methodology Problem Formulation We formulate humanoid navigation among semantically identifiable hazards with ambiguous or absent elevation signatures as a hierarchical task. Semantic Branch for Privileged Locomotion sec:semantic_branch Fig.~ fig:stage shows our locomotion training curriculum. We first learn how to use semantic hazard information for locomotion under ground-truth perception, then transfer this capability to a waist camera-based student. Augmenting the geometric locomotion policy We start from a pretrained AME policy~ he2025attention that can already walk and traverse challenging terrain. We retain its network architecture and weights, and add an independent semantic branch. The geometric branch describes terrain shape, whereas the semantic branch provides a steppability representation that distinguishes safe support from hazardous regions. The teacher generates actions using ground-truth elevation and semantic maps together with proprioceptive input. This stage builds semantic-aware hazard avoidance on top of the pretrained terrain-traversal capability. Training a robust semantic teacher We continue PPO training with curriculum-based randomization of dynamics and payload, proprioceptive observation noise, pushes, and external forces, as detailed in Sec.~ sec:experiment_setup . title: Dynamics Modeling of a Multi-UAV Slung Load System Using a Discrete-Link Cable Approach
comment: Presented at ICRA 2026 as an accepted paper
summary: A common assumption to simplify the problem of controlling a multi-UAV slung load system (MUSLS) is that the flexible cables can be modeled as massless rigid rods. In this work, we propose an alternative Euler-Newton derived dynamical model which uses a series of rigid links to model the flexible cables. The model is specifically designed to allow efficient simulation using Featherstone's articulated body algorithm. We perform real-world validation of this model on gentle, aggressive, and tension-engagement maneuvers and run a parameter sweep to determine the number of links, joint damping, and joint friction to achieve the greatest model fidelity. The model closely matches real-world flight data with mean load translation errors below 132 mm (5.5% of the cable length) and orientation errors below 11.4 degrees. We make the real-world flight data publicly available for the development of future cable models.

The model is specifically designed to allow efficient simulation using Featherstone's articulated body algorithm. Supplementary Material sect:supplementary_material Video: |https://youtu.be/VATTPYYDwYY| Code: | https://github.com/hmer101/| |musls_cable_modeling/| INTRODUCTION sect:intro A common strategy for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) payload transport is to suspend the payload from a flexible cable, yielding a slung-load configuration marques_tethered_2023 . When multiple UAVs cooperate to carry a single load (Fig.~ fig:system_symbols ), they can transport heavier payloads and, in principle, regulate the load’s full six-degree-of-freedom pose manubens_motion_2013 . As applications mature, there is a growing need to simulate multi-UAV slung-load systems (MUSLS) within off-the-shelf toolchains. In these settings, the dynamics model must be plug-and-play with standard rigid-body simulators, operate near real time, and remain stable across regimes that include loss and re-engagement of cable tension. Accurately modeling general flexible cables is difficult because they exhibit nonlinear, high-dimensional dynamics and undergo abrupt transitions when tension is lost or re-established. Approaches to cable modeling can be categorized as discrete or continuous lv_review_2020 . Discrete approaches include mass–spring systems lv_physically_2017 , multibody chains of rigid links servin_rigid_2008 , and finite-element methods wang_efficient_2013 ; continuous formulations include elastic-rod and spline-based dynamics lang_multi-body_2011, echegoyen_linked_2010 . Within the MUSLS literature specifically, prior work can be grouped into three subsets of the discrete approach. Massless rigid links. The most common approach assumes each cable is a massless, always-taut rod forming a straight line between attachment points sreenath_dynamics_2013, fink_planning_2011, michael_cooperative_2011, lee_geometric_2013, wu_geometric_2014 . This simplifies analysis and controller design but reduces simulation fidelity, particularly when cables go slack. Hybrid tension models. To handle slack-cable transitions, some works augment rigid-link models with hybrid dynamics that explicitly switch between taut and slack regimes sreenath_dynamics_2013, li_rotortm_2024 . While more physically accurate during tension re-engagement, these models still rely on custom numerical simulators and are not easily integrated with general-purpose robotics toolchains. Discrete rigid links. Discrete-link formulations have been applied to MUSLS primarily for differential-flatness-based planning and LQR control kotaru_differential-flatness_2018, kotaru_multiple_2020 and for stabilizing geometric control goodarzi_stabilization_2015 . These works emphasize control-theoretic insights rather than validating cable-model fidelity against real-world MUSLS data, and they offer no insight into how joint properties affect predictive performance. Moreover, all prior discrete-link MUSLS works concentrate link masses at joint connections rather than distributing inertia along each link. While this simplifies the state representation, it increases the number of elements required for convergence relative to rod-inertia models quisenberry_discrete_2006 and prevents treating links as standard rigid bodies. This is a key obstacle to integration with general-purpose simulators, most of which target tree-structured rigid bodies solved with Featherstone's articulated-body algorithm (ABA) featherstone_rigid_2008 . Organization and contributions This paper focuses on the construction and performance quantification of a multi-discrete-link cable dynamics model in a MUSLS context. The model is specifically designed to be easily integrated with a range of rigid-body robotics simulators. The key contributions are: a dynamical model of a MUSLS with a discrete-link cable model which includes the effect of link inertias and tunable joint properties, a systematic selection of key parameters to balance computational efficiency and predictive performance of a multi-link cable model, a quantification of the performance of a multi-link cable model over a variety of trajectories (including tension engagement), and real-world flight data made publicly available harvey_merton_code_2025 to allow the development of future cable models. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section sect:dynamics introduces the MUSLS dynamical model, with emphasis on the multi-link cable formulation and how it differs from existing approaches. Section sect:method describes the approach to testing the model with a position control based scheme. Section sect:results discusses model tuning and the performance of a multi-rigid-link cable model for MUSLS simulation. Section sect:conclusions provides concluding remarks. Unlike many prior formulations, the system is modeled as a tree of rigid bodies, making it solvable with the ABA. The section opens with notation and conventions, proceeds with the derivation of the equations of motion, and concludes with remarks comparing this formulation to existing MUSLS models. title: SURGE: Sonar-fUsed Reconstruction and localization via image-gated Graph Estimation
summary: Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) are widely used to explore and inspect underwater environments such as caves, shipwrecks, and submerged infrastructure. These missions require accurate 3D understanding of the surrounding environment, which depends on both reliable vehicle localization and metric scene reconstruction. However, external positioning is often unavailable underwater, requiring small ROVs to rely primarily on onboard perception. Optic vision provides rich visual and geometric information but suffers from scale ambi- guity and trajectory drift, whereas 2D imaging sonar provides metric range but incomplete 3D geometry. Existing underwater reconstruction approaches typically address these limitations separately or assume known sensor poses, leaving localization and reconstruction disconnected. We present SURGE, a camera sonar framework that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and target location by integrating visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph, then uses the recovered metric poses for sonar Gaussian splatting. Experiments on real underwater RGB sonar observations show that SURGE substantially improves localization consistency over conventional vision based pose estimation and produces a more compact, natively metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian splatting baselines.
