Optic vision provides rich visual and geometric information but suffers from scale ambiguity and trajectory drift, whereas 2D imaging sonar provides metric range but incomplete 3D geometry. Existing underwater reconstruction approaches typically address these limitations separately or assume known sensor poses, leaving localization and reconstruction disconnected. We present SURGE, a camera sonar framework that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and target location by integrating visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph, then uses the recovered metric poses for sonar Gaussian splatting. Experiments on real underwater RGB sonar observations show that SURGE substantially improves localization consistency over conventional vision based pose estimation and produces a more compact, natively metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian splatting baselines. Underwater perception, sensor fusion, factor graph SLAM, forward-looking sonar, Gaussian splatting, remotely operated vehicles. Introduction Remotely operated vehicles are increasingly used for underwater exploration and inspection of environments such as caves, shipwrecks, and submerged infrastructure~ hou2022underwater,labra2023net,hurtos2017underwater,molina2024containers . These missions require accurate three dimensional understanding of the environment for navigation, inspection, and spatial mapping. Building such representations, however, depends on both reliable vehicle localization and metric scene geometry. Underwater localization is particularly challenging because external positioning is often unavailable, forcing small ROVs to rely on onboard perception~ paull2014auvnav . Monocular cameras provide rich visual and geometric information but suffer from scale ambiguity and trajectory drift, especially when visibility and feature quality degrade underwater~ akkaynak2019sea . Forward looking imaging sonar provides complementary metric range measurements and remains effective under poor visibility, but conventional two dimensional sonar observes range and azimuth while leaving elevation ambiguous~ huang2015acousticsfm,negahdaripour2007optiacoustic . Neither modality alone therefore provides both reliable metric localization and complete scene geometry, as shown in Fig. fig:teaser . Recent acoustic optical methods such as AONeuS and Z Splat demonstrate the benefit of combining camera and sonar measurements for underwater reconstruction~ aoneus2024,zsplat2024 . However, these approaches largely assume known sensor poses, while other methods address pose estimation and reconstruction primarily within a single sensing modality~ sonarsplat2025,seasplat2025,watersplatting2025 . This leaves a gap between multimodal reconstruction and the localization needed to support it in real underwater operation. This separation is limiting in practice because reconstruction quality depends directly on the accuracy and metric consistency of the estimated sensor trajectory. We present SURGE, a camera sonar framework for joint underwater localization and metric reconstruction. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce a multimodal factor graph that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and the location of a compact underwater target from monocular RGB and two dimensional forward looking imaging sonar observations. We develop a multi view sonar aggregation strategy and a target extent aware acoustic residual that provide stable metric constraints for joint pose and target estimation. We use the recovered metric poses for target-scoped sonar Gaussian splatting and demonstrate improved localization consistency and more compact metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian-splatting baselines on real underwater data. Related Work sec Recent underwater reconstruction methods differ primarily in two aspects: the sensing modalities they use and whether sensor poses are known or must be estimated from the observations. These distinctions are important for SURGE because accurate reconstruction depends on both complementary visual acoustic geometry and a reliable metric trajectory. Table~ tab:landscape summarizes representative approaches and the setting considered in this work. Multi-modal Reconstruction with Known Poses Camera and sonar provide complementary information for underwater reconstruction, motivating methods that combine optical appearance with acoustic geometry. AONeuS~ aoneus2024 and Z-Splat~ zsplat2024 demonstrate that acoustic measurements can improve three dimensional reconstruction when optical observations are degraded by underwater visibility. Collado-Gonzalez~et al. similarly combine image regions with sonar range measurements for reconstruction in turbid environments~ collado2025optiacoustic . These methods establish the value of acoustic optical fusion, but primarily assume externally provided sensor poses. As a result, they address reconstruction once the trajectory is known rather than recovering localization and reconstruction from the same measurements. Single-Modality Reconstruction with Estimated Poses A parallel line of work relaxes the requirement for known poses, but generally within a single sensing modality. SonarSplat~ sonarsplat2025 extends Gaussian splatting to forward-looking sonar while jointly optimizing the acoustic scene representation and sensor poses. Differentiable space carving reconstructs occupancy from imaging-sonar observations when poses are available~ feng2024dsc , while other approaches address reconstruction under pose drift~ acoustic_drift_2025 or recover sonar geometry without supplied poses using priors from vision foundation models~ posefreesonar2026 . Together, these methods show that acoustic observations can support both pose reasoning and reconstruction despite the geometric ambiguity of imaging sonar. For optical sensing, SeaSplat~ seasplat2025 and WaterSplatting~ watersplatting2025 reconstruct real underwater scenes from RGB imagery using COLMAP poses, while AquaSplat~ aquasplat2026 introduces a dual-branch representation for underwater RGB reconstruction. These methods improve the representation of underwater appearance and geometry, but their reconstruction remains tied to trajectories recovered from visual Structure-from-Motion. Thus, pose-aware reconstruction has been explored for both optical and acoustic sensing, but primarily without using their complementary measurements jointly to recover a metric trajectory. Underwater Factor-Graph SLAM Underwater SLAM provides the complementary perspective of estimating vehicle motion from multiple sensor constraints. Existing systems combine acoustic range, inertial sensing, and optical observations to estimate trajectories and map features~ ferreira2026slam,mcconnell2022perception,li2018flsposegraph,westman2018sonarslam . Imaging-sonar multi-robot systems further recover trajectories and object-level maps from multibeam measurements~ huang2025dracoslam2,mcconnell2022dracoslam . These approaches demonstrate the value of acoustic constraints for underwater localization, but are not designed to connect monocular RGB and 2D FLIS localization directly to downstream target reconstruction. The observation model is also different for compact extended targets. Conventional landmark formulations typically associate acoustic observations with discrete features, whereas the dominant return from an extended object can move across its visible surface as the viewpoint changes. SURGE therefore models the sonar observation relative to the spatial extent of the target rather than forcing every acoustic return to coincide with a single geometric center. Position of the Present Work Prior work therefore establishes three complementary capabilities: acoustic optical fusion can improve underwater reconstruction when poses are known, single-modality methods can reconstruct scenes while estimating or tolerating pose uncertainty, and underwater SLAM can recover vehicle trajectories from acoustic and visual constraints. What remains less explored is their combination: jointly estimating metric vehicle motion and target location from monocular RGB and 2D forward-looking sonar, then using the recovered trajectory for reconstruction in real underwater environments without external positioning. SURGE addresses this gap by coupling visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph and using the resulting metric poses for target-scoped sonar Gaussian splatting. The framework therefore connects localization and reconstruction through the same complementary camera-sonar measurements rather than treating accurate poses as an independent prerequisite. Method sec:method At a high level, SURGE recovers a metric ROV trajectory and a static target centre from paired RGB and 2D sonar frames, then reconstructs the target with sonar Gaussian splatting under those poses. Vision tells where the object appears in the image; sonar tells how far it is. The factor graph fuses both, and the reconstruction stage consumes only the resulting poses. title: Seeing the Invisible: Physics-Guided Visual Prompting for Temperature- and Radiation-Aware VLA Navigation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a major paradigm for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN). However, in safety-critical facilities, invisible risks such as radiation or temperature spikes cannot be detected by an RGB camera, and handling each risk is expensive, requiring a new encoder, new data, and model retraining. We propose Physics-Guided Visual Prompting (PG-VP), a plug-and-play multimodal perception module that instead reuses what a frozen VLA model already does well: avoiding visible obstacles. Given a proximal radiation or thermal source, PG-VP performs a physics-guided risk assessment to determine the avoidance direction and overlays a corresponding virtual obstacle that moves across consecutive frames (Dynamic Visual Prompting). The navigation policy then naturally detours around this invisible hazard. The identical virtual obstacle is used regardless of hazard type, so the visual prompting pattern remains fixed as sensors are added. When no hazard is detected, nothing is rendered, and the policy behaves exactly as it would without PG-VP. We evaluate PG-VP on OmniNav using the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, where it guides the policy toward intended low-risk actions in 84.9% and 83.2% of cases, at a cost of 6.8 and 7.9 percentage points in navigation success rate. We further test it with distinct scenarios on a real robot in the presence of actual thermal and radiation sources, all without any retraining. The real test shows that PG-VP effectively avoids these invisible hazards, improving worst-10% average trajectory safety by 63.45% and 32.59% against thermal and radiation sources, respectively.

However, in safety-critical facilities, invisible risks such as radiation or temperature spikes cannot be detected by an RGB camera, and handling each risk is expensive, requiring a new encoder, new data, and model retraining. The navigation policy then naturally detours around this invisible hazard. The identical virtual obstacle is used regardless of hazard type, so the visual prompting pattern remains fixed as sensors are added. When no hazard is detected, nothing is rendered, and the policy behaves exactly as it would without PG-VP. We evaluate PG-VP on OmniNav using the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, where it guides the policy toward intended low-risk actions in 84.9 and 83.2 of cases, at a cost of 6.8 and 7.9 percentage points in navigation success rate. We further test it with distinct scenarios on a real robot in the presence of actual thermal and radiation sources, all without any retraining. The real test shows that PG-VP effectively avoids these invisible hazards, improving worst-10 average trajectory safety by 63.45 and 32.59 against thermal and radiation sources, respectively. Vision-Language-Action Models, Vision-and-Language Navigation, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Multimodal Perception, Visual Prompting INTRODUCTION Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) is a core problem in achieving generalist navigation capabilities guided by natural language instructions. In particular, implementing VLN in safety-critical facilities, such as nuclear power plants (NPPs), is beneficial for their operations and maintenance (O M). Son~et al.~ son2025use proposed a systematic catalog of potential robotic applications in NPP O M by analyzing historical nuclear incidents using domain-specific large language models (LLMs). Based on their insights, NPP O M requires multi-task robots rather than task-specific ones. Therefore, VLN systems with generalist robots can be valuable not only in everyday environments but also in safety-critical domains. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged, leveraging the foundational capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to unify the perception-to-action pipeline into a jointly trained policy that maps multimodal inputs directly to action tokens, and now represent the latest paradigm of VLN~ cheng2025navila,xue2026omninav,zhang2026qwen,chu2026abot . Still, a key challenge remains for VLA-based navigation in safety-critical environments: visual perception alone is insufficient. Invisible hazards, such as radiation or temperature spikes, can arise during navigation~ son2025use , but they leave no signature in the visible spectrum, and thus cannot be detected by a standard RGB camera. A straightforward solution would be to extend a VLA model's input modalities, but this is expensive: it requires a new encoder, new paired multimodal-language data, and retraining for every new modality~ huang2025tactile,jones2025beyond,cheng2026omnivtla,wang2026vision . More critically, the model offers no guarantee that it preserves its original navigation performance in scenarios without such invisible hazards. We propose the physics-guided visual prompting (PG-VP) module, which guides the navigation trajectory to naturally detour around invisible proximal hazards by leveraging the frozen VLA model's foundational capability to avoid visible obstacles. It assesses the risk posed by proximal radiation or thermal sources, identifies the avoidance direction, and overlays the corresponding virtual obstacle onto the VLA model's input images. Instead of overlaying a static obstacle onto the scene, PG-VP shifts the virtual obstacle across frames to smoothly guide the trajectory, which we call dynamic visual prompting. As a result, the VLA model treats the injected context as a real obstacle and implicitly avoids the invisible hazards. The main benefits of PG-VP are as follows: PG-VP is a plug-and-play visual prompting module that injects non-geometric multimodal physical context into a VLA-based navigation framework in a zero-shot manner, without touching the model weights. When no hazard is detected, it renders no virtual obstacles, fully preserving the native navigation performance. PG-VP requires only a risk assessment model per modality. Building this model is far cheaper than adding an encoder, collecting new data, and retraining. PG-VP renders the same virtual obstacle regardless of modality type. Because the model interprets a single visual prompting pattern rather than a different one for each modality, the alignment with the training distribution remains consistent across sensing modalities. We used OmniNav as the underlying navigation policy~ xue2026omninav , evaluated PG-VP's trajectory-guidance effectiveness across unseen R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits~ Matterport3D,anderson2018vision,ku2020room,krantz_vlnce_2020 , and demonstrated physical deployment under actual thermal and radiation sources. Related Work VLA-based Robot Navigation NaVid~ zhang2024navid was an early attempt to leverage video-based VLMs, directly mapping natural language instructions to low-level navigation actions from an RGB stream; Uni-NaVid~ zhang2024uni and NaVILA~ cheng2025navila established this formulation as a VLA paradigm for navigation. Since then, this has advanced along several directions: broadening generalization across embodiments, tasks, and goal modalities through large-scale training~ zhang2026embodied,hirose2025omnivla,chu2026abot ; compressing accumulated video context and improving systemic efficiency for real-time deployment~ wei2025streamvln,zhang2025mapnav,zheng2025efficient ; injecting geometric priors to recover 3D spatial understanding from RGB input alone~ zeng2026janusvln,liu2026span ; decoupling high-level semantic reasoning from low-level control in dual-system architectures~ wei2026ground,internvla-n1,huang2026sedualvln ; and post-training the policy with self-correction data flywheels~ yu2026correctnav . At the intersection of these directions, OmniNav~ xue2026omninav adopts a fast-slow design: a fast system generates short-horizon continuous-space waypoints via a flow-matching policy, while a slow system plans long-horizon sub-goals from frontiers and visual memory. We adopt OmniNav's fast system as our underlying vision-only navigation policy. Extending Perception Beyond RGB In VLA-based manipulation, depth can be reconstructed from RGB alone, but contact force, sound, and temperature leave no signature in the visible spectrum. To include these physical quantities in the VLA policy input, researchers must add an additional sensor, and several studies have pursued this approach~ huang2025tactile,cheng2026omnivtla,jones2025beyond,guo2025omnivla . Yet, adding a new sensor is costly. A new modality requires collecting additional robot data~ wang2026vision and retraining the model to recover the pretrained alignment~ li2026pointvla,sun2025geovla . Furthermore, for deployment, platforms without the additional sensor require a separate policy~ zhang2026core . In VLA-based navigation, geometric quantities, such as goal coordinates and poses, are directly incorporated into the policy~ zhang2026qwen,liu2025citywalker,hirose2025omnivla,xue2026omninav , or 3D structure is reconstructed from RGB images~ zeng2026janusvln,liu2026span . In some cases, additional geometric sensors fall outside the VLA policy. For example, NaVILA~ cheng2025navila leverages LiDAR readings for its locomotion controller, while the VLA policy itself relies only on visual input. However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior research has used non-geometric physical quantities as input to VLA navigation. Visual Prompting Overlaying marks on input images has proven effective for guiding a model's interpretation. BYOVLA inpaints a task-irrelevant region to recover the nominal behavior under visual distraction~ hancock2025run , and Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) applies a tint to the personalized target object~ lee2026bring . For navigation, waypoint prediction can be enhanced by placing markers on a navigable region~ chen2025affordances , grounding goal pixels~ bao2026goal2pixel , or, in concurrent work, segmenting traversable (green) and non-traversable (red) regions~ szvoren2026green . These visual prompts emphasize, remove, or label information already present in input images. In contrast, we inject visual context entirely absent from the scene: a moving virtual obstacle. The policy maps an RGB observation and a language instruction to an action . PG-VP overlays a virtual obstacle in the direction , converting into . The action is then inferred as , while the policy weights and language instruction remain unchanged. When no hazard is detected, . Figure~ fig:overall illustrates the overall flow. Integrated Robotic Multimodal Perception System subsec:integrated_robotic_multimodal_system Identifying proximal invisible hazards requires auxiliary sensing beyond RGB vision. Our multimodal perception system combines RGB, radiation, and thermal sensing modalities, with radiation and temperature serving as the target non-geometric physical quantities. The vision system consists of a front-facing wide-angle ELP global-shutter camera with a horizontal field of view (HFOV) and two webcams with a HFOV. The two webcams are yawed by relative to the robot's forward direction to provide left and right views. For temperature detection, we use two FLIR Lepton 3.5 radiometric thermal camera modules, each mounted on a PureThermal Mini Pro JST-SR carrier board. To extend horizontal thermal coverage, we mount the two sensors side by side and yaw them outward from the robot's forward direction. With HFOV for each sensor, this configuration provides a nominal combined HFOV of , with a overlap in the central region. All sensors are mounted on a Unitree Go2 EDU quadruped robot. Because of hardware compatibility constraints, the radiation and thermal sensors connect to an external Windows-based single-board computer (SBC). The latest radiation and thermal measurements are transmitted to a Redis server running on the robot's onboard computer, making them available in real time. title: OpenSplatGraph: From Dense Semantic Maps to Structured Scene Graphs for Open-Vocabulary Robot Perception
summary: Dense 3D mapping with semantic understanding is essential for robotic perception in complex environments. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting-based mapping approaches enable high-fidelity geometry and efficient open-vocabulary perception, but typically represent semantics as unstructured feature fields that limit object-centric reasoning. In contrast, 3D scene graphs explicitly model objects and their relationships for structured reasoning, but are commonly constructed from sparse geometric representations that do not fully exploit dense semantic maps. In this work, we present OpenSplatGraph, a unified framework that constructs persistent 3D scene graphs directly from an online Gaussian-based open-vocabulary semantic map. The proposed framework augments the dense semantic map with a reliability-aware semantic field that maintains lightweight observation statistics for confidence-aware, query-conditioned object extraction. Extracted object instances are associated with persistent graph nodes, allowing object attributes and relationships to be incrementally updated across observations and queries. By tightly coupling dense semantic mapping with persistent object-centric representations, our framework supports both language-guided object grounding and structured relational reasoning while preserving the geometric fidelity of Gaussian-based mapping. Comprehensive evaluations on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments demonstrate that OpenSplatGraph achieves competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks. Project page: https://csiro-robotics.github.io/OpenSplatGraph.

Introduction sec:intro Dense 3D mapping with semantic understanding is fundamental to robotic perception, supporting navigation, manipulation, and interaction in complex environments~ huang2023visual,jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion,zhou2024navgpt . Recent advances in vision-language foundation models~ radford2021learning,li2022blip have further enabled open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding that responds to natural language queries and generalizes to previously unseen objects. Meanwhile, ~ kerbl20233d has established an efficient representation for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction with real-time rendering. Online GS-based mapping systems~ keetha2024splatam,matsuki2024gaussian,ha2024rgbd integrate Gaussian primitives with for geometrically consistent mapping. Building on this representation, open-vocabulary approaches~ qin2024langsplat,wu2024opengaussian,yang2025opengs,nguyen2026ilov3splat incorporate vision-language features into dense Gaussian maps, enabling language-guided retrieval of scene regions. However, semantics are often represented as unstructured per-voxel or per-Gaussian feature fields rather than explicit object-level entities. Consequently, they provide limited support for object-centric reasoning and modeling inter-object relationships. In parallel, address this limitation by representing environments as graphs whose nodes correspond to objects and whose edges encode semantic or spatial relationships~ armeni20193d . Recent advances have extended scene graphs to online incremental systems~ wu2021scenegraphfusion,hughes2022hydra , open-vocabulary reasoning~ gu2024conceptgraphs,koch2024open3dsg,maggio2024clio , and large-scale robotic applications~ deng2024opengraph,yin2024sg . Most open-vocabulary scene graph methods construct graphs from RGB-D observations by projecting 2D detections into point clouds or meshes. While these approaches provide compact and interpretable scene abstractions for reasoning, they typically rely on sparse geometric representations that cannot fully exploit the dense geometric and semantic information available in Gaussian-based maps. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:comparison , robotic systems benefit from these two complementary scene representations. Dense geometric-semantic maps provide high-fidelity 3D reconstruction for language-grounded perception and localization, whereas object-centric scene graphs explicitly model objects and their relationships for structured reasoning and task planning. However, existing approaches typically emphasize one representation over the other, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve both high-fidelity mapping and structured scene understanding. In this paper, we propose , a framework that bridges these two paradigms by grounding 3D scene graphs directly in an online open-vocabulary semantic map. Rather than treating the dense semantic field and the scene graph as alternative representations, we maintain both throughout operation, allowing each to serve a complementary role. The dense semantic map preserves fine-grained geometric and semantic information for open-vocabulary perception, while the scene graph incrementally accumulates persistent object-centric knowledge for structured reasoning. To support object construction, we introduce a reliability-aware semantic field that augments the dense semantic map with lightweight observation statistics, enabling confidence-aware ranking of query-conditioned object instances. Extracted object instances are assigned persistent identities and incrementally incorporated into a 3D scene graph, allowing object attributes and relationships to be consistently accumulated across multiple queries. By jointly maintaining these two representations, preserves the geometric fidelity of dense mapping while progressively constructing an interpretable object-centric representation for language grounding, relational reasoning, and downstream robotic tasks. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce , a unified framework that constructs persistent 3D scene graphs directly from online open-vocabulary Gaussian semantic maps, enabling high-fidelity dense mapping and structured scene understanding within a single system. We propose a reliability-aware semantic field that leverages lightweight per-voxel observation statistics for robust query-conditioned object extraction under partial observations and semantic ambiguity. We design a scene graph construction strategy that associates extracted object instances with persistent identities and incrementally accumulates object-centric knowledge across queries for structured relational reasoning. We validate the framework on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks. Related Work sec:related Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Understanding Vision-language foundation models~ radford2021learning,li2022blip have enabled open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding by aligning visual representations with natural language. Early methods, such as PointCLIP~ zhang2022pointclip and ConceptFusion~ jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion , leverage language features for point cloud understanding, while LERF~ kerr2023lerf extends language-guided retrieval to representations. More recently, ~ kerbl20233d has emerged as an efficient representation for open-vocabulary 3D perception and robotic applications~ nguyen2026ilov3splat,zielinski2026neo . Representative methods, including LangSplat~ qin2024langsplat , LEGaussian~ shi2024language , OpenGaussian~ wu2024opengaussian , and InstanceGaussian~ li2025instancegaussian , associate language features with Gaussian primitives for open-vocabulary querying. However, these methods primarily represent semantics as unstructured feature fields, limiting their support for object-centric and relational reasoning. 3D Gaussian-Based Scene Mapping has been integrated into systems for efficient online dense mapping and high-fidelity rendering. Methods such as SplaTAM~ keetha2024splatam , MonoGS~ matsuki2024gaussian , and GS-ICP SLAM~ ha2024rgbd jointly optimize Gaussian representations and camera poses for real-time reconstruction. Subsequent works incorporate semantic information through supervised labels~ li2024sgs,zhu2025semgauss or open-vocabulary features, as demonstrated by OpenGS-Fusion~ yang2025opengs . These approaches provide geometrically accurate and semantically rich maps for robotic perception. However, they primarily focus on online reconstruction and semantic fusion, without explicitly maintaining persistent object-centric representations for structured reasoning and task planning. 3D Scene Graphs ~ armeni20193d represent objects as nodes and their relationships as edges, providing interpretable scene abstractions for planning and human-robot interaction~ rana2023sayplan,werby2024hierarchical . Recent advances~ catalano20253d highlight rapid progress from online incremental graph construction~ hughes2022hydra,wu2021scenegraphfusion to open-vocabulary scene understanding through ConceptGraphs~ gu2024conceptgraphs , Open3DSG~ koch2024open3dsg , and Clio~ maggio2024clio , and large-scale robotic applications~ deng2024opengraph,yin2024sg . These methods typically construct graphs from point clouds or meshes, providing compact object-centric representations for downstream reasoning. Despite these advances, many open-vocabulary approaches infer object relationships from 2D observations using , resulting in graph representations that are weakly grounded in dense 3D geometry. Recent studies~ ge2025dynamicgsg,wang2025gaussiangraph have explored grounding scene graphs directly in Gaussian representations. Our work follows this emerging direction but adopts a different architectural perspective. Rather than treating the dense maps and the scene graph as alternative world models, we explicitly maintain both throughout operation. The dense semantic field serves as the geometric and semantic foundation for reliable object extraction, while the scene graph incrementally accumulates object-centric knowledge for structured and relational reasoning. Methodology sec:method We propose , a unified framework that jointly maintains a dense open-vocabulary semantic field and a persistent 3D scene graph throughout online operation. The dense semantic field serves as a geometrically consistent foundation for query-conditioned object extraction, while the scene graph incrementally accumulates object-centric knowledge to support structured reasoning across multiple queries. Rather than maintaining a fixed object inventory, extracts objects on demand from language queries by grouping spatially and semantically consistent regions in the semantic field. Extracted instances are associated with persistent graph nodes and enriched with semantic and relational information as the map evolves. In this way, preserves the fidelity of dense semantic mapping while progressively constructing an interpretable scene representation for downstream robotic tasks. An overview of the framework is shown in Fig.~ fig:overview . Reliability-Aware Semantic Field sec:method:semantic The dense semantic field forms the perception layer of , providing a geometrically consistent representation for query-conditioned object extraction. Built upon an online open-vocabulary Gaussian semantic map, the field maintains fused semantic features together with lightweight reliability statistics that characterize the quality of semantic observations. title: BiGym 2.0: Benchmarking Learned and Agent-Developed Policies for Humanoid Household Manipulation
summary: Humanoid household manipulation requires the arms to act while the body balances, steps and changes posture. We present BiGym 2.0, an adaptation of BiGym for the Unitree G1 across 20 household tasks using a unified whole-body controller for demonstration and evaluation. The suite provides 60 native human virtual-reality demonstrations per task with synchronised multi-camera views and full-body execution records. We benchmark vision-language-action fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning, and cold-start coding agents given the interaction budget of online reinforcement learning. With the same onboard views, proprioception and whole-body controller for every method, vision-language-action fine-tuning has the highest nine-task mean, and agent-developed programs outperform every demo-driven reinforcement learning baseline on this mean and lead on bimanual reaching. Cross-workspace stacking remains open, $π_{0.5}$ stays low on pick-box, and multi-object transport is hard for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and coding agents. All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced at https://github.com/swirl-uk/BiGym2.

All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced at . Introduction Humanoid robots are expected to perform household tasks that combine walking with manipulation. Carrying an object, reaching into a dishwasher and changing working height require the arms to act while the legs support and move the body. Today, robot capabilities are produced along two distinct routes: data-driven policy learning (VLAs, imitation learning and demo-driven RL) and agentic policy development (coding agents synthesising executable programs from environment APIs). Recent simulation platforms support G1 loco-manipulation through learned controllers~ simple2026,humanoidmimicgen2026,humanoidarena2026 , but no current benchmark combines household tasks, native human demonstrations collected through active whole-body control, deterministic restoration of controller state, and common evaluation of learned and agent-developed policies. This combination matters because both routes must confront the same physical execution stack: unlike a wheeled base that executes velocity commands directly, a walking controller realises them through dynamic gaits that lag, oscillate and perturb the torso~ gysin2003grip,sato2021iros,steadytray2026 . We ask what each route can reliably complete under this execution condition, where their capabilities diverge and where they fail together. BiGym~ chernyadev2024bigym provides the closest foundation: 40 H1 household tasks with human virtual reality (VR) demonstrations. It offers a 23-dimensional full-joint whole-body mode and a mobile-bimanual mode, but its released demonstrations use the latter. Its floating base directly commands body translation, height and yaw, with planar motion equivalent to an omnidirectional autonomous mobile robot (AMR) base (Fig.~ fig:diff ). This separation isolates mobile-bimanual learning from locomotion control. We instead study legged execution, where gait and balance dynamics couple directly into manipulation. We modify BiGym for the G1 by adapting task geometry, collecting demonstrations through active whole-body control, restoring controller state at evaluation, and supporting learned and agent-developed policies. Coding agents synthesise robot policies by composing perception, kinematics and control APIs into executable programs~ liang2023code,fu2026capx,elmaaroufi2026rho,lu2026aspire . We formulate a cold-start capability audit: given environment APIs and three synchronised camera views of a single human demonstration, can a coding agent develop reliable household programs within a bounded interaction budget? To match the learned policies, the agent takes three onboard views and proprioception as input and outputs the same arm, gripper and body commands, with no camera calibration or inverse-kinematics tools. This cold-start setting measures how reliably an agent develops a program without a pre-built skill library, and gives a baseline against which later work can measure skill accumulation. We present , a G1 household loco-manipulation benchmark based on BiGym. Our contributions are: (i) adapting tasks to the G1 workspace, integrating frozen GR00T-WBC walking and balance policies~ nvidiawbc , and collecting native human VR demonstrations per task through the same controller used for evaluation (Fig.~ fig:tasks , Section~ sec:benchmark ); (ii) comparing VLA fine-tuning, imitation learning, online and offline demo-driven RL on nine representative tasks with deterministic evaluation that restores controller states (Table~ tab:main , Section~ sec:experiments ); (iii) auditing coding agents (GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5) under matched observation and action interfaces ( views, direct joint control, no IK tools), showing that their programs lead on bimanual reaching, where a program can control each arm separately, and evaluating a tool-augmented cold-start reference to quantify the benefit of classical robotics tooling (Section~ sec:agent ); and (iv) showing that vision-language-action fine-tuning leads plate and cup transport but not box transport, that multi-object transport remains difficult for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and code synthesis, and that cross-workspace stacking remains an open frontier (Sections~ sec:experiments and~ sec:agent ). title: The Robot Is Not Its Description: GaugeBench for Representation Robustness in Morphology-Aware Policies
summary: A robot description does more than specify a physical mechanism: it also encodes arbitrary conventions, such as joint-axis direction, joint-angle zero, and the order and names of links and joints. Morphology-aware policies consume interfaces built from these descriptions, yet cross-embodiment evaluation typically changes the robot while keeping those conventions fixed. This leaves a simple question unanswered: does behavior survive when the robot stays fixed but its description changes? GaugeBench isolates this case by rewriting a fixed mechanism under physically equivalent conventions, verifying that its physics and policy interface are preserved, and then evaluating the same policy weights. The result is stark: three MetaMorph policies score 4030.6 on 80 familiar robots, but only 51.6 when those same robots are equivalently re-described, while 98 genuinely held-out robots score 1489.6. A new description can therefore be more damaging than a new robot. Tracing the failure reveals that axis reversal alone reproduces the collapse, joint-angle zero changes are nearly harmless, and reordering lies between them; moreover, changing joint-state and torque coordinates alone is sufficient to cause the failure, while changing description-derived features alone is not. The same phenomenon appears in ModuMorph and an unrelated PyBullet framework. Yet it is not irreversible: exact two-description transport restores the original controller, and training across equivalent axis conventions raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6% to 80.6%. Together, these results separate mechanism robustness from representation robustness and show that cross-embodiment evaluation should test both.

Introduction One physical mechanism admits many numerical descriptions. Two files can agree on every link, mass, inertia, and joint placement and still disagree on the direction an engineer called positive for a hinge, on the pose that hinge calls zero, and on the order and names of parts. Classical rigid-body equations transform covariantly under a consistent change of generalized coordinates, so a textbook routine returns the same world-frame motion from either file~ featherstone2008rigid, murray2017mathematical . A robot is a mechanism. A description is one way of writing it down. Cross-embodiment robot learning increasingly conditions a single policy on a structured robot description, and tests it by changing the robot. Robustness here has two distinct axes, and that practice measures only one of them. Mechanism robustness asks whether a policy transfers from the machines it trained on to a new one, . Representation robustness asks whether it preserves behavior when one fixed mechanism is expressed by two physically equivalent descriptions and , with the machine itself untouched. Existing cross-robot benchmarks probe the first while keeping one description convention per robot~ parakh2025anybody . GaugeBench isolates the second (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Nothing here assumes that an unconstrained neural policy should be invariant to a coordinate convention it never saw. In general, it has no reason to be. The question is what that costs an evaluation. Cross-embodiment results are read as evidence that a policy has learned something about robots, and we ask how much of that evidence rests on a convention the benchmark never varies. Answering it requires a mechanism that stays fixed while its description changes. The answer is not graceful degradation. Across three MetaMorph policies, mean return falls from 4030.6 on 80 familiar robots to 51.6 on those same robots under certified equivalent descriptions, while 98 physically held-out robots from the same procedural generator return 1489.6. Across the three baseline policy families we evaluate, every policy loses more from re-describing a robot it was trained on than from meeting the held-out population. A new robot can be easier than a new description of the same robot. We call this comparison the Same-Robot Paradox. Changing the conventions one at a time shows that a single one is enough. Reversing joint-axis directions retains 3.6 percent of the original return against 97.7 for joint-angle zeros and 35.8 for reordering, and driving axis reversal's two channels separately, joint-state and torque coordinates alone retain 2.5 percent while description-derived features alone retain 37.6 percent. The effect is not specific to one implementation, reproducing on ModuMorph and, under axis reversal alone, on released policies from an unrelated line of work on modular robot control running in PyBullet. Exact interface transport then recovers the original controller with unchanged weights, and training over randomly drawn equivalent axis conventions raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6 to 80.6 percent. : First, an evaluation axis. GaugeBench separates mechanism robustness from representation robustness, scoring fixed morphology-aware policies on descriptions whose physics and policy interface are certified equivalent before any episode is run. Second, a same-robot representation failure, and which channel reproduces it. An equivalent description of a familiar robot costs these policies more than a physically held-out robot, and controlled interventions show that changing joint-state and action coordinates alone reproduces the collapse while changing description-derived features alone does not. Third, generality and response. The failure reproduces on ModuMorph and on an independent PyBullet system. Exact transport recovers the original controller with unchanged weights, and axis-convention randomization raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6 to 80.6 percent for the one convention family it samples. Related Work Morphology-aware policy learning MetaMorph~ gupta2022metamorph tokenizes a kinematic graph for a Transformer, ModuMorph~ xiong2023modumorph modulates a shared backbone with per-robot context, and Body Transformer~ sferrazza2024bodytransformer masks attention by embodiment graph, each treating the description as a stand-in for the robot under one convention per machine. Current work extends the interface to morphology tokens~ suzuki2026embedding and morphology-conditioned world models~ danesh2026morphology , while cross-embodiment benchmarks evaluate transfer to novel embodiments~ parakh2025anybody . Policies conditioned on images and language~ open_x_embodiment2023, pi0_2024 fix proprioception and action ordering in a comparable way, though we do not transform those interfaces and make no claim about them. We evaluate released systems whose interfaces can be reproduced and transformed exactly, which is what makes a causal test possible. Symmetry, equivariance, and canonicalization In classical rigid-body mechanics, these conventions are bookkeeping, and physical predictions do not depend on which one is chosen~ featherstone2008rigid, murray2017mathematical . Whether learned policies that consume descriptions inherit that independence is an empirical question. Four changes are easy to conflate. Cross-robot benchmarks vary the mechanism. Geometric deep learning handles a rigid motion of a whole scene under global symmetry~ bronstein2021geometric , with gauge-equivariant networks addressing tangent-frame choice on manifolds~ cohen2019gauge . Morphological symmetry exploits a symmetry a mechanism genuinely has, such as left--right limb pairs~ wei2025beyond . Ours is the fourth: a rewrite of one fixed mechanism's numbers, which leaves the mechanism and its asymmetries where they were and so exists for every robot, symmetric or not. Repairing such a rewrite is standard machinery, and we claim no novelty for it. Conjugating a fixed policy by an exact interface transport is the lifted policy of an MDP isomorphism~ vanderpol2020mdp . Canonicalization maps an input to a canonical representative, applies a base model, and transports the output back, whether by frame averaging~ puny2022frame , a learned canonicalizer~ kaba2023equivariance , or an wrapper around a trained manipulation policy~ deng2025eqbot . Proposition~ thm:repair only specializes that construction to the full policy-visible input. What is new here is the evaluation axis: certifying physically equivalent descriptions before scoring, measuring what re-description costs against what a new mechanism costs, decomposing that cost by convention, and replicating it across independent systems. Closest recent work Tai~ tai2026sameweights shows that one vision--language--action checkpoint becomes a different controller when its action-scaling metadata changes, so fixed weights can depend on non-physical metadata. That change also alters the physical action produced, so the controller itself is not preserved. We instead certify physical equivalence before evaluation and put the loss in context against held-out robots. Yang and Hatton~ yang2026coordinate make inverse-dynamics identification independent of the generalized-coordinate chart. Their object is a model-fitting objective scored by prediction accuracy, whereas ours is a closed-loop policy scored by task behavior. Robot Description Equivalence Descriptions and physical equivalence Let a mechanism be described by , with links , joints , parent-to-child frames , unit screw axes , masses, centre-of-mass offsets, inertias, and an identifier assignment naming links and joints. The evaluated policies do not consume directly. They consume a policy interface built from it: per-part feature vectors in the order the file lists them, graph edges, padding masks, and per-joint features, alongside the robot state and task observation. Write for everything the policy sees and for the action. The distinction carries the paper's causal result, because a description change can reach the interface through description-derived features, through joint-state and action coordinates, or both. [Physical equivalence] A transformation carrying to is physically equivalent if it acts by an invertible change of generalized coordinates , extended to joint velocities and torques, under which both descriptions realize the same mechanism in exact arithmetic. Chart-independent quantities agree directly: world-frame link and contact geometry, tip velocity, kinetic energy, and the trajectory a matched torque sequence produces. Chart-dependent ones agree only after transport by , which is how spatial Jacobians, the mass matrix, inverse dynamics, and forward accelerations are compared, since each transforms covariantly. def:equiv Physical equivalence is a property of the descriptions. What a policy meets is the pair of invertible conversions and that induces on the complete policy interface and on actions. Definition~ def:equiv is a statement about exact arithmetic. What can be checked is an implementation of it. GaugeBench certifies each rewrite numerically over a 100-step rollout from the environment's reset pose under actuator commands drawn uniformly from per step. Each quantity in Definition~ def:equiv is checked separately rather than pooled, in its own units and after transport where it depends on the chart, and its largest componentwise absolute difference must stay within an absolute . Certification runs in the same simulator configuration used to score the policy, which is part of the claim, because a rewrite can preserve physics under one contact setting and not another, as Sec.~ sec:independent shows. Exact mathematics and floating-point code differ slightly. title: ESP: Energy-Score Policy for One-Step Multimodal Action Generation
summary: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching have been increasingly adopted in vision-language-action (VLA) policies for their ability to capture diverse behaviors, including multiple valid action sequences under the same observation and instruction. Their iterative sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to generate each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control. We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), a teacher-free approach that maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. ESP trains the action head with the energy score rather than mean squared error. Whereas squared-error regression targets the conditional mean, the energy score is strictly proper: its expected value is uniquely minimized by the target distribution. This provides a principled objective for learning multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling, with exact recovery at the population optimum when the model can represent the target distribution. Experiments on both simulation and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline. These results support direct distributional learning as an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies.
full_text: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching have been increasingly adopted in vision-language-action (VLA) policies for their ability to capture diverse behaviors, including multiple valid action sequences under the same observation and instruction. Their iterative sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to generate each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control. We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), a teacher-free approach that maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. ESP trains the action head with the energy score rather than mean squared error. Whereas squared-error regression targets the conditional mean, the energy score is strictly proper: its expected value is uniquely minimized by the target distribution. This provides a principled objective for learning multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling, with exact recovery at the population optimum when the model can represent the target distribution. Experiments on both simulation and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline. These results support direct distributional learning as an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies. Project page Introduction sec:intro Diffusion and flow matching models are increasingly used in robot policies, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, to represent diverse behaviors conditioned on observations and instructions~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . These models can capture multiple valid action sequences for the same context rather than restrict the policy to a single deterministic prediction. Their standard sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to transform noise into an action chunk. Therefore, their action generation is inherently time-consuming, motivating faster one-step action generation with a single network evaluation. We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), where we cast conditional action generation as strictly proper distributional regression and generate an action chunk in a single network evaluation ( ). The proposed ESP predicts the entire multimodal distribution of actions that are valid for a given context. We use the energy-score objective~ gneiting2007strictly,bouchacourt2016disco ; in expectation over the data, it becomes smallest exactly when the generated actions match the distribution of the training data (demonstrations), and larger for every other distribution. Unlike previous one-step and few-step approaches, such as distillation and consistency-based methods~ yin2024onestep,song2023consistency,zhang2025flowpolicy,chen2026meanflowvla , ESP directly trains on the training data alone in a single stage, with no pretrained teacher, no trajectory or velocity targets, and no auxiliary critic. Different from recent teacher-free generators~ deng2026drifting,gladstone2026explorative , whose objectives can also be minimized by distributions other than the training one, ESP retains this uniqueness while keeping single-evaluation inference. To apply ESP to an existing VLA model, we retain its pretrained vision-language backbone and policy conditioning unchanged and replace its action head with our ESP for one-step action generation. The VLM backbone can remain frozen while the ESP action-head parameters are trained without teacher distillation. For each training context, we generate several action chunks from different noise inputs, and the energy score evaluates the generated chunks against the demonstrated chunk and against one another. At inference, one single noise draw produces one action chunk in one network evaluation, without multi-step numerical integration or candidate ranking. Experiments on synthetic regression and the LIBERO manipulation benchmark as well as real-robot experiments demonstrate that ESP can generate multimodal actions in a single network evaluation and achieves task success comparable to the flow matching baseline with substantially lower action-generation latency. These results establish energy-score training as an effective approach to fast, one-step generative action policies. . Our chief contributions are: We cast conditional action generation as strictly proper distributional regression and propose an energy-score policy (ESP) for action generation. Unlike diffusion/flow matching policy that requires multi-step integration, our ESP can learn the conditional noise-to-action generation in a single network evaluation, leading to faster action inference, while retaining the competitive task success rate. With the same action-head architecture, in one-step, ESP achieves a competitive task success rate on LIBERO compared with the multi-step flow matching policy. Increasing the number of action-head parameters further improves the mean success rate given the same inference time budget to the flow matching policy. Related Work sec:related Learning robot actions from demonstrations is a conditional distribution modeling problem: the same observation and instruction can correspond to several valid behaviors. We review multimodal prediction and generative policies, followed by objectives for efficient one-step generation. prediction and generative action policies. Early approaches modeled multimodal conditional distributions with mixture density networks~ bishop1994mixture , conditional latent-variable models~ sohn2015learning , and conditional adversarial generators~ mirza2014conditional . Generative moment matching networks~ li2015generative train feedforward generators using Gaussian-kernel MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)~ dziugaite2015training . These Gaussian-kernel MMD objectives require selecting a kernel bandwidth, whereas our energy-score objective does not require the kernel-bandwidth hyperparameter. Diffusion and flow matching subsequently emerged as expressive high-dimensional samplers that transport noise to data through a learned denoising process or vector field~ ho2020denoising,song2021scorebased,lipman2023flow . Representing such multimodal, high-dimensional distributions is particularly relevant to robot action prediction, where the same visual observation and language instruction can correspond to several successful behaviors. Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy models action sequences with conditional denoising, while more recent VLAs such as ~ black2024pi0 , ~ intelligence2025pi05 , GR00T N1~ nvidia2025gr00t , and FLOWER~ reuss2025flower use flow matching to generate action chunks. These methods can represent multimodal action distributions, but require multiple network evaluations. Our work preserves the stochastic multimodal action representation while achieving action generation only with a single network evaluation. -step generation and distributional objectives. Reducing the cost of iterative generation has motivated distillation, consistency training, and objectives designed for few-step or one-step sampling. Distillation methods compress a multi-step model into a shorter sampler~ yin2024onestep , while consistency models can learn outputs that agree along a diffusion trajectory~ song2023consistency . In robot learning, FlowPolicy imposes self-consistency on a flow field~ zhang2025flowpolicy , MeanFlow-VLA learns an average velocity~ chen2026meanflowvla , and Let It Be Simple retains flow matching while emphasizing the high-noise regime used by one-step inference~ chen2026letitbesimple . Drifting methods construct a training target by moving the generator's own samples toward the data with a data-adaptive drift, then train the generator to match this detached (stop-gradient) target~ deng2026drifting,zuo2026driftvla . However, without additional assumptions, even globally minimizing the ideal population drifting loss does not guarantee that the generated distribution matches the data distribution~ deng2026drifting . Efficiency alone, however, leaves open how a direct one-step generator should learn a multimodal distribution. Multiple-choice learning, multiple-hypothesis prediction, and IMLE emphasize the best-matching candidates through hard or relaxed assignments~ guzmanrivera2012mcl,lee2016smcl,rupprecht2017mhp,li2018implicit . Forward XM follows this candidate-selection principle: for each training example, it evaluates the loss under several sampled noise inputs and updates the generator using the lowest-loss candidate~ gladstone2026explorative . While effective, with a fixed finite candidate budget, the hard-min endpoint-distance objective is not, in general, strictly proper: its minimum does not necessarily correspond to the data distribution. Energy-score training instead follows the statistical lineage of proper scoring rules. The multivariate energy score combines distances to the observation with pairwise distances between generated samples. Under finite first moments, its expected value is uniquely minimized by the data distribution~ gneiting2007strictly . DISCO Nets train conditional generators using an energy-score objective and apply them to 3D hand pose estimation from depth images~ bouchacourt2016disco . We also use this established objective for one-step action generation, scoring the conditional action samples produced by the deployed action head. Minimizing its expected value recovers the target conditional distribution when the model can represent it. Method sec:method At each control step, we seek to sample from the demonstrated conditional action distribution without integrating a learned sampling trajectory. Rather than learning a time-dependent velocity field and selecting a numerical solver, we parameterize the action generator itself. title: StairVLA: Stage-Aware Hierarchical Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly rely on diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads to generate continuous robot actions. These action heads typically process the denoising trajectory in a largely uniform manner. However, we observe that the conditioning focus naturally shifts across denoising stages: early stages combine language instructions and visual observations to establish a coarse action trajectory, whereas later stages place greater emphasis on current visual observations for action alignment. Based on this insight, we introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local refinement. A high-level VLA performs early denoising to produce a reusable long-horizon partially denoised action trajectory, while a lightweight refiner operates at a higher frequency to refine local action chunks using the latest observations. This design amortizes expensive high-level VLA computation while preserving frequent closed-loop correction. On LIBERO, our GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% while reducing amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk. More broadly, across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, StairVLA consistently reduces inference cost while maintaining strong task performance.

Project page: Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of robot manipulation tasks kim2024openvla , combining vision-language understanding with generative action heads to translate multimodal context into continuous robot actions black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t . Specifically, these diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads are conditioned on language instructions, visual observations, and robot states to progressively transform noise into executable action trajectories chi2025diffusion . Despite this progressive generation process, multimodal conditioning is typically applied throughout the entire denoising trajectory, leaving open whether different types of conditioning information should always be processed together during action generation. Intuitively, language instructions typically specify task intent that remains stable over many control steps, whereas visual observations and robot states continuously change during execution. Task-level information therefore need not be processed as frequently as the feedback required for precise closed-loop control. Existing hierarchical VLAs exploit this temporal asymmetry by processing high-level information at a lower frequency and communicating it to higher-frequency controllers through subgoals, waypoints, macro-actions, or learned representations Fang2024MOKAOR,li2025hamster,wei2026libra, du2026cf . Such hierarchies are typically introduced through externally designed representations or model components. This leads to our central question: can such a hierarchy arise directly from the generative action process itself? In practice, we observe that the denoising trajectory itself already exhibits such a structure. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation_hierarchical_generation , substantial action structure emerges well before denoising is complete, while the interaction between evolving action and multimodal conditioning continues to change throughout denoising stages. Intermediate actions are therefore not merely noisy versions of the final prediction: they already encode meaningful structure, even as subsequent denoising continues to reshape them toward execution. This reveals a natural stage dependence in generative VLA action formation, with different denoising stages serving distinct functional roles. This behavior is also consistent with the coarse-to-fine progression commonly observed in generative denoising balaji2022ediffi,falck2025fourierspaceperspectivediffusion . This observation suggests a direct way to exploit the hierarchy already present in denoising: expensive task conditioning can be concentrated in less frequent early-stage generation, while later stages perform frequent local refinement using up-to-date observations. However, this separation raises a key challenge: how can the refiner preserve task information without repeatedly processing the full instruction? Our key insight is that partially denoised actions themselves can bridge the two stages. By the end of early denoising, they already encode task-relevant action structure while remaining open to further refinement. The low-level refiner can therefore operate directly on these intermediate actions together with the latest observation, preserving high-level task information without repeatedly processing the full instruction. Based on this insight, we introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework. A high-level VLA performs the early denoising stages over a long-horizon action trajectory and outputs partially denoised actions that are cached across multiple control steps. For each local chunk, a lightweight refiner takes the corresponding local action segment together with the latest observation and cached high-level context, and completes the remaining refinement before execution. This allows expensive task-conditioned generation to be reused across multiple control steps while keeping local actions responsive to the evolving environment. Importantly, the two stages communicate directly through intermediate states of the generative action trajectory, rather than through an externally designed action abstraction. We evaluate our approach across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot manipulation tasks. On LIBERO, our GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5 to 97.8 while reducing amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk, with consistent performance-efficiency gains on a -style VLA backbone. Although performance gradually degrades as the reuse horizon increases, further analysis shows that StairVLA maintains strong performance over longer high-level reuse horizons than prior hierarchical VLA methods. In summary, our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*, nosep] We reveal stage dependence in generative VLA action formation, showing that task-relevant action structure emerges progressively while the role of multimodal conditioning evolves throughout denoising. We introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local observation-conditioned refinement. We validate the proposed design across two generative VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, demonstrating substantially reduced inference cost while maintaining strong task performance. Related work sec:related_work Action Chunking and Unified VLA Models. Unified VLA models typically map language instructions, visual observations, and robot states into action sequences within a single policy. Recent VLA models further adopt generative action heads based on diffusion or flow matching to produce continuous actions~ black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t,chi2025diffusion . These methods commonly use action chunking, predicting a sequence of future actions rather than a single-step action to improve temporal consistency and reduce policy invocation frequency~ Zhao-RSS-23,chi2025diffusion . However, action chunking introduces an inherent horizon trade-off: short chunks require frequent invocation of computationally expensive VLMs, while long chunks weaken closed-loop feedback and real-time correction during execution~ zhang2025action . Therefore, processing different information and generating actions at a single temporal scale may be unnecessarily restrictive. Hierarchical VLA Models. Recent works increasingly adopt hierarchical structures to bridge high-level task understanding and low-level robot control. Earlier methods use explicit intermediate goals to guide low-level policies, such as subgoals, waypoints, keypoints, or language sub-instructions~ hu2023look,Fang2024MOKAOR,li2025hamster,shi2025hi . More recent works further integrate this hierarchy into the model architecture and explore different high-to-low-level interfaces, including VLM tokens, learned features, discrete macro-actions, and coarse action representations~ cui2025openhelix,guo2026brain,wei2026libra,wu2026coarse . Other dual-system approaches focus more explicitly on temporal organization, using event-driven high-level updates or allowing different levels to operate at different frequencies~ chen2026streamvla,sun2026unifs . Despite their different forms, these methods highlight a common design question in hierarchical VLA: how should high-level task intent be transferred to low-level action generation? Rather than using manually designed or learned interfaces, we directly leverage intermediate states formed during action generation as a natural high-to-low-level interface. Generative Action Models and Intermediate Denoising States. Diffusion- and flow-based generation progressively transforms noise into executable actions. In both generative modeling and robot policies, prior works assign different denoising experts to different sampling stages to better accommodate stage-specific generation requirements~ balaji2022ediffi,zhang2024improving,reuss2025efficient,du2026cf,niu2026t . Another line of work reuses partially denoised trajectories or constructs better warm starts to reduce redundant sampling and control latency~ hoeg2025fast,chen2025responsive,li2026step . Our method further uses partially denoised actions to transfer task intent across stages, enabling high-level coarse action generation and local refinement to use different conditioning and operate at different frequencies. Method sec:method Overview As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:method_comparison , we decompose VLA action generation into two stages that operate at different frequencies. The high-level VLA is invoked at a lower frequency to perform early denoising and produce a long-horizon partially denoised action trajectory, which is reused across multiple local action chunks. The low-level refiner runs at a higher frequency, taking the corresponding local action segment and the latest visual observation to produce an executable action chunk. This design reduces repeated VLM computation while preserving closed-loop correction with updated observations. Our framework is designed to be applicable to flow-matching-based generative VLAs and is trained in two stages. The high-level VLA retains the original VLA architecture with an extended action horizon. The lightweight refiner is the main additional module and follows the design of the VLA action head. It starts from partially denoised actions produced by the trained high-level VLA and performs local refinement using current observations. The high-level generation, refiner architecture and training, and multi-rate inference procedures are detailed in the following subsections. High-Level Intent Trajectory Generation sec:high_level_generation The high-level VLA retains the original generative architecture and training objective, while extending the action horizon to . Taking a flow-matching VLA as an example, training constructs a continuous path between Gaussian noise and the ground-truth : The corresponding target velocity is Given the intermediate action state , denoising progress , and VLM conditioning feature , the action head is trained to predict this velocity: At inference time, action generation starts from random noise, , and iteratively updates the action state by repeatedly predicting the velocity: A standard VLA continues this process until to obtain the final executable action trajectory. In contrast, we terminate the high-level generation at and use the resulting partially denoised trajectory

title: Efficient Gaussian Splatting Sequence Compression with Standard Video Codecs
summary: This paper presents a novel effective Gaussian Splatting (GS) sequence Compression method that utilizes the Video codec (GSCV). Existing video-based GS sequence compression relies on the Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS) and tracked primitive information to convert GS into smooth 2D videos. However, tracked information is not available for most practical applications, and without it, using the vanilla PLAS can generate images exhibiting weak inter-frame correlation, due to its stochastic nature. GSCV incorporates a simple yet efficient Inter-PLAS method to produce close images between the I- and P-frames of GS, enhancing the inter-frame performance of video codec greatly. GSCV also realizes a new pipeline based on the state-of-the-art video codecs with high bit-depth GS images, achieving higher compressibility while simultaneously providing a higher quality upper bound. Experimental results show that the proposed GSCV exhibits obviously improved performance over MPEG video and point cloud-based anchors in GS sequence compression. The code is available at https://github.com/Qi-Yangsjtu/GSCV.
