The code is available at . <ccs2012> <concept> <concept_id>10010147.10010371</concept_id> <concept_desc>Computing methodologies~Computer graphics</concept_desc> <concept_significance>500</concept_significance> </concept> </ccs2012> Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian splatting (GS) vanillaGS has greatly advanced novel view synthesis thanks to its fast generation speed and impressive quality. However, the explicit GS primitive format induces a large data volume, which attracts considerable attention for effective GS data compression bagdasarian20253dgs . To facilitate GS compression standardization, the Moving Picture Experts Group (MPEG) has established a GS compression Ad Hoc group and delineated two lines of investigation: the A-3DGS and I-3DGS tracks m71640 . A-3DGS uses 2D videos/images as the input. With any agreed-upon GS-related representation as the intermediate, A-3DGS involves training GS models as part of the encoding process (i.e., optimization-based compression). I-3DGS aims to compress the trained GS data (i.e., optimization-free compression), resulting in a symmetric output with the same format as the input, such as GGSC yang2024benchmark , HGSC huang2024hierarchical , and FCGS chenfast . At present, most GS compression efforts focus on A-3DGS. They include HAC chen2024hac and CompGS liu2024compgs . Using an effective context model and rate-distortion (RD) loss function, they can achieve a compression ratio of more than 60 to 100x without noticeable distortion xing20253dgs . However, these optimization-based algorithms typically involve a complex coding process and rigid rate control yanghybridgs based on GPU, which restricts their application to certain use cases. The lightweight requirement from the industry m72430 promotes more attention devoted to I-3DGS. One promising approach to develop lightweight solutions is to compress GS data using canonical codecs such as the video or point cloud (PC) codec sullivan2012overview, pcc-1 , where the compression is mainly performed on CPUs. A more detailed related work is presented in Appendix sec:app_related . Video-based GS compression depends on the use of Parallel Linear Assignment Sorting (PLAS) PLAS to convert GS data to a group of smooth 2D maps. PLAS is a progressive process inspired by image sorting barthel2023flas . It first randomly places the primitive attributes into 2D grids, then gradually generates a smoother image via Gaussian blurring from coarse to fine as a target to sort the pixels until the 2D grids converge to a smooth distribution. For intra-frame compression strategies, PLAS significantly improves video codec performance, reporting compression ratios of 6 to 20x on HEVC wg7-73294 . Based on the preliminary MPEG experiments, for tracked GS sequence compression (see Appendix sec:exp for an explanation of ``tracked''), the video-based anchor (GSCodec Studio li2025gscodec ) is superior to the PC-based anchor (GPCC v1 GPCCv1 ) owing to its efficient inter-frame compression m72063 . However, few works focused on GS inter-frame compression based on video codecs, and the current anchor has obvious limitations, which motivate the study of this paper. To the best of our knowledge, GSCodec Studio pioneered the open-source solution that supports GS inter-frame compression based on video codecs. In its inter-prediction mode, PLAS is used for the first frame (i.e., the I-frame), and then the I-frame PLAS index is utilized for sorting the following frames (i.e., the P-frames) within the same group of pictures (GoP) to generate videos. This operation is built upon two assumptions: 1) the arrangement of the I- and P-frame primitives demonstrates an explicit spatial correspondence, whereby primitives with identical indices constitute spatial nearest neighbors sharing close attributes; and 2) directly using the I-frame PLAS index can generate smooth and close P-frame images. Nevertheless, the above assumptions can be violated in practical applications, resulting in suboptimal results as shown in Fig. fig:motivation . For the first assumption, GS data is characterized by permutation invariance as PC li2018so . Even though the initial GS data might share some correspondence between adjacent frames (e.g., they may be generated from the same canonical reference after fine-tuning), a considerable number of preprocessing operations before compression, such as sampling and editing hanson2025pup, chen2024gaussianeditor , can scramble the primitive order. Even a simple primitive shuffle operation, which does not change GS data and rendering results, can incur obvious performance degradation (see Appendix sec:app_shuffle ). For the second assumption, GS data is not injective due to -blending tewari2022advances , which means spatially neighboring primitives in the I- and P-frames may inherently possess substantially different attributes, especially in the large motion region. This observation implies that index-based primitive matching alone is insufficient to ensure that the P-frame images are smooth and close to the corresponding I-frame images. Besides, the current video-based anchor uses 16 bit depth (BD) for coordinates and 8 BD for quantising other attributes, which is not enough for complex GS scenes. Results from wg7-69034 showed that the optimal coordinate quantization BD lies within the range of 14 to 18, depending on particular datasets. Considering that GS is very sensitive to coordinate distortion, it would be better to use a larger BD during quantization and realize quality-bitstream balance via compression. Otherwise, the quality upper bound will be limited even under lossless compression. To improve the GS sequence compression performance and robustness, we propose GSCV, a new pipeline for GS sequence Compression based on Video codec. First, an effective and simple Inter-PLAS method, which consists of two steps, is proposed to reduce the PLAS image difference between adjacent GS frames. Inter-PLAS adopts a spatial-stable initialization (SSI) module designed to address the GS permutation-invariance issue, leading to stable I-frame PLAS image generation without affecting the compression efficiency. It also enables initializing the P-frame with low complexity using the I-frame context. Additionally, Inter-PLAS has an anchor-based PLAS refinement, which is proposed to optimize the P-frame image for better inter-frame prediction. Second, we establish a new PLAS image compression framework compatible with state-of-the-art (SOTA) video codecs, including HEVC and VVC bross2021vvcoverview . For a higher quality upper bound, 10 BD images are used for video sequence generation after Inter-PLAS. The coordinate maps, which are quantized by 20 BD, are split into two 10 BD images. Channel padding is adopted for attributes (e.g., opacity and rotation) that are not integer multiples of three channels to simplify compression configuration, as well as making it compatible with different image or video codecs. GSCV reports superiority on both MPEG tracked and semi-tracked datasets over benchmark methods. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: A new GS sequence compression pipeline based on video codecs, GSCV, is proposed to take advantage of advanced video codecs for efficient inter-frame GS sequence compression; We propose a simple yet effective Inter-PLAS scheme to generate close 2D maps for adjacent GS frames to improve inter-frame prediction performance. We use high BD images to form video sequences, which can provide wider bitrate and quality ranges; The experiment results show that the proposed GSCV is superior to MPEG video- and PC-based anchors. Ablation study demonstrates the robustness and generalization capability of GSCV. Brief Review of PLAS sec:plas PLAS is a heuristic algorithm to map GS attributes into 2D maps. Ideally, the generated 2D maps should be as smooth as possible so that they can be effectively compressed using video codecs. title: From Model to Prototype: Design and Motor-Flap Propulsion Control of a Twin-Wing Metamorphic UAV
summary: This paper presents the design and control strategy for MetaMorpher, a metamorphic Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), capable of both spinning-wing hover and fixed flying-wing cruise flight. Since control of the cruise configuration is comparatively well established in the literature, this paper focuses on control of the MetaMorpher in hover mode, building on the flight dynamics model and conceptual design validated in previous work. The control algorithm is implemented using one of two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses motor thrust in synchrony with the vehicle's rotation, or flap propulsion, a novel strategy that pulses the deflection of the wing-mounted elevons. We evaluate both strategies in simulation through different flight experiments. Simulation results confirm the mathematical model and show stable reference tracking, demonstrating flap propulsion as a lightweight, decoupled alternative for hover control. Experimental testing validated the vertical-dynamics propulsion model against the physical prototype, demonstrating very good steady-state agreement across different configurations.
full_text: This paper presents the design and control strategy for MetaMorpher, a metamorphic Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), capable of both spinning-wing hover and fixed flying-wing cruise flight. Since control of the cruise configuration is comparatively well established in the literature, this paper focuses on control of the MetaMorpher in hover mode, building on the flight dynamics model and conceptual design validated in previous work. The control algorithm is implemented using one of two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses motor thrust in synchrony with the vehicle's rotation, or flap propulsion, a novel strategy that pulses the deflection of the wing-mounted elevons. We evaluate both strategies in simulation through different flight experiments. Simulation results confirm the mathematical model and show stable reference tracking, demonstrating flap propulsion as a lightweight, decoupled alternative for hover control. Experimental testing validated the vertical-dynamics propulsion model against the physical prototype, demonstrating very good steady-state agreement across different configurations. Introduction sec:introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) capable of both vertical takeoff and hovering, as well as efficient long-range cruising, are needed for tasks such as power-line monitoring Luo2023 and bridge inspection Panigati2025 , which require confined launch sites and extended range. Conventional rotorcraft and fixed-wing aircraft each satisfy only one of these requirements. Metamorphic UAVs meet both, reconfiguring their airframe between hover- and cruise-optimized shapes. However, turning from this concept into a flying, controllable vehicle requires an actuator layout and suitable control strategy. We address this challenge with MetaMorpher, which builds on previously developed spincopter Orsag2011,Orsag2013 , an inherently stable UAV whose twin-wing rotating structure generates lift by spinning two wings with a pair of propellers. MetaMorpher extends this platform into a metamorphic design that folds between the spinning-wing hover configuration and a fixed flying-wing cruise configuration. Its conceptual design and a nonlinear, segmented-aerodynamics flight dynamics model have previously been presented and validated through simulation in BosakEric2026 . Implementing position control in the hover configuration, however, poses a challenge that conventional Vertical Take-Off and Landing (VTOL) controllers do not face. In this case, the aerodynamic surfaces and propulsion units rotate with the airframe, a fixed-axis control input cannot produce a constant horizontal force. Instead, the control action should be synchronized with the vehicle's rotational phase and applied only within selected angular sectors of each revolution. The spincopter implemented this principle by pulsing the imbalance between its two motor thrusts Orsag2011,Orsag2013 , an approach that couples horizontal and vertical control since both motors also determine the vehicle's overall lift Orsag2011 . Since MetaMorpher's cruise mode already requires a pair of wing-mounted elevons for attitude control, a well-established problem ( Hu2024 ), that we do not address in detail here, motivated us to use it as an alternative channel for the novel control principle. Therefore, this paper presents the design and control algorithm for the MetaMorpher. The resulting vehicle has a 0.7 m wingspan and an estimated ready-to-fly mass of approximately 454 g, with two independently driven wing-mounted propellers and two independently actuated trailing-edge elevons. For position control in hover mode, we implement and compare two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses the motor thrust imbalance following the spincopter approach in Orsag2011 , and flap propulsion, a novel strategy that instead pulses the elevon deflection in synchrony with the vehicle's rotation while motor speed is held constant. We evaluate both strategies using a nonlinear Simulink model, demonstrating stable waypoint tracking in simulation. The main contributions of this work are: Physical design of a MetaMorpher prototype that implements the airframe and actuator layout derived from the mathematical model in BosakEric2026 . Implementation and comparison of two phase-synchronized control strategies for position control in hover mode: motor propulsion and flap propulsion, a novel scheme that repurposes MetaMorpher's cruise-mode elevons for hover-mode actuation validated through simulation tests. Parameter identification of the throttle-to-spin-rate response in simulation and on the physical prototype. An open-source Simulink code of the control strategy to support reproducibility. This paper is divided into six sections. Section sec:related reviews related work on different designs and control algorithms of MetaMorpher-like vehicles. Section sec:design describes the MetaMorpher prototype. Section sec:control presents the motor- and flap-propulsion control strategies. Sections sec:simulation and sec:experiment report the simulation and experimental setup and flight-test results, respectively, to validate the design of the vehicle. Finally, Section sec:conclusion presents conclusions and directions for future work. Related work sec:related Conventional UAV airframes typically use a single configuration, trading hover capability for cruise efficiency. Metamorphic designs avoid this trade-off through approaches ranging from bio-inspired wing folding Win2021 to dedicated tilt-rotor Anuar2025 and tail-sitter Sufiyan2021 layouts. However, most of this work stops at mechanical concepts and theoretical analysis. Accurate simulation models and physical prototypes with control strategies validated through flight tests remain rare. Few review papers address the design of morphing aircraft alongside their flight control. For instance, Chu et al. Chu2022 reviewed the broader field of morphing aircraft, covering configuration design methods, the nonlinear dynamics and aerodynamic interference introduced by wing morphing, and the flight control strategies used to address them. Authors in Parancheerivilakkathil2024 focused more specifically on control, surveying shape, flight-dynamics, and aeroelastic control strategies for a wide range of fixed-wing morphing concepts. Harvey et al. Harvey2022 took a different angle, reviewing avian-inspired morphing in which wing sweep, dihedral, twist, and camber replace conventional control surfaces to provide pitch, roll, and yaw control, including on tailless airframes; camber-morphing trailing edges, similar to elevons, provide pitch control when actuated symmetrically and roll control when actuated asymmetrically. Across these reviews, the scope remains fixed-wing or gliding flight, while none address vehicles like MetaMorpher that transition between rotary-wing hover and fixed-wing cruise. Several hardware platforms have demonstrated metamorphic hover-to-cruise flight. Low et al. Low2017, Low2018 developed the Transformable HOvering Rotorcraft (THOR), which inspired MetaMorpher’s wing sizing and models the vehicle as a rigid body in each flight mode. Sufiyan et al. Sufiyan2021, Sufiyan2022 introduced a multimodal vehicle, jointly optimizing design and control parameters through a collaborative co-evolutionary approach. State-of-the-art control papers have also focused on specific aspects of the transition problem. Yuksek et al. Yuksek2016 developed a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model for transition control of a tilt-rotor UAV and validated it through both simulation and a physical flight demonstration on their TURAC prototype. Zhao et al. Zhao2021 proposed Kriging-based control allocation for a flying-wing UAV with a morphing trailing edge, validated in simulation, addressing control-surface actuation without full airframe metamorphosis or a hover mode. Both of MetaMorpher's control strategies, detailed in Section sec:control , rely on synchronizing the control input with the vehicle's rotational phase rather than producing a fixed control force in the body frame. This principle is closely related to cyclic pitch control on a conventional helicopter rotor, where blade pitch is varied once per revolution to redirect the rotor's thrust in a commanded inertial direction Leishman2006 . On the spincopter, this principle was implemented entirely through differential motor thrust Orsag2011,Orsag2013 . Phase-synchronized flap deflection has also been investigated on single-wing, samara-inspired monocopters, where a trailing-edge flap is deflected within selected angular sectors of each revolution to produce horizontal control forces FregeneBolden2010 . To the best of our knowledge, no existing metamorphic UAV has achieved horizontal control through elevon deflection on a twin-wing spinning platform, nor directly compared it against motor pulsation on the same model. This work bridges these gaps by implementing MetaMorpher’s previously validated model as a flight-ready prototype and evaluating two phase-synchronized control strategies for its hover mode. Finally, this work lays the foundation for combining motor and flap propulsion into a single control architecture and for extending phase-synchronized control across the transition between hover and cruise flight. MetaMorpher Design sec:design Design Overview The UAV is designed to operate in both spinning-wing hover and fixed-wing cruise configurations. The transition mechanism follows a concept similar to Low2018 , where the two wings are independently rotated by servo actuators about spanwise pivot axes. Each wing is connected to the fuselage through a one-degree-of-freedom (1-DoF) revolute joint. The pivot shafts also serve as the primary wing spars, reducing the number of structural components and the overall mechanism complexity. The final vehicle layout, shown in Fig. fig:metamorpher_design , includes two independently driven wing-mounted propellers and two independently actuated trailing-edge control surfaces, referred to as flaps in the spinning-wing hover configuration and as elevons in the fixed-wing cruise configuration, reflecting their differing aerodynamic role in each flight mode. This arrangement provides separate port and starboard propulsion and aerodynamic control inputs, which are used in this work to generate asymmetric forces and moments. Further details of the mechanical layout, electronic components, and wing geometry are given in the following subsections. Actuator Layout subsec:actuator_layout The wing pivot shafts pass through the central fuselage and are positioned as far forward as permitted by the wing geometry and structural requirements. This leaves sufficient volume for the battery, flight controller, and other onboard electronics while allowing the center of mass to be placed within the required range. The pivot shafts also act as the primary wing spars, such that the wing rotation mechanism does not require an additional load-bearing element. The rotation of the wing is coupled to the actuator through a pair of gears, giving the wings a \( 90^ \) range of motion. The propulsion units are positioned near the outer wing sections to increase the moment arm of the thrust force about the vehicle rotation axis. This increases the available spin-up moment in the hover configuration and the control moment available from differential thrust. However, the local tangential velocity at the propeller distance from the center of the UAV, , increases with radial distance from the rotation axis , \(V_ = r_m _x\). The motor position was therefore selected as a compromise between thrust moment and propeller performance under the increased local inflow velocity. The final actuator placement is shown in Fig.~ fig:metamorpher_design . The elevon servo actuators are installed within recessed cavities on the upper wing surface to minimize external protrusions and the associated aerodynamic drag. A mechanical linkage

title: Cooperating with Future Collaborators: Multi-Agent RL under Staggered Participation
summary: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents are often trained under concurrent participation, while in many tasks some agents act earlier and leave task-relevant information that becomes useful to agents participating later. We study this setting as staggered participation (SP), which introduces a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency because an early action may affect the return through the information it provides and the later policy that uses it. Learning under SP therefore requires both identifying what information is useful for future decisions and learning how later agents should use it. We propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that addresses these two parts with prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents. We evaluate SPL across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns. Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average difference of 14.1%. The gains also extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab, providing evidence across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings.
full_text: In cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), agents are often trained under concurrent participation, while in many tasks some agents act earlier and leave task-relevant information that becomes useful to agents participating later. We study this setting as staggered participation (SP), which introduces a cross-time, cross-agent learning dependency because an early action may affect the return through the information it provides and the later policy that uses it. Learning under SP therefore requires both identifying what information is useful for future decisions and learning how later agents should use it. We propose Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that addresses these two parts with prospective acquisition supervision for earlier agents and outcome-supervised receiver learning for later agents. We evaluate SPL across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns. Across 60 MPE/RWARE backbone setting comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every case, with an average difference of 14.1 . The gains also extend to eight-agent teams and a physics-based UAV--UGV environment in Isaac Lab, providing evidence across algorithmic, temporal, and embodied settings. Introduction sec:intro Cooperative agents do not always participate over the same time interval. For instance, in multi-robot systems, one agent may begin sensing or exploration earlier, while another becomes active later for navigation or task execution~ rockenbauer2024traversing,sasaki2020map,9732342 . Their participation windows may partially overlap, allowing direct interaction for some time steps, or they may be fully separated. In these cases, earlier agents can acquire or leave task-relevant information that remains useful to agents participating later. We study this temporal structure as staggered participation (SP), where agents contribute to the same cooperative objective over temporally offset participation windows. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:problem , these windows may partially overlap or be fully separated, while earlier participants can leave task-relevant information that supports later decisions. Learning under SP is challenging in cooperative MARL because the effect of an early action may only become visible through the behavior of an agent acting later. An earlier agent may take an action that acquires or reveals information for downstream decisions, but the usefulness of that action depends on how the resulting information affects later behavior. The return therefore links decisions across both time and participants. When participation windows overlap, this dependency can coexist with direct interaction; when they are disjoint, it is carried through information and other consequences of earlier actions. This gives rise to two interdependent learning requirements: (i) Information Acquisition, where earlier agents learn which actions provide useful information for later decisions, and (ii) Downstream Utilization, where later agents learn how that information should influence action selection. Although a shared team return couples the two roles through a common objective, it does not provide separate supervision for acquiring useful evidence and using it effectively downstream. SP is closely related to three existing directions in cooperative MARL. First, asynchronous MARL studies agents that act or communicate at different times~ 3545946.3598752,min2023cooperative,3709347.3743915 . Second, dynamic and open-team MARL considers agents that join, leave, or interact with changing teammates~ liu2021coach,rahman2023general,10.24963/ijcai.2024/974 . Third, communication MARL learns what information is useful for decision-making. Our focus is the learning dependency that appears when information acquisition and downstream utilization are distributed across different participation windows and potentially different agents. SP therefore places these two components within the same cooperative learning problem. We introduce Staggered Participation Learning (SPL), a training-time augmentation that provides complementary supervision for the two learning requirements under SP. Prospective acquisition supervision guides earlier agents toward actions that provide useful information for future collaborators, while outcome-supervised receiver learning trains later agents to use inherited evidence based on downstream outcomes. SPL augments actor training without modifying environment rewards and introduces no additional communication or auxiliary inference at execution. We evaluate SPL across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, participation patterns, larger teams, and a physics-based UAV--UGV setting. Across the 60 primary Vanilla--SPL comparisons, SPL achieves higher observed mean task completion in every configuration, with an average gain of 14.1 . Our contributions are: (i) Staggered participation. We formulate cooperative MARL with temporally offset participation and identify the dependency between evidence acquisition and downstream utilization; (ii) Staggered Participation Learning. We introduce complementary supervision for prospective acquisition and outcome-informed evidence use while preserving the underlying reward and decentralized execution; and (iii) Empirical evaluation. We evaluate SPL across policy-based MARL backbones, temporal participation patterns, larger teams, and physics-based UAV--UGV simulation. Related Work sec:related Simultaneous vs. Staggered Participation in Cooperative MARL. In simultaneous participation, agents contribute within the same interaction period. Cooperative MARL also studies temporal variation through asynchronous interaction, dynamic team composition, and staged decision making. Asynchronous methods consider agents that execute actions, communicate, or assign credit across asynchronous interactions~ 3545946.3598752,min2023cooperative,3709347.3743915,10.24963/ijcai.2025/20,farjadnasab2025cooperative , while dynamic and open-team approaches address agents that join, leave, or interact with changing teammates~ liu2021coach,rahman2023general,10.24963/ijcai.2024/974,hu2025adaptability . Cooperative Consecutive Policies studies cooperation across consecutive decision stages~ erskine2022developing . These directions examine different aspects of when agents act and participate in a cooperative task. SP concerns temporally offset participation windows, which may partially overlap or be fully separated. In the tasks studied here, earlier participants can acquire task-relevant evidence before future collaborators begin participating, and this evidence remains available to support downstream decisions. Direct vs. Indirect Communication Protocols in Cooperative MARL. Communication methods support direct information exchange and learn what to send and with whom to communicate, including under intermittent connectivity~ zhu2024survey,hu2024learning,li2023context,yang2024team,lin2026and,ijcai2026p50 . Cooperation can also occur indirectly through persistent environmental traces or another agent's subsequent actions. Stigmergic methods support coordination through such environmental traces~ xu2021stigmergic , while MAE-MAPPO addresses indirect cooperation with invisible collaborators through marginal advantage estimation~ pmlr-v337-qiao26a . Related methods provide complementary mechanisms for retaining and interpreting information: sequence-based methods retain long-horizon context~ mahjoub2025sable , while SMPE and MA E model or reconstruct information unavailable from local observations~ kontogiannis2025enhancing,kang2025mae . Policy distillation transfers training-time coordination knowledge into decentralized policies~ pei2025policy,zhaidistilling . Informative sensing and Dec-POMDP approaches further guide information acquisition according to its expected decision value~ 2484920.2484926,3306127.3331815,3709347.3743765 . The form of SP studied here combines temporally offset participation with indirect cooperation through persistent task-relevant evidence. Within this setting, SPL focuses on evidence acquisition and downstream utilization, while related credit-assignment methods study how cooperative outcomes are attributed across agents or coalitions~ pmlr-v337-qiao26a,3709347.3743764 . SPL builds on value-aware information acquisition and policy distillation to supervise earlier participants and learn receiver preferences from attributable downstream outcomes. Persistent evidence connects the two roles without requiring additional execution-time communication. At time , the environment is in state and agent receives a local observation . Each agent maintains an action--observation history and selects an action according to , where denotes the legal-action mask. The joint action produces the shared reward and the next state is sampled according to . All agents optimize the common discounted team return . Staggered participation. Agents may participate over different temporal intervals, so teammates need not be active throughout the same period. Let denote the set of agents participating at time ; agents outside this set take a null action and make no policy decision. For each agent , let denote its participation interval, where is the first participating time and is the exclusive end time. We call agent a future collaborator of agent if and both contribute to the same cooperative objective. Their participation intervals may be disjoint, with , or may partially overlap, with . In both cases, agent can act before agent begins participating. Learning problem under SP Earlier information-gathering actions can change the evidence available to future collaborators and thereby influence downstream decisions and the shared return. This creates two interdependent learning requirements: what evidence earlier participants should acquire and how future collaborators should use it. Because the effect of an earlier action is realized through persistent evidence and subsequent decisions by another policy, its learning signal is delayed and indirect. We therefore focus on improving both evidence preparation and downstream evidence use. The next subsection introduces SPL to support these two requirements. Staggered Participation Learning (SPL) sec:spl Under SP, earlier participants and future collaborators are coupled through persistent task-relevant evidence. SPL augments the native cooperative MARL objective with two complementary actor-side training signals. Prospective acquisition supervision guides earlier participants toward evidence-gathering actions expected to support future decisions, while outcome-supervised receiver learning teaches future collaborators how inherited evidence should influence downstream action selection. Both augment native actor training while leaving the environment reward and backbone critic objective unchanged, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:spl_pipeline . Structured training supervision. SPL uses structured task knowledge available during training to construct its auxiliary targets. Receiver supervision uses fixed task-level utilities for successful and unsuccessful execution, while candidate-specific success probabilities are learned from attributable outcomes observed during training. title: PACE: Stage-Consistent Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation via Progress-Aligned Context for Execution
summary: Demonstration-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for specifying robot behavior, yet long-horizon manipulation remains difficult when visually similar states recur across different stages or when demonstrations and executions proceed at different speeds. We identify the resulting failure mode as stage confusion and introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE), a stateful method that continually reinterprets a complete demonstration according to realized execution progress. PACE compresses the demonstration into ordered multimodal prompt tokens and uses training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose its latent stage structure. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action-observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention, producing a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies. PACE improves success from 88.9% to 94.0% on LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain, from 79.1% to 83.3% on Spatial Combination, and from 33.3% to 73.3% on the two-step Block Routing tasks. Failure analysis further indicates that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion.
full_text: Demonstration-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for specifying robot behavior, yet long-horizon manipulation remains difficult when visually similar states recur across different stages or when demonstrations and executions proceed at different speeds. We identify the resulting failure mode as stage confusion and introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE), a stateful method that continually reinterprets a complete demonstration according to realized execution progress. PACE compresses the demonstration into ordered multimodal prompt tokens and uses training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose its latent stage structure. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action--observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention, producing a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies. PACE improves success from 88.9 to 94.0 on LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain, from 79.1 to 83.3 on Spatial Combination, and from 33.3 to 73.3 on the two-step Block Routing tasks. Failure analysis further indicates that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion. INTRODUCTION Enabling robots to adapt to new tasks from minimal user input without retraining is a central objective of general-purpose robotic manipulation. Recent visuomotor policies have increasingly supported task conditioning through language, goal images, and multimodal demonstrations octo2024,jain2024vid2robot,jiang2023vima,patel2026bpp . Among these, a perception--action demonstration conveys the global task objective, the sequence of operations, and fine-grained motion details, enabling policies to adapt to new execution objectives without updating model parameters duan2017oneshot,james2018taskembedded,devin2019cpv,jain2024vid2robot,xu2023xskill,fu2024icrt,patel2026bpp . However, long-horizon multi-stage manipulation requires a policy to continually track task progress and interpret the demonstration relative to the current execution state. This is particularly challenging when different stages contain similar or recurring observations: similar states may require different actions depending on what has already been completed. Retrieving a demonstration segment inconsistent with the current progress may cause the policy to regress to an earlier stage, skip or repeat a stage, or terminate prematurely. We refer to this class of failures as stage confusion, illustrated in Fig.~ fig:stage_confusion . Stage confusion primarily arises from two related factors: cross-stage observation aliasing, whereby distinct latent stages exhibit similar observations, and demonstration--execution temporal-scale mismatch, whereby the robot and the demonstrator complete the same behavioral stage at different speeds. Existing approaches address this problem only partially. Explicit stage or subgoal models often require predefined task decompositions, semantic subgoals, or manual stage annotations sutton1999options,pertsch2021spirl,shiarlis2018taco,kipf2019compile , while frame- or window-level localization is vulnerable to recurring observations and execution-speed variation sermanet2018tcn,dwibedi2019tcc . Long-context and memory-augmented policies retain longer execution histories dai2019transformerxl,ba2016fastweights,sun2024ttt,jiang2026robottt , but typically use history as additional input to action prediction rather than to continually revise which part of the demonstration is relevant. These limitations motivate a mechanism that recovers stage structure from demonstrations without manual annotations and uses causal execution history to dynamically determine which part of the demonstration should guide the current behavior. Event cognition research suggests that humans parse continuous activity into structured events and update an active event model at perceptual boundaries zacks2001eventstructure,zacks2007event,kurby2008segmentation . Inspired by this view, we adopt a functional abstraction in which an event model is realized not necessarily through parametrically independent modules, but through context dynamically constructed during execution. Specifically, the policy combines current perception with within-episode execution history to locate and aggregate demonstration segments consistent with the current progress, forming an evolving event context that enables a shared policy to produce stage-appropriate behavior. Building on this insight, we introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE), a stateful progress-alignment method for long-horizon demonstration-conditioned manipulation. During training, PACE automatically extracts and monotonically aligns action-stage boundaries, imposing dual-edge attention supervision and effective-support regularization. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action--observation transitions and modulates observation queries before cross-attention with the full demonstration. The resulting progress-aligned demonstration context conditions a unified diffusion action expert. Stage boundaries are used only for training supervision; at inference time, PACE requires neither explicit event segmentation, discrete stage prediction, nor stage-specific policies. We evaluate PACE on compositional long-horizon manipulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks. On the LIBERO-Gen Spatial Combination and Goal Chain, PACE improves the success rate from 79.1 to 83.3 and from 88.9 to 94.0 . On the two-step Block Routing tasks, which exhibit pronounced cross-stage observation aliasing, PACE raises the mean success rate from 33.3 to 73.3 . Stage-level analyses further show that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory work synergistically to suppress stage confusion. Our main contributions are as follows: We systematically study stage confusion in long-horizon demonstration-conditioned manipulation, attributing it to cross-stage observation aliasing and demonstration--execution temporal-scale mismatch. We introduce PACE, centered on a causally updated, episode-local fast-weight state that encodes realized action--observation transitions and modulates observation queries before prompt cross-attention, allowing visually similar current observations to attend to different demonstration stages under different execution histories. PACE further combines automatic stage-structure discovery with dual-edge attention supervision and effective-support regularization, without requiring manual stage annotations or stage-specific policies. We validate PACE on compositional simulation tasks and real-world robotic tasks with held-out demonstrations, and use stage-level analyses to elucidate how it mitigates stage confusion. RELATED WORK Demonstration-Conditioned Robot Policies Complete perception--action demonstrations provide a natural inference-time interface for specifying task objectives, operation sequences, and motion details without updating policy parameters. Existing methods relate human demonstrations to robot observations through cross-attention or learned cross-embodiment representations jain2024vid2robot,xu2023xskill , retrieve or align relevant demonstration segments papagiannis2024rplusx,kedia2024rhyme , encode task identity from one or a few demonstrations duan2017oneshot,james2018taskembedded , or jointly model demonstration and execution trajectories as prompted, in-context sequences jiang2023vima,fu2024icrt,patel2026bpp . In particular, Behavior Prompting Policy (BPP) treats a complete perception--action demonstration as a behavioral prompt for closed-loop action generation patel2026bpp . However, these approaches generally use the demonstration as a static conditioning sequence and do not continually reinterpret it according to realized execution progress, leaving them susceptible to cross-stage observation aliasing. Temporal Alignment and Stage-Structured Manipulation Temporal correspondence methods, including frame-level metric learning, temporal cycle consistency, dynamic time warping, and optimal transport, align sequences with different appearances or execution speeds sermanet2018tcn,dwibedi2019tcc,sakoe1978dtw,cuturi2013sinkhorn . Local correspondences become ambiguous when visually similar states recur, while sequence-level alignments are typically computed offline or remain fixed during execution. Related hierarchical approaches represent progress using skills, options, subgoals, or keyframes sutton1999options,pertsch2021spirl,shiarlis2018taco,kipf2019compile , but often require predefined decompositions, semantic labels, or separate skill policies. Although unsupervised skill discovery reduces annotation requirements eysenbach2019diayn , it does not directly establish an execution-conditioned correspondence with a new demonstration. Latent-plan methods learn reusable long-horizon structure from play or human video lynch2020latentplans,wang2023mimicplay , but likewise do not continually realign a provided demonstration using the realized execution history. PACE instead learns ordered demonstration structure without manual stage labels and dynamically interprets that structure during execution. History and Memory for Long-Horizon Manipulation Long-horizon manipulation is partially observable because similar current observations may require different actions depending on prior interactions. Recurrent policies, history-aware Transformers, and memory-augmented models address this problem by retaining execution history dai2019transformerxl,ba2016fastweights . Test-time training further represents history as recurrently updated fast weights sun2024ttt , and RoboTTT applies this mechanism to long-horizon visuomotor control jiang2026robottt . These approaches primarily use history to improve action prediction. In contrast, PACE uses an episode-local fast-weight state to modulate observation queries before prompt cross-attention, allowing execution history to determine which part of the demonstration guides the current action. At execution timestep , denotes the current execution observation, and contains all realized transitions prior to action prediction at timestep . The policy , parameterized by , predicts the execution action sequence over a horizon of steps. The superscripts and distinguish prompt demonstration and execution quantities, respectively. The parameters remain fixed at test time; any episode-local state is reset between episodes. The demonstration is the sole behavior specification, with no test-time stage label or progress signal. It is latent rather than explicitly predicted, and the relevant guidance may span a contiguous demonstration interval around . Given training tasks , we learn to maximize complete-task success on evaluation tasks , including unseen task compositions or held-out demonstrations, without manually annotated stage boundaries or predefined task decompositions. title: OpenWAM: An Open Framework for Composable World-Action Models
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://openwam.stanford.edu ; Code: https://github.com/OpenWAM/OpenWAM ; Code and project page released June 4, 2026. Equal contribution: Heng Yu, David D. Yuan, Juze Zhang
summary: World-action models (WAMs) couple future prediction with robot control, yet existing systems often vary the video backbone, interaction structure, supervision, and inference procedure simultaneously, making their design choices difficult to compare. We introduce OPENWAM, an open world-action modeling framework built around a common causal robot-video foundation and configurable video-action interaction. Starting from Wan2.2-5B, we perform causal robot-video pretraining on over 10,000 hours of video, then integrate an action expert through a shared Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled generation. OPENWAM achieves high success rates on four LIBERO suites and real-world bimanual tasks; robot-video training with causal adaptation improves VTA success on LIBERO-Long from 68.4% to 97.8%. The same configurable architecture naturally extends to inverse and forward dynamics, allowing us to study how counterfactual transitions improve independently trained dynamics models beyond demonstrations alone. When only the video predictor is adapted to a new task, a frozen local-context inverse dynamics model trained on counterfactual data and demonstrations achieves 84.0% mean success across four held-out LIBERO-90 tasks, compared with 47.0% for a full-context inverse model and 21.5% for a local-context model trained only on demonstrations. For forward dynamics, counterfactual supervision reduces RGB prediction error by 34.5% and raises outcome identification from 21.1% to 71.3% among 16 same-state outcomes. OPENWAM provides a common testbed for comparing WAM interaction designs and for studying dynamics learning from video data beyond successful demonstrations.
full_text: Introduction World-action models (WAMs) integrate future-observation prediction with robot control. Recent systems such as DreamZero~ ye2026world , DVA~ rhoda2026dva and LingBot-VA~ li2026causal, lingbotva2 use pretrained video models to couple future-observation prediction with robot action generation. However, differences in their backbones, training data, objectives, and inference procedures make it difficult to isolate the effect of video--action interaction. Two challenges arise when studying these systems systematically. First, video--action interaction spans multiple choices: video and actions can be generated jointly, sequentially, or through restricted cross-modal connections. A shared architecture and evaluation protocol would allow these interaction patterns and generation orders to be compared under controlled conditions. Second, successful demonstrations cover only a limited subset of possible action--outcome relationships. Other interactions, including failures, exploratory behavior, and counterfactual rollouts, can provide additional supervision about local dynamics. However, it remains unclear whether such data can improve the reuse of an action-grounding component when the visual predictor is adapted to a new task. We study this question by independently training local-context dynamics models and evaluating their transfer across adapted video predictors. To this end, we introduce , an open framework and model series for controlled world--action modeling, summarized in Figure~ fig:openwam-teaser . Starting from a pretrained general-purpose video model, we adapt its visual prior through causal robot-video training without action labels, then introduce an action branch through a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture~ liang2024mixture . The resulting model supports joint, sequential, and restricted video--action interaction. These configurations share the video initialization, representations, and evaluation pipeline, allowing us to compare how their interaction patterns affect the control performance. Furthermore, trains local-context inverse and forward models independently. The inverse model predicts actions from the current observation and a future visual trajectory, while the forward model predicts that trajectory from supplied actions. In simulation, we broaden their training data by executing alternative action sequences from the same initial state. This local-transition formulation is also compatible with failed and exploratory interactions, because it does not require a successful task outcome or a success label. Each recorded transition supplies dynamics supervision regardless of whether it completes the task. At inference, a video predictor can propose a visual trajectory and a separately trained inverse model can translate it into executable actions. We evaluate robot-video pretraining, closed-loop policy success across video--action interaction modes and dynamics-component reuse. In transfer experiments, task-adapted video predictors are paired with frozen inverse models to compare demonstration-only with counterfactual-augmented supervision and local-context with full-context conditioning. We additionally evaluate forward prediction under alternative actions from the same initial state. This work makes three contributions: A controlled WAM framework. combines a causal video backbone with configurable video--action models under shared training and evaluation protocols. Local-context dynamics interfaces. We independently train inverse- and forward-dynamics models from demonstrations and broader local transitions and evaluate their composition with separately trained predictors. Controlled empirical analysis. We measure the effects of robot-video pretraining, interaction design, transition coverage, and conditioning context on policy performance and component reuse. Related Work sec:related Visuomotor Policies and Predictive Control Behavior cloning provides the standard supervised formulation for visuomotor policy learning, mapping observations and task context directly to demonstrated actions. Action chunking and generative action prediction have become effective control primitives~ zhao2023learning, chi2025diffusion , while large-scale vision--language--action models extend this paradigm through language conditioning, pretraining, and cross-task or cross-embodiment learning brohan2022rt, brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, o2024open, team2024octo . Predictive control introduces an additional interface by explicitly modeling future observations or latent states. Early visual-foresight methods combined action-conditioned video prediction with model-predictive control for robotic manipulation~ finn2017deep,ebert2018visual . Subsequent work learns latent or visual dynamics to support policy learning, planning, and imagined rollouts hafner2019dream, hafner2023mastering, wu2023daydreamer, wu2024unleashing, cheang2024gr, zhou2024robodreamer . Predictive rollouts have also been used to evaluate policy behavior~ li2025worldeval, guo2026ctrl . Action-conditioned world models provide a complementary perspective by predicting how an environment evolves under supplied or candidate actions. Recent methods use such predictions for simulation, candidate evaluation, proposal refinement, and self-verifying planning huang2026learning, zhou2026tau_0, qi2026inference, zhang2026worldcoherent . Together, these lines show that predictive models can support action generation, simulation, planning, and evaluation. However, action-conditioned prediction and video--action policy generation are often developed as separate components, leaving open how explicit prediction--action interfaces affect component reuse across tasks. Video Foundations and World--Action Architectures Recent world--action models connect predictive video representations with robot control through several forms of video--action coupling. Joint generation models predict future visual content and actions together ye2026world, cosmos3, shen2026videovla, guo2024prediction , while causal video-first formulations generate or represent visual futures before action prediction~ li2026causal, rhoda2026dva . Other architectures use specialized video and action pathways with explicit cross-modal exchange yang2026covar, zhang2026deva , or leverage egocentric and large-scale video priors for robot grounding and generalization li2026egowam, zhou2026zero, wu2026zimablue, qiu2026vid2wam . A closely related line studies the interface between predictive visual information and executable actions. Predicted visual states or representations can condition inverse dynamics~ tian2025predictive, hu2024video, li2026turningvideomodelsgeneralist , while other approaches translate generated futures through dense correspondence, pseudo-action labeling, intermediate denoising features, or latent representation alignment ko2024learning, jang2025dreamgen, ma2026dit4dit, vuong2026world2act . These methods differ in where and how predictive visual information enters the action-generation pathway. Unified formulations instead expose multiple predictive and control modes within a shared system. UWM and UVA~ zhu2025unified, li2503unified support combinations of policy, inverse-dynamics, forward-dynamics, and video prediction objectives, while related systems combine action generation with world prediction, simulation, planning, or evaluation cen2025worldvla, kim2026cosmos, sun2026riemann, bi2026motus2, guo2026unified . Recent work further isolates particular choices in the WAM design space. Predictive computation can be reduced, sparsified, reordered, or scheduled asynchronously yuan2026fast, tang2026world, wang2026glancewam, ye2603gigaworld, li2026light, huang2026streaming, huang2026noisegate, pan2026selfwam . Alternative work studies the representation through which world prediction interacts with control liu2026oa, wang2026repwam, qiu2026making, zhao2026sg, shen2026ld4wam, you2026affordancewam, jiang2026rethinking , or augments world--action learning with structural, geometric, and tactile supervision zheng2026gift, gonzalez2026spatially, ma2026tacpac . Temporal abstraction, data and model scaling, humanoid control, and long-horizon memory provide additional design axes li2026wall, liu2026ge, zheng2026motionwam, zhao2026memory ; recent surveys summarize the rapidly expanding landscape wang2026world, lu2026world . Concurrent work, also named OpenWAM~ wang2026openwam , develops a modular framework for systematic WAM pretraining and design studies. Our focus is complementary: fixes a common causal robot-video foundation and training interface while explicitly varying generation order and future cross-modal visibility, enabling joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled interaction to be compared under a shared evaluation protocol. We further study the reuse of independently trained inverse- and forward-dynamics components through explicit trajectory interfaces. Dynamics Learning Beyond Successful Demonstrations Successful demonstrations provide valid transitions, but they cover only the action--outcome relationships selected by the demonstrating policy. A complementary analysis shows that observational demonstrations alone may not identify the consequences of unsupported actions~ yu2026capability . Classical imitation-learning methods address the resulting distribution shift by collecting supervision on learner-visited states, perturbing expert trajectories, or soliciting corrective interventions ross2011reduction,laskey2017dart,mandlekar2020human,hu2026rac, intelligence2025pi . These approaches broaden state coverage beyond clean expert rollouts and improve robustness to execution errors. More recent work expands supervision through synthetic failures, counterfactual augmentation, autonomous experience, and other non-successful interactions ameperosa2025rocoda,duan2024aha,li2026learning,zhao2026flare, yin2026playworld,peng2026fact,bi2026motus2,yang2026wam . Such data have been used for recovery, policy improvement, failure understanding, and predictive modeling. Particularly related to our setting, Fail2Progress~ huang2025fail2progress targets data collection toward observed failures to improve skill-effect models, while UniPi~ du2023learning decouples video planning from inverse dynamics and allows the inverse model to learn from a separate, potentially suboptimal dataset. focuses on a different question: how transition coverage and conditioning scope affect the reuse of independently trained dynamics components after visual task adaptation. We branch alternative action continuations from task-relevant simulator states and use the resulting state--action--outcome transitions as local dynamics supervision. Methodology sec:method We develop as an open framework for composing world prediction and action generation. It combines three ingredients: a causal video backbone pretrained on robot video without action labels, a common video--action architecture whose cross-modal interaction can be reconfigured, and separately trained inverse and forward dynamics components operating through local trajectory interfaces. The design supports two forms of composition. At the architectural level, we vary how future observation and action streams interact while retaining a common backbone and objective family. At the component level, we connect independently trained predictors through explicit future-observation and action-trajectory interfaces. The latter motivates local-context dynamics models that do not require the language and nonlocal history used by a task-conditioned generator. title: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Models to Unknown Visual Disruptions During Execution
summary: Visual disruptions can arise while a robot is executing a task, leaving a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to respond without knowing the disruption type or timing. We introduce Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT), which uses the leftover trajectory, the unexecuted part of the previous action chunk, as self-supervision for test-time adaptation. Because consecutive chunks overlap in time, the leftover provides a temporally aligned target for the current prediction over the same future control interval. At the onset of a visual shift, the leftover can retain a plan formed before the corruption, so updating the policy toward it anchors the adaptation across the shift (Transition Anchoring). SALT keeps the adapted policy and regenerates the current chunk, whose leftover becomes the target at the next replan, carrying the correction forward along the execution trajectory (Sequential Correction Propagation). Supervision comes entirely from the policy's own predictions, requiring no disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations, and a lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories decides when updates begin. On LIBERO-10, SALT increases average success across five persistent visual corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while largely preserving nominal performance. On a real robot, it raises task progress averaged over digital and physical disruptions from 0.49 to 0.61.

On a real robot, it raises task progress averaged over digital and physical disruptions from 0.49 to 0.61. Introduction sec:introduction Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions, enabling a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo,black2024pi0,bjorck2025groot . Despite these capabilities, reliable deployment remains challenging when unexpected changes in visual conditions occur during task execution~ fei2026liberoplus, morgan2026colosseum . Changes in lighting, image quality, or camera visibility can perturb the observation stream on which the policy relies and abruptly change its action predictions (Figure~ fig:lava_problem , right), which can substantially degrade task performance. We refer to such execution-time events as visual disruptions, which induce a visual shift from the nominal observation condition while the task is already underway. Test-time adaptation (TTA) provides a framework for adapting pretrained models to distribution shifts using signals available at deployment, such as predictive entropy~ wang2021tent,gong2023sotta or teacher predictions~ wang2022cotta,dobler2023rmt . Existing VLA adaptation methods rely on signals prepared outside the current episode, such as delayed feedback, learned progress estimates, or target-domain demonstrations~ zang2026pdf,kang2026dart,li2026fla,bai2025evolve . When a disruption arises during execution with unknown type and timing (Figure~ fig:lava_problem , left), such resources are not available, and the policy must respond within the ongoing rollout using only what execution has already produced. We ask: How can a VLA adapt online to an unknown visual disruption using only information already produced during execution? Our key observation is that action-chunked execution already exposes a useful learning signal within the rollout. At each replan, a VLA predicts an action chunk~ zhao2023act but executes only a prefix~ black2024pi0,liu2025bidirectional . We refer to the remaining, unexecuted action sequence from the previous chunk as a leftover trajectory. Because the leftover and the prefix predicted at the next replan cover the same future control interval, the policy obtains temporally aligned supervision without any new expert label. At the shift boundary, this leftover was planned from a nominal observation, so it retains the intended plan that the corrupted prediction has lost. Building on this observation, we introduce Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT), a leftover-supervised mechanism for test-time adaptation of VLAs within the ongoing episode. Once adaptation is activated, SALT uses the previous chunk's leftover as self-supervision under the current policy input, updates the policy, and regenerates the action chunk before execution. The same supervision plays two complementary roles. Across the visual shift, the nominal-side leftover can provide Transition Anchoring. Thereafter, SALT retains the adapted policy state and refreshes the leftover target at successive replans, yielding Sequential Correction Propagation along the execution trajectory. To deploy SALT when disruption timing is unknown, we use a lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories. The gate determines when these leftover-supervised updates begin without requiring annotations of the disruption type or timing. We evaluate on LIBERO-10 tasks~ liu2023libero under five persistent visual corruptions from LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus . With SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla , raises average success across corrupted conditions from 43.9 to 53.2 , and with GR00T N1.7~ bjorck2025groot , it raises success from 58.7 to 66.0 , while largely preserving nominal performance. The leftover target approaches an oracle target that is unavailable at deployment. On SmolVLA, reaches 53.2 , within 3.7 points of supervising with the policy's clean-input prediction (56.9 ), whereas other nominal targets, such as another episode's plan, remain at or below the frozen level (43.9 ). On a real robot, raises task progress from 0.46 to 0.61 under digital disruptions and from 0.51 to 0.62 under physical disruptions such as switching off the lights or covering a camera. Because relies only on the temporal overlap between consecutive action chunks for supervision, its core mechanism is compatible with action-chunked backbones without requiring architectural modifications. Related Work sec:related Robustness of VLA models under visual shifts. VLA policies have shown strong performance across diverse manipulation tasks~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,bjorck2025groot , but visual shifts such as sensor noise and lighting changes can sharply degrade execution~ fei2026liberoplus,morgan2026colosseum . Prior work improves visual robustness through training on perturbed images~ xie2026strongvla or learned visual adapters~ fu2026stablevla , intervenes on or restores observations at inference time while keeping the policy fixed~ hancock2024byovla, guarnizo2026crt , or adapts from target-domain demonstrations~ kang2026dart, li2026fla . Unlike these approaches, SALT updates the policy when a visual shift of unknown type and timing arises mid-episode, using only observations and action predictions from the ongoing rollout without target-domain demonstrations or corruption-specific training. Test-time adaptation of policies. Test-time adaptation methods for visual perception update models from unlabeled test data through entropy-based objectives~ wang2021tent, gong2023sotta , teacher predictions~ wang2022cotta,dobler2023rmt , or activation-statistics matching~ mirza2023actmad . These objectives do not directly provide targets for temporally aligned continuous action chunks. VLA-specific approaches instead use delayed episode feedback~ zang2026pdf , learned progress estimates~ bai2025evolve,liu2026ttvla , predicted and observed future images in visual-foresight policies~ park2026t3vf , a proxy task trained before deployment~ zhang2026tttvla , or additional exploratory rollouts~ chen2026t2vla . Several of these assume discrete action tokens or a future-image head and do not transfer directly to recent flow-based action experts. Unlike methods that depend on such feedback, auxiliary components, or extra rollouts, SALT uses temporally aligned leftover actions already generated during the same episode as targets for online updates, and applies to any action-chunked backbone. Reusing overlapping action chunks. Prior work uses overlapping action chunks to improve execution: ACT temporally ensembles predictions~ zhao2023act , SEAM smooths chunk transitions~ zhan2026seam , BID selects chunks consistent with previous actions~ liu2025bidirectional , and RTC freezes actions committed during inference latency~ black2025rtc . AAC adjusts the execution horizon from action uncertainty~ liang2026adaptive . These methods reuse overlapping predictions to improve inference-time continuity, chunk selection, or execution while keeping the policy parameters fixed. In contrast, uses temporally aligned leftover actions as self-supervision for online policy updates under within-episode visual shifts, which to our knowledge has not been explored before. Visual Disruptions During Execution sec:prelim_visual_shift We consider episodes that begin under nominal visual conditions. An unknown visual disruption may change the visual input during execution. We call the resulting deviation a visual shift. Let denote the first replan affected by this shift, marking the shift boundary from nominal visual observations to shifted visual observations . The task instruction, proprioception, embodiment, and action space remain unchanged. The policy's visual input is At deployment, neither the disruption type nor the shift boundary is known. The policy can use its current inputs and execution history, but has no paired nominal observation, expert action, or prior shifted-domain data. We allow access to a small set of nominal trajectories before deployment. The goal is to preserve the policy's nominal task behavior under the shifted visual input without access to the corresponding nominal observation. Method sec:method We propose Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT), which repurposes the leftover trajectory introduced in Section~ sec:prelim_action_chunking as self-supervision for online policy adaptation. Figure~ fig:method_overview illustrates the overall adaptation process. Across the shift boundary, Transition Anchoring provides a temporally aligned nominal-side action reference for correcting the policy under the shifted observation. As execution proceeds, the adapted policy is carried forward and the leftover supervision is repeatedly refreshed, yielding Sequential Correction Propagation along the execution trajectory. In deployment, a lightweight adaptation gate determines when these online updates begin. title: Commit While Futures Agree: Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking for Robot Manipulation
summary: Action-chunking policies predict multi-step control sequences, but a fundamental question remains: how much of a predicted action chunk should be committed before replanning? Existing systems typically execute a fixed-length prefix, implicitly assuming that the same execution horizon remains trustworthy across states. Some adaptive methods estimate this horizon from the similarity or stability of predicted actions. However, different actions may lead to the same successful outcome, whereas similar actions can produce different futures, suggesting that commitment should be determined by agreement among imagined futures rather than by similarity in action space. To this end, we propose Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA$^3$C), an inference-time framework built on a simple principle: commit while imagined futures agree, and replan when they diverge. Without modifying or retraining the base policy, CA$^3$C uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine the future consequences of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise. Using these imagined consequences, we formulate execution-horizon estimation as a Bayesian change-point inference problem and select the execution candidate through future consensus. Across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, CA$^3$C consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8% relative reduction in failure rate over the corresponding base policies.

Without modifying or retraining the base policy, uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine the future consequences of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise. Using these imagined consequences, we formulate execution-horizon estimation as a Bayesian change-point inference problem and select the execution candidate through future consensus. Across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8 relative reduction in failure rate over the corresponding base policies. Introduction Modern robot manipulation policies increasingly predict actions in chunks rather than one step at a time~ kim2025openvlaoft,black2024pi0,shi2025pi05 . This way captures richer temporal structure, reduces myopic switching, and amortizes expensive inference~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion . However, one fundamental question remains: after predicting an action chunk, how much of it should the robot execute? Most existing systems answer this question with a fixed execution prefix, implicitly assuming that predictions remain reliable for as long as they can be generated. Prediction capability, however, does not imply execution reliability. In free space, a policy may safely support long open-loop execution, whereas near grasping, contact, or precise placement, only a short execution prefix may remain reliable. This discrepancy becomes even more pronounced under distribution shift, where an unfamiliar object pose or scene layout may invalidate an otherwise reliable open-loop plan much earlier than expected. Conversely, frequent replanning can interrupt reliable execution, increase inference cost, and reduce motion consistency across independently generated action chunks. Taken together, these limitations suggest that execution should be adaptive rather than governed by a fixed horizon. Recent work makes execution adaptive using action entropy~ liang2026aac , agreement across prediction horizons~ jing2026moh , or stability along a flow policy's denoising trajectory~ feng2026dvac . These methods recognize the importance of state-dependent commitment, but their confidence estimates are derived solely from the policy's action generation process. Action ambiguity, however, does not necessarily imply execution risk. Different action trajectories may produce the same successful outcome, while nearly identical actions near contact can instead lead to entirely different task outcomes. Consequently, confidence measured in action space cannot directly determine whether the resulting future remains consistent and task-safe. Taken together, the key question is not whether actions appear reliable, but whether the futures they induce remain consistent. In this study, we propose ( ), an inference-time framework for consequence-aware commitment. Rather than asking whether sampled actions look alike, we ask whether their predicted effects remain mutually consistent. Specifically, we introduce world models as an imagined-future consequence comparator. At each replanning point, samples candidate action chunks and predicts their future latent trajectories while holding world-model sampling noise fixed. It then measures candidate-induced disagreement relative to the total predicted scene change. A Bayesian change-point test determines whether, and where, this disagreement begins to rise faster; no task-specific uncertainty threshold is introduced. Finally, executes the candidate closest to the future consensus up to the selected boundary. The resulting principle is concise: commit while imagined futures agree, and replan when they diverge. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We use an action-conditioned world model to select the execution length of each action chunk by locating where candidate-conditioned imagined futures begin to diverge. We use the same imagined futures to select the candidate closest to cross-candidate consensus, yielding a representative action sequence for execution. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa, and real-world AgiBot G2 tasks, consistently outperforms the corresponding base policies and strong baselines. Related Work Adaptive Action Chunking Most action-chunking policies use a fixed execution horizon: they predict a multi-step sequence and execute the same preset number of actions before each replanning step~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion,black2024pi0,shi2025pi05 . Fixed-horizon execution is widely combined with temporal ensembling, guided candidate decoding, and asynchronous chunk stitching to improve temporal consistency or tolerate inference latency~ zhao2023act,liu2025bid,black2025rtc . Recent research instead makes commitment state-dependent, using signals derived from policy outputs or the generation process~ so2025sgac,liang2026aac,jing2026moh,feng2026dvac , learned horizon selectors optimized through task feedback~ zhao2026dehp , or verification between predicted and subsequently observed futures~ wang2026ffdc . likewise adapts commitment online, but determines the execution boundary before acting from agreement among the action-conditioned consequences of multiple candidate chunks, rather than from action-space confidence or post-execution prediction--observation discrepancies. World Models for Robot Manipulation World models predict how observations or latent states evolve under actions, enabling imagined-future reasoning in robot manipulation~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2023dreamerv3,zhu2024irasim,zhu2025uwm . Existing work uses such predictions primarily for visual planning and goal-conditioned control~ finn2017deep,ebert2018visual,du2023unipi,zhou2024robodreamer,zhen2024threedvla , policy or representation learning in imagination~ hafner2023dreamerv3,wu2022daydreamer,zhu2025uwm,cen2025worldvla,zheng2025flare , and action-conditioned simulation for policy evaluation, improvement, or data generation~ zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld . Thus, imagined futures generally serve as plans, learning signals, or surrogate environments. instead uses the world model as an execution-time consequence comparator for policy-proposed chunks: disagreement among candidate-conditioned futures determines how long to commit, while consensus identifies which candidate to execute. To our knowledge, this use of a world model to jointly guide action-chunk truncation and candidate selection has not been studied previously. 2 Method Preliminaries Our framework builds on two established model classes: an action-chunking policy that models a distribution over future controls, and an action-conditioned world model that models the future consequences of those controls. We do not assume a particular policy architecture or input modality; the only requirement is that the policy can produce multiple plausible action chunks under the same condition. In the standard action-chunk execution mechanism, the policy predicts actions but the controller executes only the first actions before observing the environment and replanning. Thus, is the prediction horizon, whereas is the execution horizon; existing controllers commonly keep fixed throughout deployment~ black2025rtc,zhao2026dehp . Action-Conditioned World Models. An action-conditioned world model predicts how the environment evolves under a proposed action chunk.
