title: IronMan: Information-Constrained Video-Action Learning for Robot Manipulation
summary: Video Action Models (VAMs) couple visual dynamics modeling with action generation for robot manipulation. However, video representations are not naturally suited to action generation, as exposing the action policy to excessive visual detail can impair its generalization ability. Therefore, we introduce IronMan (Information-constRained videO-actioN learning for robot MANipulation), a robust video-action learning framework built on the information bottleneck principle. The core principle of this framework is to impose information constraints that suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues. IronMan employs a dynamics-aware bottleneck that distills noisy, entangled one-step video features into compact world representations. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong in-distribution (ID) performance and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness while maintaining efficient inference. IronMan achieves success rates of 99.0% on LIBERO and 79.4% on RoboTwin clean2clean, outperforming all the evaluated baselines. Under OOD shifts, IronMan achieves a success rate of 79.1% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.4 percentage points. Project Page: Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent class of foundation models for robot manipulation~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05,intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience,intelligence2026pi07steerablegeneralistrobotic,wu2026lingbotvla,liu2026g05autoregressivestreamrobot . However, most VLAs inherit priors from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pretrained primarily on static image--text data, and therefore lack dynamics modeling. This limitation has motivated a video-action learning paradigm that couples visual dynamics with action generation, enabling these Video-Action Models~(VAMs) to learn inverse dynamics within predictive representations~ ICLR2025_e5b5c402,hu2025vpp,bi2026motus,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam,nvidia2025cosmosworldfoundationmodel,zhang2026disentangled . These advances reveal the great potential of jointly modeling video dynamics and actions. However, video and action generation inherently impose different information requirements. A video backbone needs to preserve rich visual details to reconstruct future frames. But an action policy should primarily leverages action-relevant cues. Therefore, the rich information from video backbones is not naturally aligned with the needs of action generation. Existing approaches typically connect video features to the action policy through learned projections or attention mechanisms~ yuan2026fastwam,hu2025vpp,yan2026svam . Such interfaces do not explicitly suppress features irrelevant to action generation. This can undermine the robustness of action policy. When excessive visual cues are exposed to the policy, the model may exploit incidental correlations, which are unreliable under visual distribution shifts. For example, camera noise, light conditions, and background may become shortcuts, leading to degraded generalization in unseen scenes. Therefore, a key challenge is how to transform rich video features into compact representations that capture the dynamics essential for manipulation while avoiding spurious visual correlations. The information bottleneck~(IB) theory offers a principled way to regulate the video-action interface by constraining how much information can pass from input features, while encouraging the latent representation to retain sufficient information for prediction target~ tishby1999information,alemi2017deep . Prior work applies IB-style objectives to regularize visuomotor representations for robot manipulation~ bai2025rethinking,zhang2026information,pmlr-v162-du22b . However, these methods do not address the more challenging video-action interface, where features from a generative video backbone entangle predictive dynamics with visual details. Motivated by this, we introduce IronMan (Information-constRained videO-actioN learning for robot MANipulation), a robust video-action learning framework. As illustrated in , unlike inverse dynamics model (IDM)-based VAMs, IronMan extracts one-step video features from the video backbone, substantially reducing inference overhead. Although these features already encode physical dynamics, they remain highly noisy and entangled with redundant visual cues. Applying an information constraint on these features alone does not specify how spatial and temporal cues should be used for action generation. Therefore, we introduce a dynamics-aware bottleneck in~ which first aggregates the video features with a Qformer-style module~ li2023blip , and then maps the aggregated features to a parameterized latent distribution through a Gaussian head. These latents constitute world tokens, forming an efficient and compact video-action interface. To instantiate the information bottleneck in our video-action learning framework, we adopt a variational formulation~ alemi2017deep that penalizes the KL divergence between the latent distribution and a standard Gaussian prior, and combine this regularization with video and action supervision to form our joint learning objective. To evaluate the effectiveness of IronMan, we conduct simulation experiments across two datasets and four benchmarks covering both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings: LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin clean2clean, and RoboTwin clean2random. We further evaluate three real-world manipulation tasks under ID and OOD settings with background and layout shifts. Across these evaluations, IronMan achieves strong ID performance and OOD robustness while maintaining efficient inference. Related Work sec:realated Vision Language Action Models Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models, such as RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 , OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , ~ black2024pi0 , ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 , and GR00T~ nvidia2025gr00t , have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robot manipulation by transferring the rich visual and semantic knowledge of pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) to embodied control. Leveraging large-scale pretraining on diverse image--text data, VLAs enable robots to better understand instructions, recognize a wide range of objects and scenes, and generalize across tasks and environments beyond the limited coverage of robotic datasets. This has substantially improved the versatility and generalization of robotic policies, establishing VLAs as a prominent direction toward general-purpose robot manipulation. Despite these achievements, modeling physical dynamics remains a fundamental limitation of current VLAs. Because their VLM backbones are pretrained predominantly on static image--text pairs, they receive little direct supervision about temporal evolution. Recent approaches seek to mitigate this limitation during post-training by aligning VLM representations with features of future observations extracted by vision foundation models, thereby injecting dynamics into a VLM backbone~ zheng2025flare,su2026wog,xu2026futurevla,luo2026beingh07latentworldactionmodel,cen2025WorldVLA,cen2025rynnvla . In contrast, our work directly uses a pretrained video generative model as the source of physical dynamics priors. Video Action Models Recent Video-Action Models~(VAMs) increasingly leverage generative video models to provide rich physical dynamics priors~ ICLR2025_e5b5c402,hu2025vpp,bi2026motus,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam . A paradigm is explicit future prediction, where future frames are generated to guide action generation~ li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero, bharadhwaj2025gen2act,liang2025video,li2026turningvideomodelsgeneralist,wang2026stwamsemantictemporalworldaction . However, these methods require full video denoising, introducing substantial inference overhead. This has motivated a more efficient line of work based on implicit future prediction, which bypasses full video denoising and directly extracts one-step features from video backbones~ hu2025vpp, ma2026dit4dit,yan2026svam,pai2026mimicvideo . One-step video features are obtained at the start of denoising process and thus retain redundant visual cues for reconstruction, making them noisy and highly entangled. Existing video-action interfaces allow the action policy to attend to these redundant visual details without explicit information constraints: ~ ma2026dit4dit,pai2026mimicvideo directly connect one-step features to action tokens through cross-attention. hu2025vpp,yan2026svam transform them with learned projection modules. To address this limitation, we introduce an information-constrained interface that explicitly limits the information transferred from video to action. Information Bottleneck The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle provides a framework for learning compact representations that preserve task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variations tishby1999information . Its extensions to deep learning, particularly the Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) alemi2017deep , make such information constraints tractable and have been widely adopted to improve representation compactness, invariance, and generalization. In robot manipulation, recent works further apply IB-style objectives to suppress redundant information in visuomotor representations and retain features relevant to action prediction bai2025rethinking,zhang2026information,pmlr-v162-du22b . Building upon this theoretical foundation, we address a more challenging and specialized problem: learning compact and manipulation-relevant representations from highly noisy, redundant, and entangled video features. Such representations jointly encode rich visual details and dynamics, making it difficult to isolate information useful for control. This problem has remained largely unexplored in prior IB-based methods for robot manipulation. title: AutodidactWAM: Cross-Modal Self-Distillation from Generated Video to Robot Actions
summary: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune to a previously unseen robot, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We evaluate closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place. The native action succeeds only approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% of the time, respectively, and performs worse on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM, a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, that runs on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. Paired with the native prediction, these recovered actions provide preferred targets for fine-tuning only the action-related layers, while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare supervised relabeling with a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches approximately 75%, 47%, and 42% pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success, compared with 17%, 10%, and 7% for the native action. A hybrid objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) performs best: on Oreo, the training object, it reaches 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object, it reaches 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy, indicating that the combination of training objectives, rather than the contrastive objective alone, drives the observed gains.
full_text: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos~3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model, with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune, to a robot absent from pre-training, a Unitree~G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video--action asymmetry: the video already renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We score closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp (hand reaching a graspable pose), grasp, and pick-and-place, where the native action, on pilot objects, succeeds only / / of the time, worse still on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM: a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, run on the model's own generated video to recover an action estimate through those same three stages. Paired with the native prediction , the resulting preferred target fine-tunes only the action-related layers, with the training loss evaluated on action outputs while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare two ways to use this pair: plain supervised relabeling and a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO, rather than committing to either. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches / / pre-grasp/grasp/pick-and-place success, against the native / / . A hybrid self-distillation objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) produces the strongest policy among the configurations tested: on Oreo, our training object, it reaches pre-grasp and full-task success; on the held-out object, it reaches and . Plain Flow-DPO, trained without any additional losses, reaches success everywhere despite validation preference accuracy—evidence that it is the combination of terms, not the contrastive objective alone, that drives the gains above. INTRODUCTION sec:intro Progress on generalist robot manipulation is gated by action-labeled data: teleoperation is slow, robot-specific, and must be repeated for every new embodiment~ zhao2023aloha,chi2024umi,oxe2023 , hardest for dexterous multi-fingered hands. World-action models (WAMs) address this via large-scale pre-training that predicts both future video and actions from vision and language~ cosmos1,cosmos3,gr00tn1,gr1,unipi . Cosmos~3~ cosmos3 is one such model: video and action tokens are noised and denoised jointly within one rectified-flow sampling trajectory~ liu2023rectified,lipman2023flowmatching (Sec.~ sec:prelim ). We adapt Cosmos~3 to a Unitree~G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, an embodiment absent from pre-training, via a lightweight LoRA fine-tune on a mixed in-house G1 corpus. The two output modalities transfer very unequally: the generated video is usually visually plausible and temporally coherent, although occasional hallucinations remain and are characterized separately (Sec.~ sec:screening ); the co-generated action output looks plausible on its own but is systematically mis-targeted in space, completing the task in only of closed-loop pick-and-place trials and reaching pre-grasp in just (Table~ tab:pilot ). This suggests task-consistent information is represented more effectively in the generated video than in the co-generated action tokens, and more fine-tuning does not fix it: SFT loss decreases and DPO validation preference accuracy saturates at within the first round, while the on-policy task metric that tracks real behavior --- headline wrist DTW/path --- does not follow (Fig.~ fig:losses , Sec.~ sec:analysis ). This points to a residual cross-modal consistency problem between the video and action outputs of one generation, related to a forward--inverse asymmetry~ wav2026 , an executability gap~ eva2026 , or a mismatch between plausible video and control-relevant dynamics~ vampo2026 in concurrent work. We recover that correspondence with a frozen perception stack --- hand detection~ yolo , a hand-pose model~ hamer adapted once to the robot hand, and inverse kinematics --- run on each generated rollout to give a full action trajectory , paired with the native prediction to fine-tune the action-related layers toward the resulting target (Sec.~ sec:impl ). We compare two ways to use this pair (Sec.~ sec:obj ): plain supervised relabeling onto , and a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO~ wallace2024diffusiondpo that prefers over , since token-level DPO~ rafailov2023dpo needs a tractable likelihood actions do not have. The generated video is teacher-forced as clean conditioning in both cases, so gradients update only the action-related layers and cannot degrade video quality; using the model's own prediction as the rejected sample mirrors self-play preference optimization~ spin2024 . Every training example needs only a composited anchor frame; seeds and LLM-generated prompt variations~ leo2024 turn it into an effectively unbounded stream of tuples with no manual annotation, in the lineage of self-training and self-distillation~ star2022,noisystudent2020,spin2024 applied here across the outputs of one model. The perception stack itself carries only a one-time training cost from synthetic renders (Sec.~ sec:extractor ), so the method adds no further teleoperation as it scales; relative to recent work on the same gap, we repair the action output offline rather than with reinforcement learning~ wav2026,eva2026,vampo2026,wmpo2025 (Sec.~ sec:related ). Contributions. We identify and quantify a video--action generalization asymmetry in a jointly-trained WAM adapted to an unseen dexterous humanoid embodiment: the generated video renders the task on most seeds, while the co-generated action output produces plausible-looking but mis-targeted motion, reaching the pre-grasp pose only of the time and completing the full pick-and-place task in of closed-loop trials on the real robot (Table~ tab:pilot ). We propose AutodidactWAM, which recovers executable action targets from the model's own generated video and uses them to align the action prediction for the adapted embodiment, without collecting additional task-specific teleoperation (Sec.~ sec:obj , sec:teleopscope ). We introduce a scalable synthetic data engine that generates self-distillation pairs from a small set of static observations through seed, prompt, and object-placement diversification. RELATED WORK sec:related VLA policies and video-as-control. Action policies trained on heterogeneous robot corpora~ oxe2023,rt2,openvla,gr00tn1 , often with a diffusion action head~ chi2023diffusionpolicy , still generally need demonstrations on a robot outside the training mixture; our starting point --- Cosmos~3 with a lightweight LoRA on the new embodiment --- sits in this family, and our contribution begins where it usually ends, when the adapted action branch still does not produce competent behavior. Separately, world models have served as planners or manipulation pretraining, with a separate policy or inverse-dynamics model turning predicted frames into actions~ unipi,avdc,gr1,genie,vpt2022,lapa2024,doasido2025 . We differ in that video and action are two outputs of one model and the generated video repairs that same model's action branch rather than driving a downstream controller; the recovered target is used contrastively against the model's own , not as a plain regression target. The video--action gap, and preference optimization. Several recent methods target the same mismatch: WAV~ wav2026 frames it as a forward--inverse asymmetry with a subgoal generator and a sparse inverse model; EVA~ eva2026 names it the executability gap and RL-tunes the video branch against an inverse-dynamics reward trained on real robot data; VAMPO~ vampo2026 and WMPO~ wmpo2025 apply policy optimization to sharpen visual dynamics or run in-world-model RL for a VLA policy. We differ on four points: we correct the action branch and leave video untouched; the optimization is offline and preference-based, with no reward model, no training-time rollouts, and no real-robot inverse-dynamics data; the extractor is a hand-pose reconstructor with IK, for the dexterous contact-rich regime where low-dimensional inverse models are weakest; and every signal is a contrastive pair against the model's own for the same generation. That contrastive step builds on DPO~ rafailov2023dpo and its diffusion extension~ wallace2024diffusiondpo (Sec.~ sec:obj adapts the latter to rectified flow) and on self-improvement from a model's own outputs~ noisystudent2020,star2022,spin2024 ; AutodidactWAM applies this across modalities of one model, the stronger (video) supervising the weaker (actions). METHOD sec:method AutodidactWAM has three stages (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). First, from one anchor frame and a language instruction the world model generates a video rollout together with its native action prediction. Second, a frozen perception stack reads the generated video and recovers a second, independent action trajectory. Third, the model's action branch is fine-tuned to prefer the recovered trajectory over its own native one, with a preference objective adapted to the model's rectified-flow formulation and with the generated video teacher-forced so that only the action tokens are updated. These stages are then iterated: because the pair describes the action branch as it currently behaves, it is regenerated from the updated model at a fixed step interval (Sec.~ sec:pair ). The remainder of this section makes each stage precise: Sec.~ sec:prelim recaps the model, Sec.~ sec:pair constructs the contrastive pair and its on-policy refresh, Sec.~ sec:extractor details the extractor that recovers , Sec.~ sec:obj gives the objectives, Sec.~ sec:tf explains how the generated video is teacher-forced, Sec.~ sec:vidsrc states where the generated video comes from, and Sec.~ sec:impl lists implementation details. Preliminaries: Cosmos~3 as a joint video--action flow model sec:prelim Cosmos~3~ cosmos3 is trained as a rectified flow~ liu2023rectified,lipman2023flowmatching : for clean latent , noise , , the interpolant and the network regresses the constant velocity . One network denoises video and action latent tokens jointly under full attention; they are not two separate branches or subnetworks, but two token types produced by the same generator, distinguished only by their own encoder/decoder and modality embedding (Sec.~ sec:impl lists exactly which action-specific tensors, plus a LoRA adapter, we fine-tune --- every layer shared with video stays frozen). For brevity, the rest of the paper still calls this action-specific slice the ``action branch,'' but it names a set of I/O tensors within one generator, not a separate network. At inference in policy mode, the model is conditioned on an anchor frame and prompt (no timestep embedding on conditioning tokens) and denoises video and action tokens together along one sampler trajectory, emitting a rollout and an action chunk , , for the G1's -D action space (per-arm wrist pose, fingertip targets, a fixed head term), mapped by a fixed IK step to the robot's joint commands. title: DensiTok: Making Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting See More Views Than It Is Given
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructs a scene in a single forward pass, replacing per-scene optimization with a network trained across many scenes. Its quality, however, degrades sharply as the number of input images drops. The bottleneck is upstream of the reconstruction heads: from a few unposed views, the internal representation they read carries no evidence for unobserved regions, leaving holes, floaters, and blur. The common remedy supplies that evidence as pixels, synthesizing extra views with an image or video generator and re-encoding them, which is costly and not 3D-consistent by construction. We instead densify the evidence itself. We present DensiTok, a plug-in module for pretrained feed-forward 3DGS models that densifies their internal geometry tokens directly, making a frozen backbone behave as though it had observed many more views than it was given. DensiTok compresses those tokens into a compact latent space, completes the latents of the unobserved viewpoints in a single flow-matching step conditioned on camera geometry, and decodes them back into tokens that the original reconstruction heads. The same module design can be integrated into different pretrained predictors while keeping each backbone and its reconstruction heads frozen. Completion in a low-dimensional latent space requires no image synthesis or additional encoder passes. Across three pretrained backbones and two benchmarks, DensiTok consistently improves sparse-view reconstruction and recovers much of the gap to dense-view reconstruction.
full_text: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstructs a scene in a single forward pass, replacing per-scene optimization with a network trained across many scenes. Its quality, however, degrades sharply as the number of input images drops. The bottleneck is upstream of the reconstruction heads: from a few unposed views, the internal representation they read carries no evidence for unobserved regions, leaving holes, floaters, and blur. The common remedy supplies that evidence as pixels, synthesizing extra views with an image or video generator and re-encoding them, which is costly and not 3D-consistent by construction. We instead densify the evidence itself. We present DensiTok, a plug-in module for pretrained feed-forward 3DGS models that densifies their internal geometry tokens directly, making a frozen backbone behave as though it had observed many more views than it was given. DensiTok compresses those tokens into a compact latent space, completes the latents of the unobserved viewpoints in a single flow-matching step conditioned on camera geometry, and decodes them back into tokens that the original reconstruction heads. The same module design can be integrated into different pretrained predictors while keeping each backbone and its reconstruction heads frozen. Completion in a low-dimensional latent space requires no image synthesis or additional encoder passes. Across three pretrained backbones and two benchmarks, DensiTok consistently improves sparse-view reconstruction and recovers much of the gap to dense-view reconstruction. Project page: . Introduction Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts cameras, geometry, and appearance in a single network pass, replacing per-scene optimization with a model amortized over many scenes. This makes reconstruction practical from unposed, unconstrained image collections, and recent backbones accept an arbitrary number of input views. Such models~ jiang2025anysplat,liu2025worldmirror,lin2025depth share a common anatomy: a geometry encoder maps the input images to a set of view-aligned geometry tokens, and camera, depth, and Gaussian heads decode that shared representation into the final reconstruction. Their quality, however, tracks the visual evidence they are given. The right side of~ plots reconstruction quality against the number of input views for several recent backbones, and it degrades in the few-view regime that motivated feed-forward reconstruction in the first place. The cause sits upstream of the heads: a handful of unposed images gives the encoder little cross-view evidence, so its tokens describe only the surfaces that were actually observed. Occluded and uncovered surfaces have no tokens at all, and the heads turn that gap into holes, floaters, and blurred novel views. What the model lacks, then, is not pixels but tokens. This suggests a different target: rather than acquiring the views it never saw, synthesize the geometry tokens those views would have produced. Existing remedies differ mainly in where they supply the missing evidence. The dominant line of work operates in image space, either synthesizing extra input views with a multi-view or video diffusion model~ gao2024cat3d, zhong2025taming , or repairing those renderings, and refitting the scene to them~ chen2024mvsplat360, yin2025gsfixer . Both incur two separate costs: running a large generative model at full image resolution, and then running the geometry encoder again over the enlarged set of views. Because pixels are not a shared 3D representation, consistency across generated views is encouraged but never enforced, so the reconstruction must fit views that disagree with one another. More fundamentally, pixels are a detour. The reconstruction needs only tokens for the missing viewpoints. These methods produce entire RGB frames instead, which the encoder then compresses into those tokens, so most of what the generator produced is discarded immediately. A second line of work supplies no new evidence at all, and instead trains feed-forward architectures specialized for sparse views, extracting as much as possible from the correspondences the input views do provide~ chen2024mvsplat, xu2025depthsplat,smart2024splatt3r . Such models remain bounded by what those views cover, and they are standalone architectures tied to a small, fixed number of views. Closest to our setting, recent work~ jang2026repurposing generates directly in token space, but without a compressed latent it must run cascaded multi-step generators on features with over a thousand channels, so generation stays expensive. We introduce DensiTok, a plug-in that densifies the geometry tokens of a pretrained feed-forward 3DGS model so that its heads reconstruct as if from far more views. As shown in~ , DensiTok sits between the geometry encoder and the reconstruction heads, with the encoder frozen and the heads either frozen or minimally adapted. The encoder's output is naturally organized as a sequence of per-view token sets, one for each input image. DensiTok augments token sets for viewpoints that were never observed, so the heads receive the representation of a dense capture even though only a few images were encoded. Doing this directly on the tokens is costly: the heads read tokens from several layers of the encoder, and each layer has over a thousand channels in current backbones. DensiTok instead treats the whole stack of layers as one object: it compresses them into a single compact latent per view, completes the unobserved views in that latent space, and expands the result back into tokens for every layer. Two components realize this design. The first is a variational autoencoder (VAE)~ kingma2013auto with Level-Adaptive Modulation (LAM-VAE). Its encoder predicts how much each feature level should contribute for each token, fuses the features accordingly, and compresses the fused tokens into compact latents. This lets a single latent stand in for all layers without fixing in advance which layers matter, since that varies across backbones and even across scenes. The second is a Diffusion Transformer (DiT)~ peebles2023scalable for Geometry Latent Augmentation: it extends the latent sequence with the unobserved views, generating their latents from the observed ones in a single flow-matching~ lipman2022flow step, conditioned on their cameras. Since the input is unposed, these cameras are not given. The backbone's own camera head predicts them for the observed views, and the cameras of the new views are interpolated along the path through those predictions, so the new views densify the captured trajectory rather than extrapolate beyond it. The VAE decoder then expands the completed latent sequence back into tokens at every layer the heads expect, and the camera, depth, and Gaussian heads decode them. Image-space methods supply the missing evidence indirectly, as pixels that the encoder must process again. DensiTok produces the evidence itself, once and in a compact latent space, in exactly the form the heads already consume. We evaluate DensiTok on RealEstate10K~ zhou2018stereo and DL3DV~ ling2024dl3dv with three representative feed-forward 3DGS backbones: AnySplat~ jiang2025anysplat , WorldMirror~ liu2025worldmirror , and Depth Anything 3~ lin2025depth . DensiTok consistently improves novel-view rendering quality from sparse, unposed inputs. This comes at a bounded cost: the encoder still processes only the sparse inputs, and generation is a single step in a compact latent space, so where DensiTok reaches dense-view quality, it does so in less time than dense-view reconstruction itself. Related Work sec:related_work Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting Feed-forward 3DGS amortizes reconstruction across scenes by using a single network to predict Gaussian attributes, cameras, and depth from a set of images in one pass. Posed methods build explicit correspondence machinery, with pixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat using epipolar matching, MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat constructing cost volumes, and DepthSplat~ xu2025depthsplat adding monocular depth priors. Splatt3R~ smart2024splatt3r , NoPoSplat~ ye2025no , PF3plat~ hong2025pf3plat , and SelfSplat~ kang2025selfsplat remove the pose requirement for sparse unposed inputs. More recent general backbones, including AnySplat~ jiang2025anysplat , WorldMirror~ liu2025worldmirror , and Depth Anything 3~ lin2025depth , accept an arbitrary number of unconstrained views and jointly predict cameras, geometry, and Gaussians, typically by pairing a large geometry transformer with lightweight decoding heads. All of these models, however, are bounded by what their inputs show. With only a few views, overlap is limited, pose and depth are ambiguous, so the geometry tokens describe only the visible parts of the scene. Therefore, they render everything the tokens do not cover as holes, floaters, and blurred novel views. DensiTok instead treats sparse-view reconstruction as a completion problem inside the representation, augmenting token sets for additional viewpoints. Generative Priors for 3D Reconstruction Image-space generative priors are typically incorporated in two ways. The first augments the sparse input set with pose-controlled synthetic views before reconstruction, as in CAT3D~ gao2024cat3d , VistaDream~ wang2025vistadream , and Bolt3D~ szymanowicz2025bolt3d . The second starts from a coarse 3DGS reconstruction, renders it along novel camera trajectories, and uses a video or multi-view generative model to refine or complete the rendered sequence, as in MVSplat360~ chen2024mvsplat360 , FlowR~ fischer2025flowr , VideoScene~ wang2025videoscene , GSFixer~ yin2025gsfixer , and G4Splat~ ni2026g4splat . Both can synthesize plausible content for unobserved regions, but the generative step operates in RGB or generic video latent spaces with no shared 3D representation to respect. Consequently, inconsistencies across the generated views turn into geometric artifacts. Both also incur two separate costs: a generative model runs for many sampling steps at image resolution, and the scene must then be reconstructed from the enlarged set of views. DensiTok instead generates in the backbone's own token space, so the completed representation is decoded into one Gaussian scene by the same heads, with no image synthesis and no second reconstruction. Generation in 3D-Aware Latent Spaces A separate line avoids image synthesis altogether by generating in a latent space that decodes straight to 3D. LN3Diff~ lan2025ln3diff++ diffuses a 3D-structured latent decoded into neural fields, Prometheus~ yang2025prometheus generates multi-view RGB-D latents that a Gaussian decoder turns into pixel-aligned Gaussians, and Wonderland~ liang2025wonderland lifts camera-controlled video latents directly to 3DGS. Most recently, GLD~ jang2026repurposing uses the features of a pretrained geometry encoder~ wang2025vggt as the latent space itself, applying flow matching to selected feature levels for feature-space novel-view synthesis and deriving the remaining levels by propagating the result through the frozen encoder. This removes the need for a VAE, but the generated levels keep the encoder's full width of over a thousand channels. Therefore, GLD runs cascaded multi-step generators on them, decodes RGB with a separately trained decoder. DensiTok differs on each point. It compresses all feature levels into a single four-channel latent and completes the sequence in one step to produce a Gaussian scene rather than images. title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5 of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75 , and achieves a 1.5 inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance–efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine pretrained vision-language representations with action prediction to achieve strong performance in robotic manipulation~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,kim2025fine,black2024pi_0,Intelligence202505AV . However, their computational cost limits real-time deployment. At every control step, these models process long multimodal sequences dominated by visual tokens from camera observations. Processing these tokens through a large language backbone incurs substantial computation and latency, constraining the frequency at which the policy can respond to changes in the environment. One promising direction for closing this gap is to exploit visual redundancy through token pruning or caching. Pruning reduces the number of visual tokens processed, while caching reuses visual representations across control steps. Prior work~ wang2026specprunevla shows that VLA policies can tolerate even random token removal at moderate pruning rates, suggesting substantial redundancy in the visual input. The challenge is to exploit this redundancy more aggressively while preserving the visual information needed for effective control. Existing approaches largely fall into two categories. Training-free methods~ NEURIPS2025_f062da19,ICLR2026_1223ca2b,ma2026safe,liu2025bridging,NEURIPS2025_3a2ef31a,li2025sp,wang2026specprunevla,tan2025think freeze the base VLA and select tokens using heuristics such as attention scores, temporal changes, and motion thresholds. However, these signals only indirectly estimate token importance and do not capture the actual impact of token removal on model performance. Moreover, such methods often require carefully tuned layer- or timestep-specific hyperparameters or access to internal states and attention maps, limiting compatibility with existing acceleration techniques. Training-based approaches~ jiang2025better,feng2026see instead learn token selection jointly with the base VLA, incurring substantial backbone fine-tuning costs~ kim2025fine . This also couples the resulting VLA checkpoint to the specific pruning mechanism, limiting its deployment flexibility. These limitations motivate a central question: Can we learn effective visual token selection from its impact on downstream actions while keeping the base VLA frozen? To this end, we introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), a visual pruning framework for VLAs that trains a lightweight token selection policy based on its effect on the predicted action: actions produced from pruned visual contexts should remain consistent with those produced by the same VLA using the full visual context (Fig.~ fig:full-pipeline ). Combined with auxiliary ground-truth action supervision, this teacher-consistency objective directly links visual token selection to downstream control behavior. VLA-ACL trains a patch scoring network to assign an importance score to each visual token and retains the highest-scoring tokens per camera view before passing them to the language backbone at inference. During training, to enable gradient flow to the patch scorer, we use a soft Top- relaxation~ lapsum2025 to gate visual embeddings and gradually sharpen the selection weights, reducing the mismatch with hard pruning at inference. Our framework neither accesses nor modifies the internal states of the base model, making it broadly compatible with existing VLA architectures. Empirically, VLA-ACL requires just a few hours of training on a single GPU, using only a lightweight Transformer attention as the patch scorer, and avoids costly multi-GPU fine-tuning of the full policy. We evaluate VLA-ACL on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks. Our framework supports aggressive pruning rates up to 87.5 of visual tokens and reduces FLOPs by up to 75 , while maintaining success rates comparable to full-context inference. These results demonstrate a strong performance–efficiency trade-off against frozen-VLA pruning baselines, as shown in Fig.~ fig:libero-10-pareto and Table~ tab:main_libero_results . VLA-ACL thus establishes action consistency as an effective learning signal for visual token selection, enabling aggressive pruning while preserving the information needed for control. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models build on pre-trained vision-language representations~ zhai2023sigmoid,oquab2024dinov to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions~ Beyer2024PaliGemmaAV,Karamcheti2024PrismaticVI . Representative models include OpenVLA~ pmlr-v270-kim25c and the -series~ black2024pi_0,Intelligence202505AV . OpenVLA processes visual patch tokens and language instructions through a large language backbone~ Touvron2023Llama2O , while OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine improves action-generation efficiency through parallel decoding of action chunks. Despite these advances, processing long visual token sequences remains computationally expensive, hindering their practicality for real-world tasks. Efficient VLA Inference sec:related-efficiency VLA inference acceleration has been explored through compact architectures shukor2025smolvla,Wen2024TinyVLATF , dynamic depth control deervla , and visual token pruning. Among pruning approaches, training-free methods operate on a frozen VLA stack and offer plug-and-play inference acceleration. Building on token pruning for vision-language models chen2024image,zhang2024sparsevlm,alvar2025divprune , these methods commonly score visual tokens using text-to-vision attention magnitudes. Recent approaches further incorporate feature diversity, edge saliency, temporal feature changes, and moving averages of action-to-vision attention to guide token selection in sequential robotic observations~ NEURIPS2025_3a2ef31a,li2025sp,wang2026specprunevla,liu2025bridging . Besides selection criteria, methods further differ in layer-aware treatment, as attention patterns shift across the language backbone's layers. Attention scores from deeper layers, which more directly reflect action-relevance, are used to guide token selection liu2025bridging,ma2026safe . However, since these scores are only available from the previous forward pass, relying on them degrades performance at low retention rates luo2026gate . Other methods instead vary the pruning rate itself across layers, guided by heuristics such as attention entropy NEURIPS2025_f062da19,wang2026specprunevla,NEURIPS2025_3a2ef31a . Pruning is further regulated along the temporal dimension: full-context forward passes are executed at the beginning of the control sequence to fill up caches NEURIPS2025_f062da19,liu2025bridging or the pruning rate is adjusted according to signals such as end-effector velocity ICLR2026_1223ca2b,li2025sp,wang2026specprunevla . In both cases, these strategies rely on carefully tuned thresholds. These layer and time-varying mechanisms come with an additional cost: accessing and modifying internal attention mechanisms are incompatible with fused-attention kernels such as FlashAttention flashattention or graph-compiled inference, offsetting the very speedups they aim to provide. Taken together, training-free methods still struggle at high pruning rates, as they rely on a growing stack of heuristic-driven strategies that each require carefully tuned hyperparameters, rather than a signal tied directly to task performance. Training-based methods instead learn the pruning decision jointly with the VLA. To handle the non-differentiable hard pruning objective, LightVLA jiang2025better trains the entire VLA stack using a Gumbel-softmax jang2017categorical token selector. Grid-S feng2026see replaces discrete token selection with a differentiable grid-sampling module fine-tuned end-to-end. Both report strong performance at aggressive pruning ratios, but the pruner and the backbone have to be re-trained, which can take multiple days even on 8 frontier GPUs kim2025fine using parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA hu2022lora . VLA-ACL sits in the gap between these two regimes: like the training-free methods, it keeps the VLA frozen, and it trains only a small patch scorer in just a few GPU hours; like the training-based methods, the pruning decisions are learned. A single hyperparameter controls how many visual tokens are kept per view, applied before tokens ever enter the language backbone. This mechanism remains constant at every control step, eliminating the need for temporal controllers and keeping VLA-ACL compatible with existing inference-acceleration techniques. Crucially, rather than scoring tokens through intermediate proxies, VLA-ACL learns this scoring function by optimizing action consistency between pruned and full-context forwards of the same frozen VLA, directly tying token selection to its effect on the predicted action. Method VLA-ACL learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the original VLA model frozen. A small Transformer-based~ attention patch scorer assigns an importance score to each visual token. At inference, the highest-scoring tokens are retained before entering the language backbone. During training, the scorer is optimized to maintain action consistency between pruned-context predictions and full-context teacher predictions, with ground-truth actions providing auxiliary supervision. title: ViDAL: A Visual Dynamics-Grounded Action Latent Space for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. However, existing action representations primarily model action trajectories, with limited consideration of the visual dynamics induced by these actions. We introduce ViDAL, a Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space that anchors continuous action latents in the future visual dynamics of the scene. Specifically, ViDAL learns action latent space by training an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. When integrated into downstream robot policies, the proposed Action VAE serves as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and enables optional future-video prediction as an additional capability. Empirically, ViDAL outperforms competitive baselines on LIBERO with 98.1% average success, improves a multi-task $π_{0.5}$ policy on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random) success rates over 50 dual-arm tasks, and yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on real-world single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX robot platforms.

Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ brohan2022rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,liu2024rdt have emerged as a popular paradigm for generalist robot manipulation, directly predicting actions from visual observations and language instructions. Since actions define the interface between the VLA policy and robot control, their representation determines both the learning target and the executable control output. In recent VLA systems, action representations usually take three predominant forms: raw action chunks regressed by a continuous head~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,chi2023diffusion , discrete action tokens produced by a tokenizer~ pertsch2025fast,wang2025vqvla,zhou2025beast,faster2025 , or continuous action latents produced by a learned autoencoder~ tan2024rold . These representations primarily model action trajectories, but manipulation actions are meaningful through their effects on the scene, such as object motion, contact changes, and task-state transitions. Accordingly, as VLA gradually scales to long-horizon, multi-task and multi-scenario manipulation~ walke2023bridgedata,openx2023,khazatsky2024droid,octo2024 , an effective action representation should account for not only the action trajectory but also the visual dynamics induced by the action. Recent works have pursued two complementary directions: learning compact action representations and incorporating visual dynamics into VLA policies. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (a), early action tokenizers or autoencoders compress action chunks into compact tokens or latents~ pertsch2025fast,wang2025vqvla,zhou2025beast,faster2025,tan2024rold , yielding representations primarily optimized for action reconstruction, without modeling visual dynamics. As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser (b), VLAs with visual prediction use future video or world-model signals to guide policy learning~ assran2025vjepa2,hu2025vpp,cen2025worldvla,xu2026futurevla,shang2026dynvla,su2026worldguidance . Together, these directions suggest that visual dynamics benefit action learning, but leave open how they should shape the action representation. Since actions are visually contextual, the challenge is learning an executable, visual dynamics-grounded action latent space. We propose (Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space, Figure~ fig:teaser (c)) to inject visual dynamics directly into the action latent during representation learning. In , a frozen video VAE extracts the initial and future visual latents from each robot trajectory, and an Action VAE encodes the corresponding action chunk into a continuous action latent. A lightweight visual-dynamics predictor then maps the initial visual latent and the action latent to the future visual latent, training the action latent to preserve executable actions while explaining future scene dynamics conditioned on the current observation. For downstream policy learning, only the frozen Action VAE is required: its encoder produces action latent targets for VLA training, and its decoder maps VLA-predicted latents to executable robot actions. Thus, the decoupled design lets plug into both regression (e.g., OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft ) and flow-matching (e.g., ~ intelligence2025pi05 ) action experts without modifying the VLM backbone. The video VAE also enables future-video prediction for visualizing the learned dynamics. We evaluate on two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO~ liu2024libero , RoboTwin~2.0~ mu2024robotwin ) and two real-world platforms (single-arm Franka, dual-arm ARX), using both regression (OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft , StarVLA-OFT~ ye2026starvlaalpha ) and flow-matching ( ~ intelligence2025pi05 ) action experts as the downstream policy. Across all four settings, consistently improves the underlying VLA policies and surpasses competitive action-representation baselines on LIBERO (Figure~ fig:teaser , right): on the higher-dimensional dual-arm RoboTwin~2.0, it lifts a multi-task policy by Clean and Random over 50 tasks, and on real robots it delivers absolute gain on Franka and on ARX. These significant gains across simulation and real, single- and dual-arm settings establish visual-dynamics grounding as a better design principle for action representations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce , which, to our knowledge, is the first approach to ground action latents in future visual dynamics for VLA models, learned via an Action VAE jointly trained on action reconstruction and future visual latent prediction. We propose a plug-in action-latent interface for downstream VLA policies, where the frozen Action VAE serves as the action representation for both regression and flow-matching action experts, requiring no changes to the VLM backbone. We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation (LIBERO, RoboTwin~2.0) and real-world (single-arm Franka, dual-arm ARX) environments. Results show that consistently improves both regression and flow-matching VLA policies and surpasses competitive action-representation methods. Related Work -Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions~ brohan2022rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,driess2023palme,li2024roboflamingo,octo2024,liu2024rdt . Recent VLAs differ mainly in how their action experts generate actions: flow-matching experts in ~ black2024pi0 and ~ intelligence2025pi05 support high-frequency continuous control, while one-step regression experts in OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025openvlaoft and StarVLA-OFT~ ye2026starvlaalpha target faster inference. is orthogonal to these backbones and experts: it changes the action target to a dynamics-grounded latent and decodes the predicted latent back to executable actions, without modifying the underlying VLA architecture. Representations for VLA Models. VLA action representations take three predominant forms, each shaped by a different supervision signal. Raw action chunks are regressed under behavior-cloning~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05,liu2024rdt,chi2023diffusion,zhao2023act ; discrete action tokens compress trajectories via quantization~ pertsch2025fast,wang2025vqvla,zhou2025beast,faster2025 ; and continuous action latents use an autoencoder bottleneck without quantization~ tan2024rold . All three are shaped only by reconstruction, token efficiency, or imitation losses, and rarely consider how the scene visually evolves under each action. explicitly introduces visual dynamics as a direct supervision signal for the action latent, anchoring the representation to the visual effect of each action chunk. Dynamics for VLA Policies. There is also a complementary line that uses visual dynamics to guide VLA policies. JEPA-style methods pretrain on video to provide dynamics-aware features that condition the policy~ assran2025vjepa2,sun2026vlajepa . Future-prediction approaches inject future-frame or video-diffusion signals into the VLM backbone or the policy as auxiliary supervision~ hu2025vpp,jia2025video2act,dreamzero2026 . Other methods use dynamics or world-model signals for action reasoning~ cen2025worldvla,shang2026dynvla,xu2026futurevla,su2026worldguidance . These designs entangle dynamics learning with policy training and tie the visual signal to a VLA architecture, so the dynamics machinery must be retrained for every new backbone. confines visual dynamics to the action latent during representation learning and freezes it before policy training, so the same dynamics-grounded Action VAE can be plugged into different VLM backbones and action experts. Method Overview learns a reusable action representation whose continuous latent is grounded by visual dynamics. As shown in Figure~ fig:method_overview , given a robot trajectory with observation clip and action chunk , an Action VAE encodes the action chunk into a continuous action latent that is jointly supervised by action reconstruction and visual-dynamics prediction based on video VAE model(Section~ sec:method_visual_dynamics ). Then the frozen Action VAE serves as a plug-in action representation for downstream VLA policy learning (Section~ sec:method_vla_policy ), where the video model is no longer required. Learning the Action Latent Space sec:method_visual_dynamics The central challenge in learning action latents is that action reconstruction alone does not determine which aspects of an action chunk are relevant to policy learning: a low-dimensional latent may reconstruct actions while failing to encode how those actions interact with the current scene. addresses this by adding visual-dynamics supervision, encouraging the action latent to be informative for predicting the future visual latent conditioned on the initial observation. We sample with the standard reparameterization trick and decode it back to the original action chunk: The continuous bottleneck preserves smooth trajectory structure and is compatible with both regression and flow-matching action experts. -Dynamics Supervision. A frozen video encoder extracts an initial visual latent from the current observation and a future visual latent from the subsequent frames as the prediction target, and a lightweight predictor regresses from the initial visual latent and the action latent: Conditioning on is essential because the same action chunk can correspond to different scene transitions in different contexts. The predictor therefore drives to retain action-relevant scene-transition structure rather than only low-level action statistics. Both and are used only during representation learning and discarded afterwards, so deployment requires no video model. Objective. The Action VAE is jointly trained with four complementary terms, where reconstructs the action chunk in the time domain, follows FAST's DCT-based action tokenization~ pertsch2025fast to preserve temporal frequency structure, regularizes the latent distribution, and aligns the action latent with future scene evolution; the stop-gradient operator keeps the visual target space fixed. title: VOMMI: Collecting and Leveraging Portable Demonstrations for Mobile Manipulation
summary: Portable mobile-manipulation demonstrations can help alleviate data scarcity for embodied intelligence, but obtaining reliable, low-cost, and robot-free motion supervision from RGB observations remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on teleoperation or specialized devices equipped with additional sensing hardware, while directly using estimated visual odometry (VO) trajectories can introduce inconsistencies due to accumulated drift and imperfect motion supervision. We present the Visual-Odometry-Conditioned Mobile Manipulation Interface (VOMMI), a portable demonstration collection and learning framework that connects portable RGB demonstrations to vision-language-action (VLA) post-training through offline trajectory reconstruction and online visual-motion conditioning. VOMMI synchronizes body and hand views to capture navigation context and local object interactions without requiring human-robot kinematic correspondence calibration. R2-VO refines offline demonstration trajectories using sparse geometric anchors and produces causal local-motion tokens over multiple prediction horizons for online policy conditioning. An action-group residual adapter incorporates these tokens only into the base branch. Experiments use a 500-trajectory portable for each task, with 75 trajectories held out for RGB-VO evaluation, and 200 robot demonstrations as references. Our policy, post-trained only on portable demonstrations, achieves 18.2% lower base-velocity error than a policy trained with robot-collected demonstrations, while maintaining comparable end-effector translation accuracy. Offline reconstruction reduces absolute trajectory errors for the body and hand streams by 24.6% on average relative to the best evaluated baseline for each stream. The complete system improves the mean success rate by 8.3 percentage points over OpenPI 0.5 across three real-robot tasks.

Introduction Mobile manipulation is a foundational capability for embodied intelligence, enabling robots to interact with the physical world in applications ranging from domestic assistance and infrastructure inspection to industrial automation. Mobile manipulation data collection typically involves long-horizon tasks, composed of multiple sequential stages, requiring a generalizable policy that can coordinate precise whole-body motion with fine-grained end-effector (EE) manipulation. Recent whole-body vision-language-action models (VLAs) jiang2026wholebodyvla,hu2026openhlmempiricalrecipewholebody and world action models (WAMs) li2026omega0latentpredictiveworld, zheng2026motionwamfoundationworldaction advocate learning mobile manipulation as an integrated whole-body behavior rather than as separate navigation and arm-manipulation skills, but scaling such learning remains challenging due to the limited availability of demonstration data. Existing demonstration-collection paradigms often rely on teleoperation, which is expensive, slow, and difficult to scale for scene generalization. Cross-embodiment collection methods, such as UMI chi2024umi and its variants FastUMI ,IPhUMI,xu2026hommi,huang2026mobileumi , use handheld grippers with mounted cameras to collect manipulation demonstrations, while egocentric approaches use head-mounted cameras to capture broader scene context shi2026egohumanoid . For mobile manipulation tasks, existing methods have shown that portable demonstration collection is feasible ha2024umionlegs,huang2026mobileumi,xu2026hommi . However, these approaches commonly depend on special devices, such as high-quality IMU sensors, GoPro cameras, iPhones, and VR headsets, which raise the hardware barrier for more accessible data collection and limit the number of demonstrators who can participate. Using visual odometry (VO) can reduce the complexity of the data-collection hardware, but it remains vulnerable to drift over long trajectories and large rotations, which can degrade data quality or even make the data unusable. Existing portable collection pipelines typically require accurate device calibration to recover reliable trajectories, placing strict demands on data post-processing, especially for mobile manipulation tasks. As shown in Figure~ fig:motivation , we propose a VO-conditioned mobile-manipulation interface (VOMMI) to establish the data pipeline for training whole-body VLA policies from portable demonstrations. VOMMI records RGB videos from body and hand views and uses VO to recover local motion cues, enabling low-cost demonstration collection. Collection-time pose references are used only for offline metric supervision and evaluation, while deployment relies solely on RGB observations, camera intrinsics, timestamps, and robot proprioception. To improve trajectory quality during offline data processing, VOMMI can leverage pretrained visual geometry for base movement. These tokens are fed into the VLA post-training interface and connected only to the base-action residual adapter, while the manipulation residual remains blind to body motion. This design provides the missing local visual proprioception for navigation-conditioned mobile manipulation without claiming global localization or a new general-purpose VO algorithm. VOMMI is designed to test whether portable RGB demonstrations can improve long-horizon mobile-manipulation competence in a VLA policy, while making the answer auditable by separating portable-data supervision from robot-data supervision. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose a portable data-collection protocol for mobile manipulation with separate body and hand views, requiring no access to the target robot or human–robot kinematic correspondence calibration. We present R2-VO, a real-time and refined RGB motion reconstruction module that produces low-latency local motion tokens for online VLA inference and anchor-refined trajectories for offline dataset processing. We define an action interface with dimension-specific reference pose supervision and action-group residuals, so that the manipulation residual remains independent of the body-motion token. Related Work Portable Demonstration Interfaces Portable data collection is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy for mobile manipulators in diverse environments. UMI chi2024umi records in-the-wild manipulation with a portable handheld interface and transfers relative EE actions to a robot. To enhance mobility, UMI-on-Legs combines this interface with a manipulation-centric whole-body controller ha2024umionlegs , while Mobile UMI huang2026mobileumi introduces multiple views and decoupled planar-base and EE representations for mobile manipulation. HoMMI xu2026hommi and EgoHumanoid shi2026egohumanoid further use egocentric human demonstrations to capture whole-body task context. These systems demonstrate the value of extending portable whole-body data from fixed-base to mobile manipulation tasks, but they require customized, dedicated hardware. In contrast, VOMMI addresses a complementary sensing question: how to recover the demonstrator's motion from RGB observations without requiring metric pose or IMU measurements as policy inputs. Robot Learning for Mobile Manipulation Mobile manipulation requires coordinated locomotion and manipulation over extended workspaces. HomeRobot integrates perception, navigation, and manipulation in realistic environments yenamandra2023homerobot . Recent whole-body learning methods address complementary control challenges, from force-aware compensation for contact-rich loco-manipulation to latent policies for unified loco-manipulation jiang2026wholebodyvla,ding2025quarvlavisionlanguageactionmodelquadruped . In addition, bimanual manipulation learning uses egocentric demonstrations to learn active perception behaviors chuang2026lookfocusactefficient . DECOWAM~ DECOWAM trains adapters by separating base and arm latents and conditioning on base velocity to improve both future-video and action prediction. Despite these advances, existing portable-demonstration-based mobile manipulation policies often lack an explicit representation of recent ego-motion when learning from portable RGB demonstrations. VOMMI addresses this gap by incorporating visual-odometry (VO) observations directly into the VLA and introducing separate residual pathways for body and manipulation actions. This design enables motion-aware whole-body correction without requiring metric pose or IMU measurements as policy inputs at deployment. Visual Body Motion for Policy State Learning-based VO systems such as DROID-SLAM and DPVO improve sequential motion estimation, while VGGT and VGGT-SLAM 2.0 extend feed-forward geometry toward camera and real-time scene reconstruction teed2021droidslam,teed2022dpvo,wang2025vggt,maggio2026vggtslam2 . Beyond geometric reconstruction, recent robot learning studies also explore recovering actionable trajectories from human or egocentric demonstrations, such as observation-only imitation and scalable egocentric data collection karnan2021voilavisualobservationonlyimitationlearning,kareer2024egomimicscalingimitationlearning . However, these approaches either optimize geometric consistency or focus on embodiment alignment, rather than extracting policy-oriented motion for mobile manipulation. VOMMI considers visual motion from a policy-oriented perspective. This causal local representation reduces sensitivity to constant world-frame offsets while preserving short-term ego-motion cues relevant for whole-body control. The resulting token provides a compact visual proprioceptive state for policy conditioning rather than a globally consistent trajectory or localization memory. Data Collection System Dual-view capture and temporal alignment VOMMI is designed around a specific robot-free data-collection requirement: each demonstration must capture both the demonstrator’s locomotion and hand–object interaction using only RGB observations, without relying on additional sensing or target-robot instrumentation. Fig.~ fig:pipeline summarizes the data flow. The demonstrator wears a chest-mounted fisheye RGB camera for scene context and body motion and carries a second fisheye RGB camera on the UMI-style gripper module for interaction. These two views are recorded as complementary streams and reconciled later through local timestamps and trajectory-based compensation, resampled at 15~Hz after validity checks. Each episode stores the language instruction, both videos and intrinsics, tool center point (TCP) and gripper signals, and validity masks. The resulting episode contains both the observations required for RGB reconstruction and the action targets necessary to train a whole-body policy. Collection-time sensor-derived trajectories serve as privileged offline references for R2-VO supervision and evaluation, but are not policy inputs at deployment. As shown in Table~ tab:hardware-cost , the cost of our VOMMI's hardware is significantly lower than that of current portable data acquisition methods. Episode schema and split protocol The collection contains 500 portable episodes per evaluated task. For each task, 75 complete episodes form a fixed held-out RGB-VO evaluation split and are excluded from estimator fitting, canonicalizer fitting, and model selection. The remaining 425 episodes support model development and downstream VLA training under the experimental protocol. title: Catastrophic Forgetting in Sequential Thermal Anti-UAV Detection: The Role of Scale-Conditioned Gradient Imbalance
summary: Counter-UAV systems based on thermal infrared detection must stay accurate as operational datasets evolve, yet sequential fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting of prior tasks, a problem that remains insufficiently characterized in this domain. This continual-learning study measures the stability-plasticity trade-off in YOLOMG, a YOLOv5-based detector run as a single thermal-infrared stream with the motion channel disabled, trained sequentially across three anti-UAV benchmarks of rising scale difficulty: Anti-UAV-RGBT, Anti-UAV410, and CST Anti-UAV. Naive fine-tuning on CST yields a Forgetting Measure of -0.605 against the Stage 1 ceiling, corresponding to a 90% capability loss, with -0.572 occurring in Stage 3 alone. In contrast, knowledge distillation from a frozen teacher is associated with FM = -0.033 +/- 0.004 across three seeds, corresponding to 95% retention. Because no Stage 2 no-KD control is included, this result establishes retention under KD training rather than a causal KD effect. Per-stratum analysis shows large-target detection collapsing to near zero within the first epoch, despite an inter-stage cosine similarity of 0.987 over the gradient-updated weights, pointing to scale-conditioned gradient imbalance, rather than weight drift, as a candidate mechanism. Scale-Stratified Herding (SSH), a 300-exemplar buffer balanced across four UAV size strata, roughly halves the forgetting (FM = -0.605 to -0.311) and keeps large-target detection non-zero. An ablation attributes the gain primarily to scale stratification rather than herding: random-stratified replay performs at least as well (FM = -0.221 versus -0.311 for SSH). These replay results are single-seed and should therefore be treated as preliminary.
