Introduction sec:introduction The proliferation of commercial drones has created urgent demand for counter-unmanned-aerial-vehicle (C-UAV) surveillance systems capable of reliable detection across diverse operational environments~ zhao_vision-based_2022 . Thermal infrared (TIR) imaging is increasingly favoured over visible-spectrum cameras for this role: it operates independently of ambient lighting, remains effective against low-visibility backgrounds, and provides a distinct radiometric signature for airborne targets~ bohuang_410,zhu_evidential_2023 . Deep learning detectors, particularly YOLO-family architectures~ jocher2020yolov5 , perform strongly on individual TIR anti-UAV benchmarks~ guo_yolomg_2025 . But practical C-UAV systems must stay accurate as new datasets emerge, sensors are upgraded, and the threat profile shifts toward smaller, harder-to-detect targets. The core technical challenge this creates is catastrophic forgetting~ mccloskey1989catastrophic,goodfellow2013empirical : when a neural network is sequentially fine-tuned on a new dataset, the weight updates that improve performance on the new task interfere with representations learned for previous ones, causing abrupt performance degradation on earlier tasks~ mermillod2013stability,Kirkpatrick_2017 . The field of continual learning (CL) exists to manage this stability-plasticity trade-off~ wang2024comprehensive . Rehearsal methods store a subset of past training data and interleave it during subsequent training~ rebuffi2017icarl,chaudhry2019tiny,deng_unlocking_2025 ; regularisation methods penalise changes to important parameters~ Kirkpatrick_2017,lopezpaz2022gradientepisodicmemorycontinual ; gradient projection methods constrain new-task gradient updates to subspaces orthogonal to previous tasks' gradients~ farajtabar2019ogd,saha2021gpm ; and knowledge distillation (KD) methods use a frozen teacher model to constrain the updated model's output distribution~ hinton2015distilling,li2017lwf . Shmelkov et al.~ shmelkov2017iod introduced distillation-based CL for general object detection, showing that distillation can reduce forgetting when new classes are added. To our knowledge, these approaches have not been systematically evaluated in the thermal anti-UAV domain, where distributional shifts may include sensor, scene, weather, and target-scale changes. Existing thermal anti-UAV benchmarks capture complementary facets of this problem in isolation. Anti-UAV-RGBT~ jiang_anti-uav_2023 provides 318 paired RGB-TIR video streams of standard-scale drones; Anti-UAV410~ bohuang_410 contains 410 purely thermal sequences spanning a wide range of drone sizes; and CST Anti-UAV~ xie2025cstantiuavthermalinfrared focuses on extreme tiny targets in cluttered thermal scenes, with 87.9 tiny and 11.9 small bounding boxes and effectively no large targets. We are not aware of prior work that has chained these datasets into a single model's training history and measured the resulting stability-plasticity trade-off. Prior continual learning work has also not examined gradient starvation~ pezeshki2021gradient , a phenomenon in which dominant features suppress gradient signals for weaker but relevant ones, as a driver of forgetting after distributional shift. This is the research gap this work addresses. We investigate the following hypothesis and three research questions using YOLOMG~ guo_yolomg_2025 , a dual-modal YOLOv5-based detector (run here with its motion channel disabled), trained sequentially on Anti-UAV-RGBT (Stage 1), Anti-UAV410 (Stage 2), and CST Anti-UAV (Stage 3). All three datasets are thermal infrared, so the input modality is held constant across the curriculum; the shifts under study are the moderate cross-dataset domain shift of Stage 2 and the extreme scale-distribution shift of Stage 3. H1: Under the training protocol used here, the Stage~3 transition to the extreme tiny-target CST Anti-UAV distribution produces substantially greater Task~1 forgetting than the Stage~2 transition. Because Stage~2 uses KD while the Stage~3 baseline uses naive fine-tuning, this comparison is descriptive rather than a causal isolation of distribution-shift type. RQ1: Does knowledge distillation preserve Task 1 performance during Task 2 training under domain shift? Specifically, does the KD loss term in Stage 2 (Anti-UAV410) training prevent the model from forgetting its Anti-UAV-RGBT detection capability, despite the thermal cross-dataset domain shift between the two benchmarks? RQ2: How does scale shift characterise the pattern of catastrophic forgetting during Task 3 training? Specifically, does the extreme size distribution of CST Anti-UAV (87.9 tiny, 11.9 small, 0 large) produce stratum-specific forgetting in which large-target detection collapses disproportionately fast, and how is this reflected in per-stratum mean Average Precision (mAP), the Forgetting Measure, parameter drift, and the gradient signal reaching each detection head? RQ3: Does re-injecting scale-stratified exemplars via replay mitigate the Stage 3 forgetting? A 300-exemplar buffer that selects exemplars across four UAV size strata (tiny, small, normal, large) by iCaRL-style greedy herding restores the gradient signal for the under-represented strata during Stage 3, and is compared against naive fine-tuning and a random-stratified control that isolates the effect of the stratification. In brief, sequential training produces substantial and measurable forgetting. Stage~2 training with knowledge distillation retains most Task~1 performance, although the absence of a no-KD Stage~2 control prevents attributing that retention causally to distillation. The Stage 3 results point to a scale-induced forgetting pattern whose evidence is, tentatively, more consistent with a scale-conditioned gradient imbalance than with outright weight overwriting. Scale-Stratified Herding (SSH) roughly halves this forgetting, which suggests that scale-stratified replay can offset the imbalance. The remainder of this work is organised as follows. Section~ sec:related_work surveys related work on continual learning, thermal UAV detection, and knowledge distillation. Section~ sec:methodology describes the experimental design, datasets, and methods. Section~ sec:results presents the empirical results. Section~ sec:discussion interprets the findings and discusses limitations. Section~ sec:conclusion concludes with implications and future directions. Related Work sec:related_work To our knowledge, prior work has not combined a continual-learning protocol with thermal anti-UAV detection across multiple real operational datasets or examined scale-conditioned gradient imbalance, a form of gradient starvation, as a candidate driver of forgetting under scale-distribution shift. This section situates the research within four bodies of literature that together delimit this gap. Thermal Anti-UAV Detection Counter-UAV surveillance using thermal infrared imaging has received growing attention due to the sensor's independence from ambient lighting and its distinct radiometric signature for airborne targets. Zhao et al.~ zhao_vision-based_2022 provide a broad survey of vision-based anti-UAV detection and tracking, identifying the shift from visible to thermal modalities as a key trend driven by operational requirements at night and in degraded visibility. Jiang et al.~ jiang_anti-uav_2023 introduced Anti-UAV-RGBT, a paired RGB-TIR benchmark of 318 video sequences that remains the most widely used dual-modality anti-UAV evaluation resource. Huang et al.~ bohuang_410 extended this with Anti-UAV410, a purely thermal benchmark of 410 sequences spanning a wider range of acquisition conditions and drone distances. Both datasets focus on standard-scale commercial quadcopters; the more recent CST Anti-UAV~ xie2025cstantiuavthermalinfrared shifts attention to extreme tiny targets in cluttered thermal scenes, creating the near-complete scale inversion relative to Anti-UAV-RGBT that motivates the forgetting analysis in this research. Detection in such conditions shares challenges with the broader infrared small target detection (IRSTD) literature, where methods such as DNA-Net~ li2021dnanet use dense nested attention to preserve sub-16-pixel target features that deep pooling layers would otherwise discard. On the detector side, YOLO-family architectures~ jocher2020yolov5 have become a common choice for real-time anti-UAV detection because of their favourable speed--accuracy balance. Guo et al.~ guo_yolomg_2025 extended YOLOv5 with a pixel-level motion-difference channel (YOLOMG), fusing appearance and motion at three feature-pyramid scales (P3, P4, P5)~ lin2017fpn . Recent anti-UAV work has also examined complementary reliability failures. Suttorp et al.~ suttorp2026uncertainty studied uncertainty-aware RGB--thermal fusion under modality disagreement, while Golovchits et al.~ golovchits2026evidential evaluated evidential learning and sensor-gating across thermal and multimodal anti-UAV settings. Birkental et al.~ birkental2026fog quantified detector degradation under controlled fog severity and showed that robustness can change sharply as visibility deteriorates. Together, these studies reinforce that operational anti-UAV reliability depends on distributional conditions beyond aggregate benchmark accuracy, but they do not study catastrophic forgetting under sequential cross-dataset adaptation. Zhu et al.~ zhu_evidential_2023 likewise investigated evidential detection and tracking, while domain adaptation from RGB to thermal and across weather conditions has been explored by Zhang et al.~ zhang_ttsda-yolo_2025 and Zheng et al.~ zheng_foggy_2025 . These works address uncertainty or single-step robustness/adaptation rather than retention of earlier datasets after subsequent training. Continual Learning The instability of neural networks under sequential training has been studied since McCloskey and Cohen~ mccloskey1989catastrophic documented catastrophic interference in connectionist models. title: MIM-VLA: Learning Physical Interaction Representations from Gripper Motor Feedback
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures. Jaeyoung Lee and Jiyeon Koo contributed equally
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies infer grasp actions primarily from visual observations and robot state, but do not explicitly represent the physical response observed after contact. We present MIM-VLA, a motor-feedback-based architecture that encodes recent gripper current, position, velocity, and signal validity as a 128-dimensional interaction token. A motor-only Motor Interaction Module (MIM) is pretrained with human-reviewed contact and interaction-phase labels and then conditions only the gripper-action pathway of SmolVLA; arm actions and the position-control interface remain unchanged. The same token supports the MEM selector VLM that compares candidate interactions and produces evidence-conditioned selections and explanations. We evaluate MIM-VLA in three real-world settings: comparing the interaction resistance of visually different objects, disambiguating visually similar real and replica objects through active probing, and gently grasping fragile objects, including held-out instances. Across 13 object pairs, MIM-VLA selects the higher-resistance object in 75.0% of trials, compared with 48.8% for the SmolVLA baseline. For the evaluated tasks, the approach uses motor feedback already available from the gripper and does not require an additional tactile array, force-torque sensor, calibrated force estimate, or direct current control.

We present MIM-VLA, a motor-feedback-based architecture that encodes recent gripper current, position, velocity, and signal validity as a 128-dimensional interaction token . A motor-only Motor Interaction Module (MIM) is pretrained with human-reviewed contact and interaction-phase labels and then conditions only the gripper-action pathway of SmolVLA; arm actions and the position-control interface remain unchanged. The same token supports the MEM selector VLM that compares candidate interactions and produces evidence-conditioned selections and explanations. We evaluate MIM-VLA in three real-world settings: comparing the interaction resistance of visually different objects, disambiguating visually similar real and replica objects through active probing, and gently grasping fragile objects, including held-out instances. Across 13 object pairs, MIM-VLA selects the higher-resistance object in 75.0 of trials, compared with 48.8 for the SmolVLA baseline. For the evaluated tasks, the approach uses motor feedback already available from the gripper and does not require an additional tactile array, force--torque sensor, calibrated force estimate, or direct current control. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect images and natural-language instructions to robot actions openvla,smolvla . Their visual-language priors support object recognition and task planning, yet appearance does not fully specify how an object will respond after contact. Visually similar objects may have different compliance, while fragile objects of different sizes cannot be safely grasped by replaying one closing position. Joint position alone also cannot distinguish free closing, contact, stable holding, and continued compression. Force- and tactile-aware policies address this limitation using dedicated sensors or force-aware control forcevla,tactilevla,biact . We instead ask whether actuator telemetry already exposed by a smart gripper can provide useful physical grounding. Motor current is not calibrated force and depends on motion and actuator dynamics; consequently, we model its temporal relation with measured position, velocity, and signal validity rather than applying an instantaneous current threshold. MIM-VLA, shown in Fig.~ fig:mim_vla_architecture , uses a GRU-based Motor Interaction Module (MIM) to encode recent gripper history as an interaction token . MIM is pretrained with binary contact and five interaction-phase labels--- , , , , and . Video supports label generation but is excluded from the motor-only encoder (Fig.~ fig:mim_pretraining ). During policy learning, a lightweight projector injects the token only into a dedicated gripper pathway. The SmolVLM backbone and arm pathway are preserved, and the final outputs remain position commands rather than current or force commands. For these interaction states, position and velocity describe aperture and closure progression, while current supplies the corresponding motor-load response. MIM remains motor-only to avoid appearance shortcuts; vision stays in the SmolVLM pathway and is not claimed to be replaced by telemetry. The same representation supports interaction-level reasoning through the Material Explain Module (MEM). Candidate-specific token histories are summarized for a selector VLM, which compares measured interaction responses, selects a candidate, and renders a short explanation; low-level execution remains with the action policy. MEM demonstrates reuse of the same physical token beyond low-level control. We evaluate three capabilities: (i) comparing relative interaction resistance across visually different objects, (ii) probing visually similar real and replica objects to identify the more resistant candidate, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:material_selection , and (iii) minimally compressive grasping of seen and held-out fragile objects. Comparisons include vanilla SmolVLA, raw-motor conditioning, and a TA-VLA-inspired temporal-current baseline under the same position-action interface. Our contributions are: a motor-only interaction representation pretrained from temporal gripper telemetry and contact/phase supervision, without calibrated force sensing; a gripper-specific integration that preserves the pretrained visual-language backbone, arm pathway, and position-control interface; and a shared token interface for closed-loop gripper adaptation and higher-level evidence-conditioned comparison and explanation through MEM, evaluated in three complementary real-world settings. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-language-action models translate pretrained visual-language representations into robot actions. OpenVLA presents an open-source generalist policy pretrained on diverse robot demonstrations and supports efficient adaptation to new settings openvla .~More recent VLAs employ continuous generative action models: adopts flow matching for general robot control pi0 , while GR00T N1 couples a vision-language module with a diffusion-transformer action module for generalist humanoid manipulation grootn1 . FLARE augments generative policy learning with future latent representation alignment, encouraging the policy to model consequences in a control-relevant feature space flare . SmolVLA combines a compact flow-matching architecture with asynchronous inference for efficient deployment on affordable hardware smolvla . These methods learn rich representations for action prediction, but they do not explicitly preserve object-associated evidence acquired through prior physical probing. Building on SmolVLA, our approach summarizes gripper motor-response histories as interaction tokens that can be associated with explored objects and used to condition subsequent gripper control. Physical Interaction for Robot Manipulation Recent work incorporates physical feedback at different levels of the perception--action hierarchy. Among the approaches most closely related to ours, ForceVLA fuses real-time force--torque measurements with vision-language features through a force-aware mixture-of-experts during action decoding forcevla . TA-VLA studies torque-aware adapters, temporal torque history, and auxiliary torque prediction for integrating physical feedback into existing VLA architectures tavla . ForceVLA2 introduces force prompts for task-level reasoning and combines them with hybrid force--position control forcevla2 . Tactile approaches align touch with vision and language for contact-rich insertion, as in VTLA vtla , or use tactile feedback at both the planning and action-refinement levels, as in VLA-Touch vlatouch . Bi-ACT instead learns position, velocity, and force behavior from demonstrations collected with bilateral control biact . These approaches primarily use explicit force or tactile signals to improve ongoing planning and control, or require a force-aware demonstration and execution interface. In contrast, MIM operates on the temporal current, position, and velocity signals already exposed by the gripper. Wrist video is used only to generate and review auxiliary pretraining labels; it is not an input to the motor-only MIM. We do not interpret current as calibrated force. Instead, MIM encodes the joint evolution of motor load and finger motion into an interaction token, allowing the original position-action interface to be retained. Interaction Grounding with Vision-Language Models Vision-language models connect visual observations with linguistic descriptions. Qwen2.5-VL supports spatial object localization and temporal event localization in long videos qwen25vl , while SmolVLM provides a compact architecture for image and video understanding smolvlm . Visual evidence alone, however, may not reveal the physical response produced during grasping. PaLM-E demonstrates that continuous robot-state estimates can be interleaved with vision and language to support embodied reasoning palme . Other work uses VLMs to reason over candidate robot behavior: RoboMonkey samples actions from a VLA and applies a VLM-based verifier to select among them robomonkey , whereas Uncertainty-Aware Policy Steering chooses whether to execute, request clarification, or obtain a corrective intervention according to calibrated semantic and action uncertainty ups . These systems do not retain candidate-specific motor evidence from the robot's preceding contact with an object for later comparison. Our Material Explain Module (MEM) summarizes the MIM interaction histories of two probed candidates and provides them to a selector VLM together with the task instruction. The VLM predicts the selected candidate and relative position/current responses, and generates a short explanation conditioned on the same summaries, while the action policy remains responsible for low-level position commands. We evaluate candidate selection in real-robot trials and analyze the effect of interaction- summary capacity using structured response prediction, explanation consistency, and candidate-swap consistency. Method sec:method Overview sec:method_overview MIM-VLA separates physical-interaction representation from task-level vision and action generation. First, the Motor Interaction Module (MIM) encodes a causal window of measured gripper telemetry as . Second, the Material Explain Module (MEM) summarizes candidate-specific token histories for a selector VLM that compares prior interactions and produces a structured choice and explanation. Third, the current interaction token conditions a gripper-specific SmolVLA pathway smolvla while the original visual-language and arm pathways are preserved. Training follows the same separation. MIM is pretrained with contact and phase supervision. The interaction-memory summarizer and selector are then trained with MIM fixed. For downstream robot control, MIM is initialized from the pretrained encoder and jointly fine-tuned with the action pathways, while its auxiliary classification heads remain frozen. Motor Interaction Module sec:mim MIM processes measured gripper position, velocity, and current together with motion, torque-enable, validity, and timing signals. Commanded and target positions, current limits, and saturation indicators are excluded from the encoder input. Sensor and reception timestamps are used to construct causal history windows containing only measurements available at the corresponding observation time. The motor-only input is deliberate. Measured position gives the gripper aperture and cumulative closure, velocity indicates motion direction and whether closing slows or stops, and current describes the simultaneous motor load. Their joint temporal evolution provides the information needed for the contact and phase distinctions supervised in this work. Excluding wrist video also prevents the MIM token from learning an appearance shortcut. This does not imply that telemetry replaces vision for general manipulation: camera observations remain inputs to SmolVLM, whereas MIM is restricted to encoding the physical response during gripper--object interaction. Formally, for an observation issued at time , MIM receives the causal sequence where each concatenates normalized measured position, velocity, and current, their first-order differences, motor-status bits, validity masks, and timing information. Samples whose acquisition or reception time exceeds are excluded even when they occur in the same logged image interval. When a signal or temporal difference is unavailable, its validity entry is cleared so that zero-filled normalized values cannot be mistaken for a physical zero. This construction is important for deployment, where sensor packets arrive asynchronously and the policy must never depend on future telemetry. title: ActTune: Action-Aware Precision and GPU Operating-Point Adaptation for Energy-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke inference to control robots, making graphics processing unit (GPU) energy a recurring cost of task execution. Reducing energy per inference call, however, may not reduce energy per successful task if numerical errors increase failures or slower inference prolongs execution. We therefore target GPU energy per successful task while preserving task success and keeping the inference-latency increase within 10\%. Our approach builds on two observations: quantization sensitivity varies across action classes, model layers, and weights versus activations; and numerical precision changes the workload, shifting favorable GPU operating points. We introduce ActTune, an action-aware framework that connects layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection over requested frequency--power-cap pairs. A lightweight decision tree learns its splits and leaf precision configurations directly from configuration action errors, then selects precision before each policy call. The controller forecasts the next workload and applies the selected GPU operating point asynchronously using a lookup table calibrated under a latency budget. A shared resident quantized weight bank enables configuration switching without weight reconstruction or additional policy evaluations. On LIBERO, a benchmark for lifelong robot learning, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3\% relative to state of the art. Relative to the original BF16 implementations, it delivers up to $2.02\times$ faster inference and, with GPU operating-point adaptation, reduces energy per successful task by up to 76.8\%.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction VLA models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions~ kim2024openvla . For battery-powered robots, repeated onboard inference consumes limited battery energy and can shorten operation between charges. Reducing inference energy is therefore important for extending robot endurance. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) offers a direct way to pursue this goal by lowering power consumption~ tang2019dvfs . However, lower frequencies prolong inference, which can offset energy savings and delay action updates. The need for timely responses therefore limits how aggressively frequency can be reduced. Numerical precision and GPU operating-point control offer complementary ways to reduce this cost. Quantization lowers weight and activation precision, changing computation and memory traffic, but the resulting numerical errors can also perturb predicted actions. We define a GPU operating point as a requested frequency--power-cap pair. Adjusting these settings trades execution speed against power consumption. Lower frequencies may reduce power, yet longer inference can offset these savings and delay the robot's response to new observations. Crucially, these two controls are coupled: precision determines the workload on which GPU operating-point control operates. An energy-efficient operating point for one precision configuration may therefore be less effective for another. Exploiting both controls requires connecting the precision needs of robot actions to the hardware characteristics of the resulting inference workload. Existing work provides useful foundations for this connection. VLA quantization methods use action or task sensitivity to allocate precision~ xu2026qvla,akbari2026actquant,ranjan2026mixqvla , while temporal-dynamic-aware quantization for VLA models (DyQ-VLA) and motion-aware vector quantization (MotionVQ) adapt precision during execution using motion signals~ zheng2026dyqvla,song2026vqvla . However, compression objectives such as model size and bit-operation budgets do not directly capture GPU energy during task execution~ ranjan2026mixqvla . Other work studies energy efficiency through quantized robotic policies or device--edge execution placement~ park2025sqil,zhou2026ecovla , and PiQi, a framework for partially quantized inference, combines partial quantization, processor placement, and DVFS for general deep neural network (DNN) inference~ aghapour2024piqi . Building on these directions, we investigate how action-aware precision allocation and workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection can work together to reduce energy per successful robot task. Our approach is motivated by two observations. First, quantization sensitivity depends on both the action being performed and where numerical error is introduced in the model. For example, coarse approach motion may tolerate small deviations, whereas final alignment may require greater accuracy (Figure~ fig:action_precision_intuition ). Using a fixed set of action classes learned from training actions, short quantized interventions reveal sensitivity differences across action classes, Transformer blocks, and weight versus activation precision (Figure~ fig:motivation_action_combined (b--c)). Second, hardware measurements show that different numerical precisions can favor different GPU operating points (Figure~ fig:hardware_energy_time_full_grid ). Together, these observations suggest a two-stage adaptation strategy: use action sensitivity to guide precision allocation, then use the resulting workload to guide GPU operating-point selection. We introduce ActTune, an action-aware framework that implements this strategy. Before each action chunk is generated, a lightweight decision tree uses current proprioception and the preceding predicted action chunk to select a layer-wise weight and activation precision configuration. Offline calibration learns the tree splits and leaf configurations directly from action error against the BF16 reference policy under precision and storage budgets. A shared resident quantized weight bank supports configuration switching without reconstructing weights or storing a complete model copy for every leaf. This design enables action-aware precision selection with only one policy inference call per action chunk. ActTune profiles frequency and power-cap settings on replayed training workloads with the precision selector fixed. It selects the candidate table with the lowest estimated energy while limiting the mean inference-latency increase to 10 relative to the same precision selector at the fixed reference GPU operating point, subject to action equality and memory checks. After each call, the controller forecasts the next workload and applies the selected GPU operating point asynchronously. Precision selection uses the current observation. Because matching actions on replayed inputs does not guarantee unchanged closed-loop behavior, the final assessment must consider complete episodes. We therefore evaluate closed-loop task success and energy per successful task, and check the 10 budget using the measured inference latency. Our contributions are: 0pt 0pt 1em 0.5em Empirical characterization. We firstly characterize how quantization sensitivity varies across action classes, Transformer blocks, and weight versus activation precision, and show that favorable GPU operating points depend on numerical precision. Action-aware precision and GPU operating-point adaptation. We propose ActTune, which connects action-conditioned layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection. A lightweight decision tree and a shared quantized weight bank enable online adaptation with one policy call per action chunk. Quantitative evaluation. In the evaluated LIBERO comparisons, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3 relative to QVLA, an action-centric VLA quantization framework, and action-guided quantization (ActQuant). It also reduces static model storage by up to 29.3 relative to the compared general-purpose quantization baselines at W4A8/W4A4 (Table~ tab:quantization_performance ). Compared with the original BF16 implementations, it achieves up to inference speedup and up to 76.8 lower energy per successful task with GPU operating-point adaptation.

title: WareFly-VLA: A Vision-Language-Action Framework for UAV Navigation and Human Tracking in Smart Warehouses
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved impressive results in robotic manipulation and ground-mobile navigation, yet language-conditioned control of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart warehouses remains largely unexplored, hindered by the lack of benchmarks that jointly provide continuous low-level flight actions, fine-grained natural-language target descriptions, and realistic industrial environments. This paper introduces WareFly-VLA, a photorealistic UAV VLA framework and dataset for language-guided human search, localization, and tracking in warehouse environments. It contains 507 human-teleoperated flight episodes and 8,504 high-resolution RGB transitions collected in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each paired with a human-written appearance description of the target worker and a synchronized four-degree-of-freedom control command. Two aerial tasks are covered: target approach and person following, under occlusion, long-range search, altitude variation, and clutter. A unified benchmark of four open-source VLA architectures (SmolVLA, GR00T N1.7, pi_0 and OpenVLA) is established under a leakage-free episode-level protocol at two control rates. The results show that language-conditioned aerial control in warehouses is far from solved: performance drops substantially under strict generalization settings, continuous action modeling consistently outperforms discrete action tokenization, only the forward channel is reliably learnable from a single frame, and current foundation-model interfaces transfer poorly from ground and humanoid embodiments to aerial platforms. The synchronized video, language, action, pose, and difficulty annotations further support world-model research. The dataset, baselines, and evaluation protocol are released to support language-grounded aerial autonomy in smart warehouses.

Vision-language-action models Unmanned aerial vehicles Person following Warehouse robotics Language-conditioned control Imitation learning Dataset and benchmark Introduction A long-standing objective of embodied artificial intelligence is to enable robots to interpret natural-language instructions, ground them in visual observations and execute appropriate low-level actions in dynamic environments. Recent Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models such as PaLM-E driess2023palme , RT-1 brohan2022rt1 , RT-2 brohan2023rt2 , Octo octo2024 , OpenVLA kim2024openvla , RDT-1B liu2024rdt , black2025pi05 , SmolVLA shukor2025smolvla , TinyVLA wen2024tinyvla and Qwen-VLA qwenvla have demonstrated that large-scale multimodal training can produce policies that generalize across tasks, environments and robot embodiments. These advances suggest that a unified perception--language--control paradigm may provide a scalable foundation for future autonomous systems. Despite rapid progress, contemporary VLA research remains heavily concentrated on robotic manipulation and ground-mobile platforms. Large-scale datasets and benchmarks predominantly focus on tabletop manipulation, mobile navigation or humanoid interaction, whereas aerial robots remain significantly underrepresented, even though vision-based control of multi-rotor aerial vehicles is a mature and active research area nascimento2026review . This gap is particularly notable because unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) present a distinct embodiment with substantially different sensing, motion and control characteristics. Being different from manipulators that operate within constrained workspaces or ground robots that navigate primarily in two dimensions, UAVs perform continuous motion in three-dimensional space while simultaneously regulating position, altitude and heading. Visual observations are highly dynamic due to rapid viewpoint changes, target scale variation and frequent occlusions. Consequently, transferring VLA paradigms developed for ground or manipulation settings to aerial systems is far from straightforward. Among the many tasks relevant to aerial autonomy, language-guided human search and following represents a particularly compelling benchmark for embodied intelligence. Consider the instruction: ``Track the worker wearing a yellow hard hat and a purple safety vest.'' Successfully executing this command requires the integration of multiple capabilities. The UAV must first interpret fine-grained appearance descriptions, identify the correct individual among visually similar distractors, actively search when the target is not immediately visible, maintain target association over time and continuously generate flight-control commands that ensure safe and reliable tracking. In contrast to conventional UAV tracking benchmarks, where the target is initialized through a bounding box or visual template, language-guided following requires semantic target specification and persistent multimodal grounding throughout the entire trajectory. This setting naturally combines visual grounding, embodied language understanding, active perception and continuous control within a single task. Existing datasets do not adequately support this problem formulation. Classical approaches such as Chen et al. chen2018objTracking , aerial tracking benchmarks such as UAV123 mueller2016uav , and subsequent UAV tracking datasets zhao2022antiUAV provide extensive flight recordings but rely exclusively on visual target initialization without language supervision. Vision-language navigation datasets such as AerialVLN liu2023aerialvln , AirNav deshpande2026airnav , EmbodiedCity zhang2024embodiedcity , UAV-VLN wang2024uav and GeoText-1652 mei2024geotext introduced natural-language instructions but formulated navigation primarily as waypoint prediction or route planning rather than continuous low-level control. In a similar vein, large-scale drone footage datasets exist and are used to extract ground vehicle trajectories for driving research wang2025dadd ; however, the lack of ergo-centric controls makes them unsuitable for aerial embodied AI. Recent UAV-oriented VLA datasets and benchmarks remain limited in scope. CognitiveDrone cogdrone2025 focused on simulation-based trajectory generation. UAV-VLA sautenkov2025uavvla targets mission-level reasoning from aerial imagery and RaceVLA serpiva2025racevla addressed drone-racing policies. Although these resources have advanced aerial embodied learning, none simultaneously provide appearance-grounded language descriptions, continuous flight-control supervision, human-demonstrated trajectories and warehouse-scale person-search-and-follow tasks. To address this limitation, this paper introduces WareFly-VLA, a Vision--Language--Action dataset for language-guided human search and following in industrial warehouse environments. The dataset is collected from human-teleoperated UAV demonstrations performed in a photorealistic warehouse environment constructed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Each trajectory contains synchronized high-resolution RGB observations, fine-grained appearance-based language descriptions and continuous 4-DoF flight actions represented as body-frame motion commands. In contrast to scripted navigation policies or automatically generated expert trajectories, the dataset captures realistic human decision-making behaviors during target search, target acquisition and continuous following. The resulting trajectories naturally include recovery maneuvers, viewpoint adaptation, target re-identification and other behaviors that commonly arise during practical aerial operation. WareFly-VLA is designed around two complementary embodied tasks: approach-and-locate and person-following. The dataset further incorporates diverse warehouse layouts, worker appearances, target distances, altitude changes, partial occlusions and cluttered industrial environments. Structured difficulty annotations enable systematic evaluation across multiple challenge dimensions and support future research on generalization, robustness and language grounding under realistic operating conditions. Beyond dataset construction, a unified benchmark is established to evaluate representative open-source VLA architectures using a common leakage-free episode-level split. The benchmark spans multiple model families and action-representation paradigms, providing a standardized framework for studying aerial embodied intelligence. Experimental results indicate that language-conditioned UAV control remains a challenging open problem, highlighting substantial opportunities for future advances in multimodal representation learning, continuous action prediction and cross-embodiment transfer. The main contributions of this work are as follows: WareFly-VLA, a human-teleoperated UAV Vision--Language--Action dataset for language-guided human search and following in warehouse environments, containing synchronized visual observations, appearance-grounded language descriptions and continuous 4-DoF flight actions. A human-demonstration data collection pipeline built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim that captures realistic aerial search, target localization, target acquisition and continuously following behaviors from teleoperated quadrotor trajectories. Aerial embodied benchmark tasks covering approach-and-locate and person-following scenarios under realistic challenges, including occlusion, altitude variation, long-range search, viewpoint changes and cluttered industrial environments. A unified aerial VLA benchmark for evaluating representative open-source VLA architectures under a standardized leakage-free evaluation protocol. An open-source research platform including dataset artifacts, benchmark configurations, training pipelines and evaluation tools to facilitate future research on aerial embodied intelligence, language-grounded UAV autonomy and Vision--Language--Action learning. Open world-model research directions enabled by WareFly-VLA, including predictive representation learning, action-conditioned latent dynamics, language-conditioned planning and sim-to-real transfer for aerial embodied intelligence. Related Work sec:related Vision--Language--Action models VLA models have emerged as a unified paradigm for embodied intelligence by jointly learning perception, language understanding and control. Early efforts such as PaLM-E driess2023palme demonstrated the feasibility of integrating visual observations into large language models for robotic decision making. Subsequent systems including RT-1 brohan2022rt1 , RT-2 brohan2023rt2 , Open X-Embodiment padalkar2023rtx , Octo octo2024 , OpenVLA kim2024openvla , RDT-1B liu2024rdt , black2025pi05 , SmolVLA shukor2025smolvla , TinyVLA wen2024tinyvla and Qwen-VLA qwenvla have demonstrated increasingly strong generalization across tasks, environments and robotic embodiments. Recent research has further explored large-scale pretraining and cross-embodiment transfer. Open X-Embodiment padalkar2023rtx aggregated demonstrations from multiple robot platforms to investigate shared policy learning, while OpenVLA kim2024openvla , RDT-1B liu2024rdt and black2024pi0 explored foundation-model approaches capable of adapting to diverse downstream tasks. Inference-time policy steering has further been proposed to deploy pre-trained VLAs on new tasks without fine-tuning li2026vlapilot . title: RIWANav: Recursive World-Action Models with Self-Improvement for Urban Navigation
summary: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.

Introduction Long-horizon urban navigation requires an agent to reach a language-specified destination from street-level observations and recent motion history. At each step, the agent must translate the global goal into a local decision, recover from mistakes, and determine when to stop. Existing methods commonly learn this behavior by imitating expert trajectories~ liu2025citywalker,mei2026urbannav . Although imitation learning (IL) provides strong initialization, it mainly supervises successful expert actions and cannot learn from policy-induced failures, as shown in Fig.~ fig:intro (a). This limitation is particularly consequential in urban navigation, where one inaccurate local motion changes the next observation and can compound over subsequent decisions~ zhu2026wmpo . Reinforcement learning (RL) can learn from such failures, but collecting long-horizon trial-and-error interaction is costly. Navigation post-training therefore needs outcome feedback without requiring every candidate action to be physically executed. Action-conditioned world models serve as learned simulators for policy improvement. Navigation world models (NWM)~ bar2025nwm and recent world action models~ zhu2026wmpo,ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fastwam predict future observations conditioned on candidate actions. Their imagined outcomes allow a policy to compare local decisions before execution. However, a world model used for policy optimization should not remain frozen, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro (b). As the policy improves, the frozen world model does not adapt to the evolving distribution of urban navigation behaviors. Inaccurate predictions can then distort subsequent policy updates, making the frozen model a bottleneck of model-based post-training. We therefore seek a training framework that adapts the world model alongside the policy. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates a training process in which each improvement stage changes the conditions for the next~ schmidhuber2007godel . We bring this principle to navigation post-training by coupling policy optimization with world-model adaptation. The improved policy determines which demonstrations the world model should learn next, while the refined world model provides updated feedback for subsequent policy learning. Self-improvement therefore emerges from a recursive training loop between the policy and world model. We introduce (Recursive Self-Improvement of World--Action Models for Navigation), a post-training framework that recursively improves a world model and an action model (policy). Each cycle alternates two coupled updates, as shown in Fig.~ fig:intro (c). First, the action-conditioned world model predicts visual outcomes for multiple policy actions. Their relative quality provides imagined feedback for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~ shao2024deepseekmath . Second, the improved policy constructs candidate action--video pairs for adapting the world model to the policy's evolving behavior distribution. To maintain valid supervision from the offline dataset, we retain candidates that remain locally consistent with recorded expert motion. A grounded self-curriculum then prioritizes these samples according to behavioral novelty and current prediction error. The refined world model supplies the imagined feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive training loop. Our contributions are concluded as follows: We introduce , a post-training framework that recursively improves a navigation policy and a visual world model. We develop a self-curriculum that filters policy proposals by expert consistency and prioritizes accepted action--video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across seen and unseen environments, with real-world deployment further validating practical effectiveness. Related Work Real-World Navigation Real-world navigation policies are learned from diverse robot trajectories and goal-conditioned supervision~ shah2022recon,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad . CityWalker~ liu2025citywalker scales urban navigation learning with large collections of walking and driving videos. ~ mei2026urbannav aligns city-scale human trajectories with landmark-grounded language. OmniVLA~ hirose2026omnivla learns a shared navigation policy across image, language, and mixed goal modalities. Other works explore generative guidance: NoMaD~ sridhar2024nomad uses a goal-masked diffusion policy, whereas VENTURA~ zhang2025ventura generates instruction-conditioned visual paths for downstream control. These methods primarily improve navigation through data, supervision, and policy design. Our work instead focuses on post-training. World Models for Policy Learning World models support planning and policy learning through learned future dynamics~ chua2018pets,janner2019mbpo . PlaNet~ hafner2019planet and Dreamer~ hafner2020dreamer established latent imagination for policy learning, with later works scaling to broader domains~ hafner2023dreamerv3,hansen2024tdmpc2 and high-dimensional visual observations~ micheli2023iris,hansen2023modem . Recent world models extend to navigation and embodied control~ zhou2025dinowm,yao2025navmorph , while increasingly connect visual prediction with policy optimization~ zhu2026wmpo,yang2026rise . NWM~ bar2025nwm ranks navigation trajectories using controllable video prediction, whereas Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam jointly models video and actions to improve policy learning without explicit future generation. Rather than treating the world model as a fixed source of imagined feedback, we study how the world model and policy can continually adapt to one another as policy behavior evolves. Recursive Self-Improvement Recursive self-improvement traditionally studies systems that improve their own problem-solving process~ schmidhuber2007godel . POET~ wang2019poet co-evolves environment--agent pairs, generates new challenges, and transfers solutions across environments. Model-based policy learning faces a related problem at the level of learned dynamics. Uncertainty-aware prediction and short rollouts reduce exploitation of model errors~ chua2018pets,janner2019mbpo , while conservative objectives penalize uncertain transitions~ yu2020mopo,kidambi2020morel . PDML~ wang2023pdml adapts model learning toward the current policy distribution. Other approaches prioritize experience through learning progress, novelty, or curiosity~ kim2020activewm,sekar2020plan2explore,kauvar2023curiousreplay . In this paper, we connect these directions: the world model improves the policy through imagined feedback, and the evolving policy guides the next world-model update. This closed loop enables the two components to improve one another recursively. As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , each cycle alternates between policy optimization and world-model adaptation. First, the current world model predicts the visual outcomes of candidate actions, providing a basis for comparing actions and improving the policy. Second, the improved policy generates candidate actions, and those consistent with expert motion are paired with recorded future frames to build the policy-induced replay pool. The grounded self-curriculum prioritizes these pairs by behavioral novelty and current prediction error for world-model adaptation. The refined world model then supplies imagined feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. title: Fast Non-Parametric Heteroscedastic Imitation Learning With Geometric Priors
summary: When learning probabilistic policies from human demonstrations, data-efficient learning and fast adaptations to new scenarios are key requirements. One popular way to achieve intuitive and reliable adaptations is through non-parametric, typically kernel-based, methods. However, existing solutions either fail to account for the geometry of manifolds common in robotics, limiting data efficiency, or, when geometry-aware, provide unreliable uncertainty estimates or require retraining to adapt. We propose a non-parametric approach leveraging geometric priors in scenarios of data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainties for probabilistic modeling. We utilize the method to formulate policies based on time or robot state, where non-separable diagonal kernels allow capturing uncertainty relations between degrees of freedom for same-sized in- and outputs. Fast updates, requiring less than 3 ms for a trajectory involving both position and orientation are possible through an optimized formulation. Our approach supports both manifold-valued input and manifold-valued output with large orientation changes. Using task parameterization, adaptation to different object poses is easily possible. We evaluate the approach on a set of toy examples and on real robot manipulation tasks both in autonomous execution and in shared control scenarios.

Human-Robot Interaction, Imitation Learning, Uncertainty Quantification, Task and Motion Planning Introduction Probabilistic representations of movement primitives are key in applications with requirements in robustness and safety guarantees, as for example in space robotics~ muehlbauer2025control , underwater robotics~ schmidt2025conceptual or healthcare assistance~ quere2024probabilistic . Parametric approaches such as ~ zeestraten2017manifold,calinon2020gaussians provide an aleatoric (inherent to the data) uncertainty estimate while non-parametric approaches like ~ williams2006gaussian provide epistemic (lack of data) uncertainty huellermeier2021aleatoric . ~ huang2019kernelized and their extensions~ huang2021toward,silverio2023nonparametric have shown remarkable qualities regarding modeling capability and adaptability, while in parallel providing both uncertainty estimates. Both uncertainty types are required in applications -- the epistemic uncertainty estimate can, e.g., be used to render the robot compliant when unsure about its actions knauer2025interactive while the aleatoric uncertainty helps to compute control gains encoding task variability muehlbauer2025unified . Heteroscedasticity allows our method to model different uncertainties for different phases of a task, which is a key requirement in policy arbitration muehlbauer2024probabilistic,muehlbauer2025unified . have already been applied to a range of learning problems, such as manufacturing tasks~ knauer2025interactive , in space applications~ muehlbauer2025control or to guide reinforcement learning~ padalkar2025towards . Currently, these approaches are however only designed for Euclidean~ huang2019kernelized,silverio2023nonparametric or ~ huang2021toward , linearizing curved manifolds at one point, thus inducing distortions~ jaquier2024unraveling and not allowing to incorporate prior geometric knowledge. In contrast, approaches for multiple tangent spaces as already developed for ~ zeestraten2017manifold induce much less distortion through the utilization of multiple linearization points. Additionally, each of the still suffers from issues resulting from using a single linearization point. Conversely, lopez2023non developed a kernel-based, on-manifold approach which, however, uses different distributions per manifold which are hard to join in product manifolds and computationally slow. This approach also only outputs aleatoric uncertainty, neglecting epistemic uncertainty which is fundamental in many imitation learning problems. title: NMPP: Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning for Agile UAV Flight in Cluttered Environments
summary: Flying a quadrotor through a cluttered environment requires not only planning a collision-free reference trajectory based on perceived obstacles, but the reference also needs to be dynamically feasible and within the actuation limits of the vehicle, so that the controller can track it precisely. Existing methods either optimize a smooth polynomial inside a convex corridor, which limits agility, or treat obstacles as soft costs traded against tracking performance. We propose a Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning (NMPP) that imposes perceived obstacles as hard geometric constraints and hands a full-state reference to an obstacle-blind SE(3) controller. Our planner achieves a 58-67 % lower position RMSE than a linear Model Predictive Control trajectory planner and a 41-70 % lower RMSE than a polynomial trajectory planner. It also completes all forest flights with up to 9.5 m/s speed without collisions, and achieves 86 % flight success rate under a more aggressive speed profile where a state-of-the-art planner has only 26 % success rate. The real-world deployment showed reliable execution flying up to 5.5 m/s in an unknown cluttered environment.

Supplementary Material Video: Introduction Multirotor are increasingly deployed in missions that require flight through cluttered and initially unknown environments, including search and rescue Doherty_2007_SAR and infrastructure inspections Burri_2012_plant_inspection . In such missions, the achievable flight speed determines how much of the environment can be covered within the vehicle's limited endurance, which motivates operating the platform close to its dynamic limits. Flying fast between obstacles requires a reference trajectory that is not only collision-free but also respects the 's dynamics and actuation limits. The obstacles are perceived by the onboard sensors only during the flight, so the trajectory has to be planned online. The trajectory is often generated with simplified vehicle dynamics, causing a mismatch between the planned and flown trajectory Teissing_2024_PMM_mintime . Moreover, collision avoidance and dynamic feasibility are commonly handled in separate stages, where a collision-free path is first found in a map and then converted into a trajectory for the controller. Thus, the path ignores the dynamics and the trajectory ignores the obstacles. This paper addresses the generation of such a trajectory in a single onboard optimization, which respects the dynamics and actuation limits while remaining collision-free with respect to the obstacles perceived by the onboard sensor. The planner relies only on onboard sensing and has to return a solution within a few milliseconds of each planning period. The result is continuously handed to an geometric controller lee2010geometric as a full-state reference, so that the controller can follow it without deviating into the obstacles it was planned around. Meeting these requirements in one optimization is difficult for three reasons. First, the free space around obstacles is nonconvex, so imposing the obstacles as hard constraints makes the problem nonconvex and prone to local minima and infeasibility. Second, the sensor returns a variable and unbounded number of obstacles, while the problem has to keep a fixed size for its computation time to stay predictable. Third, a solution that is feasible at the discrete prediction nodes can still intersect an obstacle between two of them. Existing work addresses these difficulties in two ways. Corridor-based polynomial optimization restricts the trajectory to a convex subset of the free space, which removes the nonconvexity and allows online computation wang2022geometrically, ren2025safety . However, the smooth polynomial representation keeps the vehicle from flying close to its dynamic limits. Placing the avoidance inside the control loop instead preserves the reaction to what is currently perceived liang2025pointcloud, harms2025safe, pochobradsky2026geometric , but the obstacles are then expressed as soft costs, so that the avoidance is traded against tracking rather than guaranteed. To this end, we propose , which uses as a trajectory planner that generates a full-state reference for a separate controller rather than actuator commands. Each optimization is initialized from the previously generated prediction rather than from the noisy state estimate, which allows imposing the obstacle constraint exactly. The accumulated point cloud is converted into ellipsoids, of which a fixed number enters the problem, keeping its size constant regardless of the scene. The hard constraint is complemented by a soft obstacle penalty and a softened acceleration-level condition xiao2022hocbf . The full obstacle set validates the trajectory between prediction nodes. To enforce actuation limits efficiently, the uses the thrust rate as its control input. The thrust and angular-acceleration limits thus become linear constraints. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first planner that imposes -perceived obstacles as hard constraints on the full quadrotor dynamics with thrust dynamics and runs onboard. In simulation, is compared with two trajectory planners, one based on linear baca2018model and one based on polynomial trajectories wang2021large . All three provide their reference to the same unmodified controller lee2010geometric , so the reference is the only component that differs. Across five constraint profiles with speed limits, achieves a 58-- lower position than the linear trajectory planner and a 41-- lower than the polynomial trajectory planner. The obstacle avoidance is evaluated in a Poisson forest against SUPER~ ren2025safety , with both planners flying in the same world towards the same goal. completed all flights without collision at speeds up to (super fast profile), whereas the success rate of SUPER dropped to under that profile. Under a more aggressive profile, the two planners reached the goal in and of fifty flights, respectively. Last but not least, we deployed the planner on a real quadrotor and validated it in a cluttered outdoor environment, as illustrated in . Related Work sec:sota Methods for autonomous navigation in cluttered environments range from reactive collision avoidance to global, optimization-based, and learning-based trajectory planning. Reactive methods compute avoidance commands directly from the current perception data. represent obstacles through repulsive potentials khatib1985realtime , while Velocity Obstacles identify control velocities that may lead to a future collision fiorini1998motion . Extensions such as ORCA support reciprocal collision avoidance between multiple agents vanDenBerg2011reciprocal . Reciprocal velocity constraints have also been integrated into for mutual collision avoidance in agile flight kratky2025rvc . These approaches are computationally efficient, but their local decisions can lead to local minima and usually rely on simplified vehicle dynamics. Global motion planners instead search for a collision-free path in a representation of the environment. Graph-search and sampling-based algorithms, such as A*, RRT, and RRT*, can find paths through complex obstacle configurations karaman2011sampling . The resulting path is commonly used to further plan a smooth trajectory that can be tracked by the . Minimum jerk/snap polynomial trajectories are widely used for this purpose because the differential flatness of a quadrotor allows smooth position trajectories to be mapped to reference attitude and thrust mellinger2011minimum, richter2016polynomial . Efficient polynomial representations further enable the generation of long trajectories with many segments wang2021large . Minimum-time formulations based on a point-mass model exploit the maneuverability of the more effectively than polynomial trajectories, at the cost of a reference that is only partially feasible for the real vehicle~ Teissing_2024_PMM_mintime . However, these methods generally require predefined waypoints or a collision-free corridor and do not themselves determine how to avoid newly perceived obstacles. Optimization-based planners incorporate smoothness, dynamic feasibility, and collision avoidance into a single trajectory-planning problem. Corridor-based methods such as GCOPTER~ wang2022geometrically efficiently optimize polynomial trajectories while enforcing smoothness-based formulations. Receding safe corridors can also be constructed incrementally along the flight, so that high-speed smooth trajectories are planned within them ren2022bubble . The corridor, however, restricts the trajectory to a convex subset of the free space, so the motion that can be produced is limited by how the corridor was carved rather than by the capability of the vehicle. provides an alternative in which the future vehicle motion is optimized over a receding horizon. It naturally supports state, input, and actuation constraints and has therefore been applied to trajectory tracking and collision avoidance baca2018model . An controller that integrates the dynamics of the low-level flight controller was shown to reduce the tracking error on agile references gupta2025lol . There, the optimization is placed at the controller level, where it produces the commands for the actuators, whereas the method proposed here places it at the planner level, where it produces a reference for a separate controller. The CIAO and CIAO* methods, presented in schoels2020nmpc, schoels2020ciao , respectively, formulate collision avoidance through convex inner approximations of free space, providing recursively feasible predictive motion planning in static and predictable dynamic environments. The principal difficulty is that a nonlinear geometric constraint has to be introduced for every obstacle that the optimization accounts for, so the size of the problem grows with the number of obstacles that are taken into account. When the environment is measured online, that number is neither known in advance nor bounded, which is what the following approaches, and have to address. Several planners therefore reduce or avoid dense volumetric mapping. NanoMap stores a local history of depth measurements and performs uncertainty-aware proximity queries without fusing all measurements into a global voxel-map~ florence2018nanomap . EGO-Planner removes the need for an by extracting obstacle information only when the optimized trajectory intersects an occupied region zhou2021egoplanner . SUPER generates polyhedral flight corridors directly from point clouds and optimizes an exploratory and a backup minimum-snap polynomial trajectory within them, to distinguish high-speed progress from motion guaranteed to remain in observed free space ren2025safety .
